Speaker 1 很多人觉得现在 AI 已经可以把数学做得这么好。如果我们现在要从小培养孩子，他们的时间应该花在数学上吗？还是应该把更多精力放在 AI 解决不了的问题上？

Ed H. Chi 我觉得这个问题有意思的地方在于，快十年前 Google 开发 AlphaGo 的时候，很多人在它跟棋王对决之后就说：“完了，人类以后不下棋了。”结果后来下棋的人反而更多了，想研究围棋的人也更多了。

我觉得数学也一样。很多人会觉得，既然现在能用这种方法解决 Navier–Stokes 方程，以后就没人想学数学了。我觉得可能恰恰相反，会有更多人觉得数学这么有趣，想要去研究它。过去可能有人是为了 exploration，也就是探索知识的边界；现在会有很多其他动机，比如 understanding、entertainment 或者乐趣。所以以后做数学研究的人，可能会更多是出于内心的 curiosity。

Speaker 1 有没有可能以前数学的门槛很高，但如果能通过 AI 把数学变成一种工具，很多文科生也可以利用它解决更多、更有创意的问题？

Ed H. Chi 以前学围棋，你得请教练、请老师，还要找棋力相当的朋友一起下棋，花很多时间。现在你拿个手机，就可以下载一些相当不错的围棋 application。它反而带动了围棋界很多学习，小朋友也都在用这些软件，所以事实上激励了很多人。

这也跟 search engine 有关系。当时很多人觉得，大语言模型来了，search engine 就没那么 relevant 了。但 Google 反而看到很多 search application 在增加，而不是减少。所以我觉得还是可以保持一些乐观。当然我不否认，它会改变我们现在既有的很多结构，但也会带来新的可能性。

Speaker 1 对。

Speaker 1 嗯，非常感谢。

Ed H. Chi 哪里。

Speaker 1 非常非常感谢。

Ed H. Chi 谢谢，谢谢。

来源：小宇宙

item.title: AI 落地最大的障碍不是模型，是运维｜对话 Datadog 首席产品官李严冰
item.category: 硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector
item.description: 李严冰称，AI扩张瓶颈转向运维、可信度及超预算 token 成本，observability 关乎商业 ROI。她称头部 AI 公司需要 Datadog observability，其运维数据训练的模型接近前沿质量、成本至少低一个量级；数据泄露与 API key 暴露仍制约采用。
item.content:encoded:
硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector · 李严冰、曹卿云 Qingyun Cao · 2026-10-19 · 16 min · 原语言 ZH

李严冰称，AI扩张瓶颈转向运维、可信度及超预算 token 成本，observability 关乎商业 ROI。她称头部 AI 公司需要 Datadog observability，其运维数据训练的模型接近前沿质量、成本至少低一个量级；数据泄露与 API key 暴露仍制约采用。

TL;DR

  • 李严冰的核心判断：AI 落地推广、大规模采用的最大障碍是“如何对它进行运维管控”。 企业关注点从 AI 能否 work，转向能否信任和控制它，再到 token cost 超预算；大家关心 AI 能否给出正确结果、可控可信，并真正带来商业 ROI。背后的关键环节是 observability。
  • Datadog 年初随 SaaS 板块市值大规模滑落，但率先从低谷中脱颖而出，年初至今市值已翻倍。 她给出的依据是，世界上最大的十家 AI 公司都需要使用 Datadog 帮助实现可观测性；市场共识已变成“AI 需要更多的 observability”。
  • 对 Datadog 护城河的追问，她给出三层答案：问题复杂度、数据、自研智能。 她以自己在 Aurora 做自动驾驶卡车的经历类比：开车只有加速、减速、打方向盘三个控制，而大规模生产系统运维的复杂度远远超过自动驾驶；Datadog 拥有世界上最大的运维数据，用 observability 数据训练的专属模型质量与最前沿模型非常接近，成本至少降低一个量级。
  • 一家排名前列的 AI lab 曾询问能否购买 Datadog 标注好的运维数据。 这说明即使最前沿的实验室在专业化场景也缺少积累。她认为，post-training 已很常见，能让自有数据成为护城河；Datadog 去年还收购了 RL 公司 Adaptive ML，以加速相关投入。
  • Datadog 做明年研发或 AI 预算时发现投入增长远超预期；工程师使用 coding agent 的支出可能是最大预算支出之一。 公司能把 token 使用与 PR 速度、产品稳定性、feature shipping 和产品安全性等 outcome 对应起来，衡量投入是否转化为 engineering velocity。
  • 她担心的企业级 AI 风险不是“世界末日”头条，而是业余 agent 的基本功失守。 销售、HR 等非工程师用 vibe coding 做出的工具，可能没有优化 token 使用或充分考虑安全，存在泄露商业数据、暴露 API key 等风险；这是企业进一步采用 AI 的重要障碍。

Digest

1. 华人已成 AI 圈的重量级力量：NeurIPS 作者 57% 本科来自中国

  • 李严冰引用一项刚出炉的 Carnegie Mellon 研究：对 NeurIPS 作者的统计发现，57% 的作者本科教育来自中国，其中包括在中国、美国及世界其他地方的作者。她还提到，来自中国的 founder 或 co-founder，已在美国有 41 家十亿美元量级以上的公司。
  • 她将今年 HYSTA 的 AI 大会定位为关注 AI 真正 scaling：议题既包括最前沿的研究与企业应用，也包括取得商业成功的 founder。

2. AI 落地的三阶段焦虑：从“能不能 work”到“ROI 在哪”

  • 李严冰描述了企业关注点的变化：最初想知道 AI 能不能 work；很快转向能否信任它的安全保障；到了今年，又发现 token cost，也就是 AI 预算成本，远远超出预算。大家关心 AI 能否产生正确结果、是否可控可信，以及能否带来商业价值，而不是只是在“token maxing”。
  • 这些问题背后的共同点是 observability：深入了解 AI 在做什么、agent 之间是什么关系，以及它产生了什么价值。她认为，AI observability 是 AI 量产化、大规模采用的重要环节，Datadog 正处在风口。

3. 市值翻倍的背后：产品从“给人用”变成“人和 agent 共用”

  • 年初 SaaS 板块市场状况复杂，各家市值大规模滑落，Datadog 也在其中，但“率先从低谷中脱颖而出”；从年初到现在，公司市值已翻倍。她强调，世界上最大的十家 AI 公司都需要使用 Datadog 帮助实现 observability。市场共识已从“AI 会取代 observability”转为“AI 需要更多的 observability”。
  • 产品形态也在变化：过去 Datadog 有丰富的用户体验、UI 和 dashboard，主要为人设计；未来将由人和 agent 共同使用。交互从以网页和 mobile 为主，变成“我们在哪里工作，工具就应该在哪里”：在 CLI 里编程可以访问，在 Slack 里和团队交互也可以访问。她认为，AI 改变了用户对产品原有边界的认知。

4. 护城河三件套：运维复杂度、运维数据、自研智能

  • 面对“模型会写代码了，Datadog 不可替代性在哪”的追问，李严冰先用自己在 Aurora 做自动驾驶的经历作比。她称 Aurora 是美国第一家、并认为目前也是世界上唯一一家能在公共高速公路运营自动驾驶商用卡车的公司。驾驶只需了解视线所及的本地场景，控制方式只有加速、减速和打方向盘三种；相比之下，大规模生产环境中的软件、硬件和基础设施系统，还有复杂的 AI agent，运维复杂度远远超过自动驾驶。要实现大规模生产运维的完全自动化，还有很长一段距离。
  • 她补充说，coding 虽然也有技术难度，但相对而言主要是产生 code；运维则非常多元化。因此 Datadog 不担心被 AI 取代，而且公司自己也在研发很多 AI。
  • 她给出的另外两层护城河是多年的 domain expertise、世界上最大的运维数据，以及对 research 和 foundation model 的投入。通用大模型能解决很多问题，但有时速度慢、成本高，在非常专业的领域也不一定给出最好的答案。她举例说，Datadog 用 observability 数据训练自己的 observability frontier model，质量与最前沿模型非常接近，成本至少降低一个量级。
  • 她前几天访问的一家排名前列的 AI lab 也是 Datadog 的客户，双方互为客户。对方询问：“严冰，我们非常想在运维场景上做得更好，你能不能把你们标注好的数据卖给我们？”她以此说明，即使最前沿的 lab，在专业化场景也可能缺少积累。她认为未来不会由最前沿的 model 一统天下，也不会只有几家 frontier model 提供所有模型；post-training 已经很常见，可以把自有数据变成护城河。Datadog 去年还收购了一家领先的 RL 公司 Adaptive ML，以加速相关投入。

5. 内部 AI 账本：预算增长超预期，现实安全风险在业余 agent

  • 李严冰刚为明年的研发经费或 AI 经费做预算时“大跌眼镜”，因为增长远超直觉和预期。产品方面，客户对 AI-enabled 产品的使用率越来越高，使用量成倍增长；research 投入则需要长期回报，因为 GPU、AI 基础架构和 training run 都成本很高。
  • 内部效率方面，工程师使用 coding agent 的开支可能是目前最大的预算支出之一。Datadog 的优势是能看到 token 用量和使用位置，也能追踪 outcome：PR 速度、产品稳定性、feature shipping，以及产品安全性的提升，从而衡量投入是否转化为 engineering velocity。
  • 她更担心面向 knowledge work 的 AI 使用：不少人还处于 vibe coding 状态，例如销售人员自己写销售工具，或 HR 团队为自己的场景写工具。这类 agent 可能比较业余，token 使用没有优化好，安全方面也可能考虑不足。
  • 她指出，企业实际考虑的安全风险比“AI 杀死人类”或“几千个 agent 从 sandbox 跑出来攻击其他公司”这类头条更基本：例如 agent 不小心泄露商业数据，或未经充分 AI review 和控制的工具暴露 API key。她认为，这些都是企业进一步采用 AI 的重要障碍。

Full transcript

李严冰 AI 落地推广最大的障碍，就是如何对它进行运维管控。今年年初，整个 SaaS 板块的市值都大规模滑落，Datadog 也在其中，但我们应该是率先从低谷中脱颖而出的。现在市场上的共识是，AI 需要更多的 observability。我们在哪里工作，工具就应该在哪里。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 严冰你好。今年的 HYSTA，你觉得跟往年的会议有什么不一样？

李严冰 卿云你好。我觉得 HYSTA 的会议每年都会上升一个新高度，尤其是最近几年，我们的主题都是 AI。随着中国人在 AI 方面的影响力越来越大，我感觉今天的盛会无论是参与者、话题还是嘉宾，质量都有了质的提升。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今年的会议主要讲哪些主题？

李严冰 今年我们主要关注 AI 真正 scaling 的主题。我知道卿云你也很关注华人在 AI 行业的影响力。前几天我看到一个非常令我惊讶的数据：一项刚刚出炉的 Carnegie Mellon 研究对 NeurIPS 的作者进行了统计，发现 57% 的作者本科教育来自中国，其中既包括在中国的作者，也包括在美国和世界其他地方的作者。大家可以看到华人在 AI 圈的分量。

我们华人不只是做 AI 研究，也把 AI 转化成创业项目和企业。我还看到另一个让我非常惊讶的消息：来自中国的 founder 或 co-founder，已经在美国有 41 家十亿美元量级以上的公司，其中很多公司今天都会参加我们的盛会。所以，HYSTA 今年 AI 大会的主题不仅包括最前沿的研究和企业应用，也包括很多真正取得商业成功的 founder。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 您是 Datadog 的首席产品官，也是硅谷华人女性中非常杰出的代表。我想向您请教，在 AI 时代，您看到 AI 运维会有什么样的发展趋势？最好的机会会在哪里？

李严冰 我觉得这个问题问得非常好。从我作为 Datadog 首席产品官的角度来看，AI 落地推广、大规模地被广泛采用，最大的障碍就是如何对它进行运维管控。最开始，大家对 AI 感到兴奋，只是想知道它到底能不能 work。很快，大家又意识到：“哇，我们知道 AI work 得非常好，那我能不能相信它的安全保障？”到了今年，大家又意识到，即使我能相信 AI，它的 token cost，也就是 AI 预算成本，还是远远超出预算。

所以，无论是 AI 能不能产生正确的结果，我们能不能觉得 AI 可控、可信任，还是 AI 能不能真正提供商业价值，而不是大家都在 token maxing，最终能不能 deliver 商业 ROI，我觉得这些都是大家最关注的问题。这些问题背后有一个很重要的点，就是 observability，也就是深入了解 AI 究竟在做什么、agent 之间是什么关系，以及它究竟产生什么样的价值。

所以 Datadog 现在正处在一个非常好的风口上。AI observability 是 AI 量产化、大规模采用的重要环节。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 我们看到 Datadog 的市值一路飙升，现在也处在历史高位。以前可观测性可能是给工程师用的，让他们观测系统；未来则要给 agents 观测，而且可观测数据量也变大了。未来这样的产品形态会有什么变化？

李严冰 今年年初，整个 SaaS 板块出现了复杂的市场状况，大家的市值都大规模滑落，Datadog 也在其中，但我们应该是率先从低谷中脱颖而出的。从年初到现在，我们的市值已经翻倍了。当然，这其中很多并不是大家主观上认为“AI 需要更多 observability”，而是有真实数据支撑的。比如，世界上最大的 10 家 AI 公司都需要使用 Datadog 来帮助他们实现 observability。

大家已经完全抛弃了“AI 会取代 observability”这个观念。现在市场上的共识是，AI 需要更多的 observability，这也是我们的机会。从产品形态的角度来看，以前 Datadog 的产品有非常丰富的 user experience，有很漂亮的 UI 和 dashboard，是设计给人使用的。我觉得未来会由人和 agent 共同使用这样的产品，产品交互也会从以网页和 mobile 为主，变成“我们在哪里工作，工具就应该在哪里”。

如果你在 CLI 里编程，就可以访问它；如果你在 Slack 里和团队交互，也可以在那里访问它。我觉得 AI 完全改变了我们对产品原有边界的认知，让用户在任何时候、通过任何工作方式都可以访问产品。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今年早些时候，大家觉得 OpenAI 可能会自己做这些产品，而且现在模型能力这么强，还会自己写代码。您觉得 Datadog 未来的护城河在哪里？它的不可替代性是什么？

李严冰 我觉得护城河有几点。首先，运维不只是 mission critical，它的复杂度也非常高。我之前做过自动驾驶，在 Aurora 工作过。Aurora 是一家自动驾驶卡车公司，是美国第一家——我认为现在也是世界上唯一一家——能够在公共高速公路上运营自动驾驶商用卡车的领先公司。我们做自动驾驶的时候，觉得从有人驾驶到无人驾驶的突破是一个非常难的问题。

但仔细想想，自动驾驶比起运维大规模生产环境中的软件和系统，复杂度其实低得多。开车时，你只需要了解视线所及的本地场景，而且只有 3 种控制方式：加速、减速和打方向盘。而在一个软件、硬件和基础架构都非常复杂的大规模系统里，还有很复杂的 AI agent，复杂度远远超过自动驾驶。所以，要真正实现大规模生产运维的完全自动化，还有很长一段距离。

我想说的是，运维的复杂度非常高。相比之下，coding 虽然也有很多技术难度，但相对来说是一件简单的事，就是产生 code；运维则是非常多元化的事情。所以我们不担心自己被 AI 取代，因为我们自己也在研发很多 AI。

回到你的问题，第一，这个问题非常复杂，所以我们积累了多年的 domain expertise。第二是数据，我们拥有世界上最大的运维数据。第三，我们也在 invest in intelligence。通用大模型可以解决很多问题，但有时候比较慢、成本很高，而且在非常专业的领域里不一定能给出最好的答案。

比如，我们有自己的 AI research。我这周刚看到一个结果：我们用 observability 数据训练自己的 observability frontier model。和最前沿的模型相比，我们特制的模型质量非常接近，但成本至少降低了一个量级。所以我们认为，自己的数据、对 research 和 foundation model 的投入，以及专注这个领域所积累的经验，都是我们的护城河。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 所以您觉得像 Datadog 这样的 enterprise，最后还是会选择用开源模型，再用自己的数据训练自己的模型，不一定需要用 frontier lab 的 API？

李严冰 我觉得……

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao API。

李严冰 我觉得这是各取所需，因为不同的 model 有不同的强项。我相信现在业界的共识是，未来不会是最 frontier 的 model 一统天下，也不会是几家 frontier model 就提供世界上所有的 model。大家做 post-training 已经非常常见，因为这样可以把自己的数据变成真正的护城河。

前几天我去访问了一家世界上排名前列的领先 AI lab，因为我们是它的客户，它也是我们的客户。但讨论中最有趣的话题是，对方说：“严冰，我们非常想在运维场景上做得更好，你能不能把你们标注好的数据卖给我们？”所以可以看到，即使是世界上最前沿的 lab，在某些非常专业化的场景里，也缺少这方面的积累。

当然，即使大家有数据，我觉得通用大模型也很难最好地服务所有应用场景，所以我们在这方面有自己的投入。去年我们还收购了一家领先的 RL 公司，叫 Adaptive ML，以加速这方面的投入。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao Datadog 在企业内部采用 AI 时遇到过什么样的挑战吗？你们现在的 AI adoption 比例大概有多少？

李严冰 我觉得我们遇到的挑战和很多企业都类似。作为一家开发工程师产品的公司，我们可能起步早一些。但我刚刚为明年的研发经费或 AI 经费做预算时，真是大跌眼镜，因为增长远远超出了我们的直觉和预期。

AI 投入一方面是提升内部效率，另一方面是把 AI 放进我们的产品里。这两方面都有非常大幅度的提升。产品方面的提升是个很好的现象，说明客户对我们 AI-enabled 产品的使用率越来越高，使用量都在成倍增长。大家觉得这方面的 AI 投入非常值得。

产品投入还包括 research。这方面的投入需要长期回报，因为无论是买 GPU、搭建 AI 基础架构，还是进行多少次 training run，成本都非常高。内部效率提升则有两方面。一个是工程师使用 coding agent，我觉得这可能还是目前最大的预算支出之一。我们主要要看如何把这方面的投入真正转化成 engineering velocity。好在我们就是做这方面的，所以不仅知道大家用了多少 token、在哪里用，也知道最后的 outcome 是什么。比如 PR 的速度、产品稳定性、feature shipping，以及产品安全性的提升，我们都看得很清楚，也能看到 AI 投入产生了什么结果。

我现在比较担心的是面向 knowledge work 的 AI 使用，因为很多人还处在 vibe coding 的状态。比如销售人员不是工程师，却自己写了一个销售工具；或者 HR 团队为他们的场景写了一些工具。我觉得这类 agent 现在非常多，也比较业余，很多时候 token 使用并没有优化好，更重要的是安全方面可能没有充分考虑。

安全是 AI 现在非常热门的话题。大家想象的都是世界末日的场景，比如 AI 杀死人类，或者几千个 AI agent 一起从 sandbox 里跑出来，攻击其他公司。最近的头条新闻很多都是这种性质。但从企业 AI 的实际情况来看，我们考虑的安全问题要现实得多。比如，一个比较业余的 AI agent 不小心泄露了商业数据，或者一个不专业、没有经过充分 AI review 和控制的工具暴露了 API key。我们现在考虑的很多安全问题都更基本，还不是世界末日那样的问题。我觉得这也是企业进一步采用 AI 的一个重要障碍。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 谢谢您今天的分享。

李严冰 谢谢，你的问题非常专业。

来源：小宇宙

item.title: The Business of Seinfeld (Audio)
item.description: Nearly three decades after production ended, Seinfeld reached 72 million U.S. viewers through August 2026, while Netflix reportedly paid well over $500 million for five years of rights. FIN-SYN-era ownership left creators and Castle Rock with back-end stakes, while Sony’s distribution rights require market bidding; open-market availability differentiates Seinfeld as a streaming retention asset.
item.content:encoded:
Acquired · Ben Gilbert、David Rosenthal · 2026-10-18 · 230 min · 原语言 EN

Nearly three decades after production ended, Seinfeld reached 72 million U.S. viewers through August 2026, while Netflix reportedly paid well over $500 million for five years of rights. FIN-SYN-era ownership left creators and Castle Rock with back-end stakes, while Sony’s distribution rights require market bidding; open-market availability differentiates Seinfeld as a streaming retention asset.

TL;DR

  • Seinfeld is still arguably the single most valuable piece of television ever made: Ben verified with Nielsen that 60 million Americans watched the show in the first six months of 2026, rising to 72 million through the end of August — nearly three decades after production ended. Netflix's 2019 deal, reported at well over $500 million over five years, was the largest sum a streamer had paid an outside studio for an out-of-production series. The hosts tally roughly $7B+ in lifetime returns against about $250 million in total production costs — “a 30X on its costs,” with production costs ending in 1998.
  • The economics are “essentially a complete accident of history,” shaped by the FCC's FIN-SYN rules, which prevented NBC from owning a financial interest in the show it aired. Because NBC guaranteed production before a studio was attached, Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David held all the leverage and reportedly took about 15% each of the back end, with about 50% to Castle Rock and successors, about 5% to agents Shapiro/West, and about 15% to Sony as distributor. Sony's distribution rights mean deals have to face bona fide market bids: TBS once bid about $200 million for cable rights to a show whose owner was its parent company.
  • Ben argues that Jerry turning down Jack Welch's offer of $5 million per episode — $110 million for a 10th season — was “the best business decision Jerry Seinfeld ever made.” David calls that an interesting hypothesis and sees its logic: going out on top may have helped preserve the show's appeal. The hosts cite estimates that three to five times as many people have watched Seinfeld since it ended as watched it during its run. Jerry's own framing: “if you can get off, they'll scream even louder. They'll never forget you.”
  • Castle Rock made a costly timing bet: it sold to Ted Turner in December 1993 for roughly $400 million all-in, before the first syndication cycle generated over $500 million in 1995. The hosts estimate Castle Rock's share of the waterfall ultimately produced $2–2.5 billion — captured instead by Turner and then Warner Bros. Jerry has personally earned an estimated three-quarters of a billion dollars from the back end.
  • The product thesis is “no hugging, no learning”: static characters with little development made Seinfeld “the most perfect syndication show ever created,” watchable in any order and across generations. The hosts identify counter-positioning as a source of value today: Friends and The Office are tied to their owners' streaming strategies, while Seinfeld can still be sold on the open market as a retention asset.
  • Everything about the show violated conventional wisdom and it nearly died more than once: the pilot memo said “no segment of the audience was eager to watch the show again,” NBC passed on it for The Nut House and Sister Kate, and the show got a four-episode order using the budget for a canceled Bob Hope special. Larry's response: “It's fine. I think four episodes is all I got in me anyway” — he went on to head-write 135 episodes. The hosts' caveat on letting geniuses work their way: “if you're gonna let a genius be a genius, you need to be sure you're working actually with a genius.”
  • Ben and David offer hypotheses for why there are few Seinfeld-like shows today: streaming emphasizes subscriber acquisition, while comedy can take time to catch on and may travel less easily internationally. Ben speculates that shorter seasons make economic sense when new shows are acquisition vehicles rather than ad-inventory carriers. The hosts also argue that the 1995 FIN-SYN repeal may have been “one of the worst things to happen to the industry,” ending an independent-studio ecosystem with power-law equity upside. Jerry's HBR line stands as the episode's credo: “If you're efficient, you're doing it the wrong way. The right way is the hard way.”

Digest

1. A show that ended 30 years ago still commands 20% of America

  • Ben's hook: he and David picked this topic purely on “what episode would we have the absolute most fun making,” then found the astonishing stat — 60 million Americans watched Seinfeld in the first six months of 2026. Ben called Nielsen to verify: through the end of August the number was actually 72 million, “almost the same audience size as the Seinfeld finale when it aired.”
  • The business frame set up top: Netflix's 2019 deal, reported at well over $500 million across five years — $100 million-plus per year, decades after new episodes stopped — was the largest sum a streamer had ever paid an outside studio for a series no longer in production. And the ownership structure behind it is “essentially a complete accident of history.”
  • The through-line Ben promises: an entrepreneurial story of obsession and craft, where the creators “didn't care what anyone else thought or what the numbers looked like at first,” and a small, passionate early fan base with a slow burn became their greatest asset. Ben even bought a DVD player and a copy of the Seinfeld DVDs on eBay because some pilot facts “only exist in the DVD commentary.”

2. Jerry's one and only goal: become a successful stand-up

  • Born in 1954 in Brooklyn, Jerry's family moved to Massapequa when he was young. His father, Cal, was known as a funny guy; Jerry believes comedy is genetic, that it “can't be taught,” only honed. At about 12 he fell in love with Bill Cosby's stand-up album Why Is There Air?, back when comedy records were the era's Netflix specials.
  • At Queens College he built an independent study around stand-up — writing papers analyzing comedians' sets, then going on stage himself — and debuted at Catch a Rising Star in 1976 at 22. Ben's summary of Jerry's interviews: “I had one goal... become a successful stand-up comedian. That's it” — no career-ladder goals, family goals, or other goals.
  • Ben's framing of why stand-up forged him: it's the one performance discipline with “a real-time scorecard from the audience on something that is entirely within your control” — no band, no arrangement, just you, your material, and brutally honest laughter or silence.

3. Carson, the material treadmill, and a million dollars a year

  • After a recurring role on Benson ended when his character was dropped after three episodes in 1979, Jerry was spotted performing in LA clubs by legendary manager George Shapiro, who with partner Howard West had helped get Andy Kaufman on Taxi and placed comics on The Tonight Show. For the 1981 Carson debut Jerry “trains like he's training for the Olympics” — practicing the five-minute set about 200 times in clubs, jogging to the Superman theme on his Walkman. Johnny flashes the okay sign mid-set.
  • Ben's point on where Jerry's discipline comes from: your first Carson spot takes the best six minutes of a 40-minute act built over five years; the next spot gets your second-best six. Jerry watched comics churn out of bookings once they exhausted their material, so he adopted the regimen of writing for hours daily in steno pads — “you kinda always do need to be on this treadmill of developing material.”
  • By the mid-'80s Jerry is making about $25,000 a week touring — call it a million dollars a year — which matters because, as David flags, “this is why he has leverage with NBC.” The whole flywheel: clubs → late-night exposure → national touring, where “there's not that many people at any given time” making a real living.

4. The 5:15 p.m. meeting and NBC's new GE religion

  • Shapiro runs a letter-writing campaign to NBC Entertainment president Brandon Tartikoff. Jerry's quote on the absurdity: “Imagine you have this kid who's been on The Tonight Show 30 times, and on Letterman 30 times... Nobody ever thought, ‘Why don't we talk to this young man?’” On November 2, 1988, at 5:15 p.m. local time in Los Angeles, NBC finally meets him — but via the specials department, not the comedy department. They settle on a one-off special in an empty SNL slot: “come back with a script.”
  • Ben's context on NBC: after a strategy-free late '70s, Tartikoff's philosophy — smart content for urban 18–49 audiences — helped make them number one, and GE's 1986 acquisition brought Jack Welch-style discipline. David's sharper point: it was novel “for a broadcast network to just have a corporate strategy, period” — pre-GE, networks assumed “America watches what we put on TV.”
  • Jerry on being asked what he wanted from the meeting: he hadn't thought about it — “success as a comedian is getting this meeting.”

5. Larry David in November 1988: a 41-year-old nobody

  • David's blunt answer to “who was Larry David?”: “He is nobody” — 41, single, broke, in subsidized artist housing, a “comic's comic” whose humor landed with other comics but not audiences, “chewed up and spat out of the industry.” The pre-Seinfeld Larry stories are, as David puts it, “George Costanza stories you already know.”
  • The canonical one: writing on Fridays (ABC's wholesale SNL knockoff, where he meets eccentric young comic Michael Richards), then one year at SNL where exactly one sketch airs. He rage-quits on the spot, panics about rent, and his next-door neighbor — the real Kenny Kramer — advises: “why don't you just go back in tomorrow and pretend like nothing happened?” It works, and later becomes a George episode.
  • Two load-bearing details: Larry bonds at SNL with another under-used cast member, Julia Louis-Dreyfus; and NBC “hated this guy” — “to the extent he had any reputation, it was as a loser” who couldn't function in any corporate environment. “And he turned out to be a genius.”

6. A Korean deli, a diner, and the actual premise (not “a show about nothing”)

  • Three days after the NBC meeting, Jerry finds Larry after sets at Catch a Rising Star. In Lee's Market they riff on the shelves — Jerry on fig bars: “It looks like somebody made these in their basement” — and Larry stops him: “This is it. This is what the show should be... two guys just talking like this.”
  • The next midnight at the Westway Diner, Jerry raises the number-one question comics get — where do you get your material? — and Larry says “Bingo. That's how we set up the show.” The premise: how stand-up comedians get their material. Ben's correction to the lore: “nowhere in there did David say the words ‘a show about nothing’” — that phrase comes from the season-four arc where Jerry and George pitch a fictional NBC, and was later co-opted as the show's origin myth.
  • The premise dictates that Jerry plays himself — his sensibilities, his observational humor — because, as Ben notes with affection, “we all know Jerry can't act.”

7. FIN-SYN: the regulatory accident that created the cap table

  • The history lesson: networks and studios were separate companies, with networks “deficit financing” 60–80% of production costs in exchange for a limited license to air, while studios owned the IP and back end — syndication, international, merch, home video. When networks overreached in the '60s and demanded syndication cuts anyway, the FCC's 1970 Financial Interest and Syndication rules barred networks from holding a financial interest in the shows they aired, especially future syndication rights.
  • David's framing of the resulting ecosystem: “it's almost like Silicon Valley startups, this capitalistic entrepreneurial incentive” — independent production companies with real ownership, and, as Ben adds, genuine power-law dynamics: “most shows fail, but the shows that succeed do so massively,” with profits flowing to individuals on a cap table rather than a conglomerate.
  • The incentive split, as Ben lays it out: studios lose money on every episode by design and don't get paid until syndication five-plus years out; networks run “a very short-term business” renting content they legally can't own and betting ad sales exceed rent. The networks had won the repeal by 1993; the transcript later describes the repeal taking effect in 1995. Seinfeld is “one of the last ones out of this system.”

8. Castle Rock: funded by Coca-Cola, distributed by Sony

  • The chain: Coca-Cola buys Columbia Pictures for $750 million in 1982; Castle Rock forms in 1987 with five partners including Rob Reiner (“a studio by artists, for artists”), and Coke invests $30 million at founding for 40%. Ben's kicker: “the studio that funded and created Seinfeld was itself Coca-Cola money.” David: “Why do you think Jerry drinks Diet Coke in Seinfeld?”
  • The structurally crucial term: Columbia gets distribution rights to anything Castle Rock makes. When Sony buys Columbia in November 1989, those distribution rights — plus a minority, non-controlling stake in Castle Rock — travel to Sony, while the actual IP stays with independent Castle Rock. David flags it: “this is all gonna become very, very important.”

9. The most valuable deal in television history

  • The inversion David emphasizes: normally production companies make pilots and beg networks to air them; here NBC guaranteed production to two individuals first. His Silicon Valley analogy: “it's like if you're investing in a Series A and somebody has already guaranteed that they're gonna mark it up 10X in a Series C afterwards.” Jerry and Larry could write their own terms with any studio — and chose Castle Rock because “they seem nice enough.”
  • The reported waterfall: about 15% each to Jerry and Larry, about 5% to West and Shapiro, about 50% to Castle Rock and successors, and about 15% to Sony off the top as distributor. Exact terms have never come out — only the principals know.
  • Ben on the pair's interview technique when confronted with their earnings: they never quite deny. Someone throws out $600 million and they say, “‘That's preposterous. That's an insane number’... but you didn't say that it wasn't in the ballpark.”

10. Stand-Up Diary becomes The Seinfeld Chronicles — approved by the wrong department

  • Unable to generate 90 minutes of stand-up (“it's really hard to be funny for 90 minutes”), Larry proposes shrinking the special into a standard 30-minute sitcom pilot — 22 minutes of content — retitling Seinfeld's Stand-Up Diary as The Seinfeld Chronicles. Jerry's quote: “Every step of the way we were waiting for somebody to come in and say, ‘You can't do this on network TV.’ But nobody did.”
  • The structural fluke David underlines: NBC's late-night and specials department okays a sitcom pilot — “this has never happened before” — skipping the comedy department's scripts, notes, checklists, and committees entirely. And NBC says yes partly because 30 minutes is easier to schedule than 90.

11. Casting: a Tony winner, a headstand, and the funniest name

  • Rob Reiner suggests Broadway actor Jason Alexander for George — he was about to win a Tony, and the role needed a polished actor opposite Jerry. Alexander initially reads the character as Woody Allen and auditions with a Woody impression, only later realizing George is loosely based on Larry.
  • Kramer starts as “Kessler,” partly to avoid a potential rights issue or payment to the real Kenny Kramer — until Larry and Jerry, staring at the page, concede that “of all the names we can think of, Kramer is actually the funniest name. Funny is the most important thing. Everything else is secondary.” Michael Richards auditions doing his lines in a yoga headstand; Tartikoff: “Well, if you want funny...”

12. The pilot tests horribly — and the memo goes on the bathroom wall

  • NBC executives' screening verdict: too New York, too Jewish. David's rebuttal: “basically the entire origins of American comedy are New York and Jewish” — the vaudeville lineage just changed its names, and by the late '80s “everybody knew Woody Allen was Jewish. He was the biggest name in comedy.”
  • The testing process: researchers cold-call to recruit 400 households to watch an unused cable channel. The verbatim feedback: “You can't get too excited about going to the laundromat,” George “isn't a forceful character,” and “Why are they interrupting the stand-up for these stupid stories?” David's favorite line from the research report: “No segment of the audience was eager to watch the show again, and the overall pilot performance was rated as weak.” Jerry and Larry later hung the memo in the production-office bathroom.
  • NBC burns the pilot off on July 5, 1989 — a dead slot — and passes on the show for fall, picking up The Nut House and Sister Kate instead. Ben's recurring refrain: “nobody knows anything.”

13. A canceled Bob Hope special buys the smallest season order in TV history

  • Littlefield and Ludwin can't let it go — “I'll be damned if it's not funny” — so they cancel a two-hour Bob Hope special and use that budget to order four episodes. Littlefield's account of the call: “Jerry finally asked me, ‘Has any show in the history of television ever succeeded with just four episodes?’ I didn't know, and that's exactly what I told him.” Larry's reaction: “Ah, it's fine. I think four episodes is all I got in me anyway” — he'd go on to head-write 135.
  • The road not taken: assuming NBC was out, they shopped it; Fox guaranteed 24 episodes. Jerry passed because startup-era Fox “wasn't the major leagues, and I wanted to be in the majors.”
  • Ben's startup read on why the pilot's cult reception mattered: “You're not trying to be a seven for everyone. You're trying to be a 9.9 for a very small group of people” who evangelize.

14. “You need a girl” — and the subversion that defines the show

  • NBC's one good creative note in the show's history, per David: the pilot's worst-scoring demographic was women, so add a female lead. But the note's subtext was to give Jerry a love interest — Sam and Diane, Ross and Rachel. George Shapiro's quote: “That was normal network thinking. Fortunately, we had two creators who didn't give a crap... they were ready to walk away from the show because of it.”
  • The solution: Elaine is a former love interest — the relationship already failed, so viewers never need to go there. The one episode exploring it, “The Deal,” is even more subversive: they revisit the relationship, then “just never mention it again. There's no resolution... It's just, eh, that didn't happen.”

15. No hugging, no learning: stand-up grafted onto the sitcom

  • David's definition of what Seinfeld is: a merger of stand-up and sitcom. Like a sitcom, it has continuity of characters and places; like stand-up, it has little character development — “Jerry's always Jerry. George is always George... they never learn anything.” Larry's famous one rule — “no hugging, no learning” — was, per Ben, not formally stated, but a shared ethos.
  • Jerry's own articulation, quoted by David: “What Larry and I brought to the sitcom format was a stand-up comedian's structural sensibility. We didn't really have time to tell what the characters were all about because we had jokes to do.” Writer Jeff Schaffer's test, via Ben: “the plot itself has to be funny when you retell it” — which is why episodes end unresolved, freeze-frame, with no consequences.
  • Ben's read on the audience contract: it was respect — “you're in on the joke with us” — and the characters are wish fulfillment: “George is an avatar of our worst qualities. We've all wanted to grab the éclair from the top of the trash can, but we have restraint.” David's addition: the hugging and learning of other sitcoms “was all fake,” and audiences eventually saw it — which is why Seinfeld still plays.

16. Summer 1990: custom Nielsen data helps the show, then a half-hearted pickup

  • The four episodes air after Cheers reruns starting May 31, 1990. The title is shortened from The Seinfeld Chronicles to Seinfeld to avoid confusion with ABC's The Marshall Chronicles — “drop the ‘The,’ it's cleaner.” That same month Tartikoff leaves and champion Warren Littlefield becomes president of entertainment.
  • Littlefield commissions custom Nielsen reports by metro area to test the “only plays in New York” thesis. The result: audience retention from Cheers into Seinfeld is similar — and high — in New York, Chicago, Houston, Seattle, and San Francisco. “There is something universal to this show.”
  • The later pickup is half-hearted: 13 episodes as a mid-season replacement. And NBC, knowing notes won't be taken, drafts executive Perry Simon as hatchet man. His quote from Littlefield's memoir: “I tried to wing typical network notes... they walked out the door, and I knew that they were just like, ‘Fuck that.’ And now I think, thank God. It's a good thing they didn't listen.”

17. The Chinese Restaurant blow-up — and the genius caveat

  • NBC considers shutting down production over an episode that never leaves a restaurant lobby. Rick Ludwin walks Larry around the lot; Larry erupts: “This is what the show is. This is my vision. If you don't like it, I quit. Fine. The show's over.” David: “nobody did this.”
  • Ben's crucial pushback on the lesson: “the lesson here isn't be a blowhard... insist your vision is correct, take no notes ever, and then succeed. For most people in most situations, that is failure.” David relays Littlefield's answer to why no one ever made a show this way again: “if you're gonna let a genius be a genius, you need to be sure you're working actually with a genius” — and, like founders, “most people are not.”
  • The second-season finale, “The Busboy,” introduces the interweaving-storylines structure — four concurrent plots converging in “a violent, unexpected blowup that ruins all of their lives concurrently.” David's explanation for why they cracked it: “this is how every truly great stand-up routine ends” — the moment you realize everything was building to one callback.

18. The invisible production innovations

  • The structural stats Ben assembles: a typical two-act sitcom had seven scenes in 22 minutes; Seinfeld ran 14–25 and threw out act structure entirely. Larry wanted single-cam like a movie; NBC refused, but they brought in filmic lighting and an unusually high number of location shoots.
  • Purity rules: no artificial laugh track — off-set scenes were screened for the live audience to record real laughter, which doubled as a real-time feedback mechanism to rewrite jokes that didn't land, “because these guys come from stand-up.”
  • Ben's light-bulb discovery: episodes weren't live camera-switched but edited in post, enabling tighter cuts and jokes impossible in a live-switch show — like The Contest's montage cutting between characters either sleepless or “sleeping like a baby.” They “invented a novel production process to get the best of both worlds.”

19. The Contest: written in secret, saved by MTV's advertisers

  • Season four, episode 11 — the “master of your domain” episode, based, like many Seinfeld stories, on Larry's life. Scared it was “too much,” they wrote it in secret, keeping it off the office whiteboard, revealing it only at the table read six days before shooting — “as close to the point of no return as Larry and Jerry could engineer.”
  • Broadcast Standards chief Dr. Roz Weinman, apoplectic, ultimately relents: “it might be enough that this show has a pact with its audience, that we can get away with this.” Ben's explanation of the call: no explicit word is ever said, so the concern is whether the audience loves or hates it — and Seinfeld had cultivated an audience where “this is entirely okay, especially done this artfully.”
  • When advertisers pull out, Littlefield's fix: go to MTV's sponsor roster — including alcohol brands and Nike — to backfill the episode. Sponsors who stayed got leather-bound, cast-autographed scripts. In 2009, TV Guide ranked it the greatest TV episode of all time; it made Seinfeld “a water-cooler conversation show.”

20. Thursday night: the Larry/Jerry split and the slot worth more than all other nights combined

  • NBC moves the show to Thursday, where it airs after Cheers. Larry's furious, purist reaction: “If they didn't watch us on Wednesdays, I don't want them watching us on Thursdays.” Jerry's response, and why the partnership worked: “Thank you very much. We will take the new time slot.” Ben's gloss on Larry: George's pathetic dial turned to 11, but the same duality — “thinking he's the greatest thing to ever walk planet Earth... coupled with extreme self-consciousness, self-loathing, and self-doubt.”
  • Why Thursday mattered, which Ben admits he never understood: it was advertisers' last chance to reach audiences before weekend movie releases and shopping. David's stat: NBC's Thursday lineup “was more profitable than all of the other nights combined.”
  • The result, in February 1993: ratings rise 57%, and the show goes from the 45th most popular TV show on air to fifth in one week — and, shocking even the network, Seinfeld gains audience over Cheers rather than dropping off. NBC rolls out the “Must See TV” slogan for the Thursday lineup. Larry to the LA Times, at a point when viewership was averaging around 30 million per episode: “This probably means that a catastrophe is imminent.”
  • The timing bonus: catchphrases (“yada yada yada,” “shrinkage,” Festivus) hit just as the internet arrives. David's anecdote via Steve Case: AOL's connection numbers only dipped when Seinfeld aired — “and then they would go right back up as everybody came on AOL to talk about Seinfeld.”

21. The grind: a seven-day machine and a last-minute live rewrite

  • The process (via writers Alec Berg, David Mandel, and Jason Alexander): start Wednesday, shoot the following Tuesday, so the weekend becomes extra rewrite time — fine, because “they had no personal life to speak of.” Alexander's ritual description: after the table read “they would give their notes, then Larry would quit. Then the notes would be thrown away. Then Larry would agree to stay.” Scripts had no stage direction — just dialogue, because they're comedians — so actors stayed on set for scenes that weren't theirs and blocked collaboratively.
  • Talent pipeline: Jerry and Larry, no longer living in the world, mined fresh writers annually — including the Harvard Lampoon crop — “stealing all the best material from everyone's life and then moving on to the next one.” Festivus and the tip-jar bit both came from writers' real lives.
  • The Marine Biologist story: the shot of George walking into the ocean fails to get the expected laugh, so they huddle on the spot. Larry writes a full-page monologue live, and Tony-winning actor Jason Alexander says, “Put me in, coach,” then performs “The sea was angry that day, my friends” cold — first read, no rehearsal — paying off Kramer's golf balls from earlier in the episode. “Is that a Titleist?”

22. Syndication cycle one: $500 million — and Castle Rock sells at the wrong time

  • At the roughly 100-episode threshold, Sony sells Seinfeld to a record 224 local stations for over $500 million in 1995 — just the first five-year window, local affiliates only, no cable yet. Stations running reruns started beating live programming, including local news, in their time slots. It's “the most perfect syndication show ever created”: no continuity means any episode, in any order.
  • Castle Rock sells to Turner in December 1993 for $100 million cash plus about $300 million of debt, roughly $400 million total. Ben's spoiler: Castle Rock's share of the waterfall ultimately earned “somewhere between two and two and a half billion dollars,” captured by Turner and then Warner Bros. His revised verdict: “Castle Rock absolutely should not have sold, but no one could have known that Seinfeld would go through six syndication cycles.”
  • The wild footnote, carefully hedged: David raises the story that Steve Bannon was an investment banker on the Turner deal and may have taken commission in Seinfeld equity; Ben says the details are murky but that he's seen reports that Bannon still receives syndication royalties.

23. Larry's lockup ends; the cast fights for its only payday

  • Larry leaves in 1996 — burned out, married, and, in David's startup analogy, “the company went public and the lock-up ended”: the 1995 syndication payday put him in the money forever, regardless of new episodes. The cost to the show: Larry was “the CPU” who made every script great, so now all writers work weekends — Alec Berg once realized he'd come to the office every day for 56 straight days.
  • The economics by 1997: Seinfeld generates $200 million in profit for NBC that year — roughly 20% of the network's approximately $1 billion total — and even that understates it, because a $30 million Seinfeld ad buy required committing $200 million across NBC primetime. “Bundling, baby.”
  • The cast — employees with no back end, whose lifetime guild residuals Alexander has been quoted as estimating at around a quarter-million dollars each — holds out after season eight. Jerry backs them, refusing to return for season nine unless all three sign; they get $600,000 per episode ($14.4 million each for the season), while Jerry's salary reaches an unprecedented $1 million per episode, the highest-paid TV actor in history at the time — separate from his ownership.

24. Jack Welch's $110 million offer — and Ben's case for why saying no was the best business decision

  • At the end of 1997, at brunch in Bob Wright's Trump Tower apartment, Welch presents slides arguing the show hasn't peaked, closing with “Everybody who talks to me, they only wanna know one thing: Is Jerry Seinfeld coming back for another season?” Then he pulls Jerry aside and writes on a piece of paper: $5 million, 22 episodes, $110 million — a firm salary offer for a 10th season, five times Jerry's existing record salary, equal to 11% of NBC's annual profit, from Mr. Six Sigma cost discipline himself.
  • On a Central Park bench — the same bench where 21-year-old Jerry told his dad he was going into stand-up — Howard West says he'd love to do one more season; George Shapiro says it would be great to go out on top. On December 26, 1997, the New York Times runs the news top-left on A1. Jerry's reasoning: “When you've been on the stage for a pretty long time and they're still screaming, if you can get off, they'll scream even louder. They'll never forget you.”
  • Ben argues that saying no was “the best business decision that Jerry Seinfeld ever made,” protecting the cultural relevance that powered decades of syndication. David calls it an interesting hypothesis and says he can see the logic. The data they cite: estimates of three to five times more people having watched Seinfeld since it ended than while it was on air — “the majority of Seinfeld's audience have come after that Christmas decision.” Ben's explanation is that it's “the taste left in people's mouth.”
  • The 2017 HBR exchange both hosts have quoted for a decade: asked why he didn't find a more efficient way to make the show — what would McKinsey have said? — Jerry: “Who's McKinsey?... Are they funny? Then I don't need them... If you're efficient, you're doing it the wrong way. The right way is the hard way.” David's generalization: in a creative or entrepreneurial field, “if you want outlier results, you need to take the hard way.” Ben connects it to Bezos's “invent and wander.”

25. The finale nobody loved (and it didn't matter) — plus the $1.1 billion second cycle

  • The May 14, 1998 finale — Larry returns to write the gang's trial for violating Good Samaritan laws, with dozens of guest stars testifying they're bad people — draws 76.3 million viewers, 58% of everyone watching TV that night. NBC sells 30-second spots for up to $2 million, 54% above the 1998 Super Bowl's $1.3 million; Apple runs a one-time Think Different ad adding Jerry to the campaign. David's read: the finale is “a thank you” to the guest stars, and its unpopularity “maybe adds to the lore — nobody learns anything, so we're not even gonna give you a satisfying finale.”
  • Ben's observation: *M*A*S*H*, Cheers, and The Fugitive had bigger finales — “and no one's paying anything to get the streaming rights to them now. They didn't transcend generations.”
  • The 1998 syndication cycle adds cable: TBS, which owned Castle Rock, bids $1 million per episode, almost $200 million — effectively buying rights from a company it owned, because Sony's distribution rights require the rights to go out to market. The total 1998 cycle brings in a reported $1.1 billion, bringing cumulative syndication to $1.6 billion before the show even ends. The 25-year comedic coda: the 2024 Curb finale lands Larry in jail until Jerry appears — “you don't want this. Trust me, nobody wants this.”

26. Three decades of stewardship: ambassadors, DVDs, and one near-catastrophe

  • The post-run totals: a record six-plus broadcast syndication cycles; $2.7 billion in syndication revenue by 2010, $3.1 billion by 2013; DVDs released a season or two at a time, followed by the box set, adding an estimated $500 million — and the cast held out again for DVD back-end participation, reportedly getting low tens of millions each.
  • David's framing of Jerry and Larry's second careers: their “main economic job from now on is to be on a permanent book tour for Seinfeld” — Curb, Comedians in Cars, and the specials follow the Disney-flywheel idea of generating IP around the core without disrupting it. “Larry David made a fraction as much from 25 years of doing Curb as he did from seven years of doing Seinfeld.”
  • The Michael Richards 2006 racist outburst, scoped to the business: “it puts the business model at risk.” Ben's analysis of the communications tightrope — condemn enough that Jerry clearly doesn't have his head in the sand, but not so much that viewers decide “I don't like Kramer either.” David: the asset's value “is so tied to present-day cultural relevance” that even subconscious ick is dangerous.

27. Streaming: the last free agent, and the $7 billion scoreboard

  • The sequence: Hulu in 2015 at $150 million for five years; then in 2019, when Netflix loses Friends (reclaimed by Warner Bros. for HBO Max at a stated $425 million) and The Office (reclaimed by NBC for Peacock at $500 million). Warner Bros. controls distribution of Friends; NBC owns The Office. Sony, with no streaming service of its own, is the independent distributor of Seinfeld, and Netflix pays a reported $500 million-plus for five years of worldwide exclusivity. Ben: Seinfeld is the only one of the three “where there's actually a company paying another company.”
  • The 2026 Netflix renewal: reported as slightly below the original deal, but exclusive to the U.S. and Canada — Sony's bet that it can monetize international streaming rights separately, which it will begin doing shortly. David expects “another billion plus in streaming rights stacked on top” each decade.
  • The lifetime math: about $5 billion through the Seinfeld cap table from syndication, streaming, and DVDs, plus about $2 billion in NBC first-run ad profits — $7B+ against about $250 million in total production costs. “It's a 30X on its costs.” Jerry's personal take from the back end: an estimated three-quarters of a billion dollars; Castle Rock, by design, lost money on the first-run production, “like the first nine years of an early-stage venture portfolio.”

28. Why streamers pay, why there may be fewer Seinfelds, and what power it actually has

  • Ben's acquisition-versus-retention framework: new shows help acquire subscribers (hence eight-episode seasons, in his hypothesis — the 14th episode's $10 million might be better spent on another show's sixth), while Seinfeld is “the single perfect retention vehicle” — comfort food that can reduce churn two ways: you get hooked while browsing, and you won't cancel knowing it's there. Ben suggests comedy's international reach is one reason it can be harder to justify in a scale-economies business; David adds that comedy is a slow burn that may not work as an acquisition hook. Ben's brain-buster, which David buys with qualifications: NBC's '90s ad model incentivized attracting educated audiences; in streaming, “you're just a vehicle for your 12.99.”
  • Could it happen again? Both agree that creator-led work with no committee exists now mostly outside the system (YouTube, podcasts), because “the stakes are too high” inside it; and owning enough of a show to personally make $500 million is much harder in TV now. Ben's theory is that modern distributors are tech companies trained to invest upfront and own operating leverage. David says he expected NBC executives to regret not owning Seinfeld's back end, but found they were happy with the arrangement: “one-year payback on a multiple of invested capital.” Both also argue that FIN-SYN's repeal may have been “one of the worst things to happen to the industry,” consolidating where content can come from.
  • Seven Powers, run on the Seinfeld cap table: counter-positioning (Friends and The Office are “structurally hamstrung by their ownership situations” and can't compete in the same way on the open market); network economies, not scale economies (“the fact that you know all the memes from Seinfeld is extremely valuable to me”); cornered resource — “that might just all be it”; and, during production, process power. David says Larry couldn't repeat the Seinfeld process on Curb, which was improvised and made differently.
  • Quintessence, where the hosts emphasize different parts of the story: David thinks going out on top helped preserve the show's “greatest show of all time” standing; Ben's version is “viewership begets viewership” — the successful '95/'98 syndication cycles made it omnipresent, “in the water,” and passed it from generation to generation. The stat: per Nielsen in 2021, 41% of the then-current audience were toddlers or not yet born when the series ended. Ben's proof point: his three-year-old pointing at the screen — “Is that Jerry Seinfeld?”

29. Trivia worth keeping: Lego music and a data obsessive

  • The theme: composer Jonathan Wolff treated Jerry's monologue voice “like the lyrics of a song,” found Jerry's stand-up tempo at about 110 bpm, and built not a fixed theme song but a system — composing variations of the music for each episode. His quote: “I needed to architect it modularly so that it could be shiftable, changeable like Lego music.” The network executives, naturally, hated it — which David calls “a signal of quality.”
  • Assorted gems: Julia Louis-Dreyfus is from the French commodities-trading Louis-Dreyfus family; her grandfather raced a privately owned Ferrari 166 at Le Mans. Jerry's on-screen Nikes came from an NBC-Nike relationship that let sitcom stars visit Nike's LA warehouse. Carve-outs: David's episode picks (The Marine Biologist above all, plus The Jacket and The Dinner Party); Ben's find, seinfeld.visualizingdata.com — Andy Kirk's 121-page, entirely hand-labeled data visualization of scenes and laughs, built “on his couch with a spreadsheet open... before AI.”

The typical sitcom schedule would start on a Monday with rehearsals, leading up to a Friday shoot. On Seinfeld, they realized, “Well, actually, we could start the week on Wednesday and shoot the following Tuesday. They had no personal life to speak of. They were obsessed with this, so that’s just what they did.

It’s just dialogue, because they’re comedians. That’s what they write.

Ben Gilbert Right.

David Rosenthal So the actors had to figure it out. Day 4 is camera-blocking day. This is when the cameramen come in and start learning their shots: who’s taking what. The episode is finalized enough to figure out what shots they need and which cameras they’re assigning. It’s a very difficult thing, because it’s not like the 4 cameras just sit there and don’t change. Let’s say you’re camera 1. You’re responsible for a wide shot. It comes off you and goes to camera 3. You have 5 seconds to scramble, shift, and zoom, and get a two-shot on 2 characters, because when it flips back to you, that’s where you’re supposed to be.

Ben Gilbert Yep.

David Rosenthal It’s a real ballet and art. They all rehearse as a unit, the cameramen and the actors, because the next day they’re in front of a live audience.

David Rosenthal So any of the stars of any NBC sitcoms could go to the Nike warehouse in L.A. and get all the swag they wanted. So how do you think Jerry Seinfeld started wearing Nikes on Seinfeld episodes?

David Rosenthal Freebies. We talked about this on the Nike episode: they had their athlete strategy, then they got into entertainment, and this was part of it. Jerry Seinfeld was one of the first big parts of Nike’s “get into entertainment” strategy.

Ben Gilbert All right.

David Rosenthal All right, that’s what I got for trivia.

Ben Gilbert Carve-outs?

David Rosenthal Carve-outs. For this one, appropriately enough, I decided I’ve got to do Seinfeld episode recommendations. The Marine Biologist, number one by far. It’s just the most masterful piece of 22-minute episode crafting I’ve ever seen.

Ben Gilbert It’s great.

David Rosenthal A couple of deep cuts I’m partial to: one, The Jacket, which I already mentioned, and two, the first Seinfeld episode I ever watched. I vividly remember it like it was yesterday. I was 9 years old when this episode came out. I saw it air live on TV. I had a babysitter for the night, my parents were out, and I got to stay up late with the TV on. It was The Dinner Party, which is the episode with the black-and-white cookie. I’ll always remember Jerry eating a black-and-white cookie and talking to Elaine: “Elaine, the world needs to look to the cookie. Racial harmony here in the cookie. What we can learn from the black-and-white cookie.” Then, at the end of the episode, he throws up due to food poisoning from the cookie.

Ben Gilbert Oh, Jerry.

David Rosenthal Oh, Jerry. All right, what you got?

Ben Gilbert For me, I have another Seinfeld-related one. If you have a browser open right now, go to seinfeld.visualizingdata.com. There’s the most insane web project I’ve ever seen, called The Seinfeld Chronicles: An Unnecessary Data Exploration by Andy Kirk. It’s a coffee-table book that the author then put online, a full data visualization of a zillion different ways you could slice and dice Seinfeld. What laughs happened when in each episode? What do the patterns look like? How do they accrue to each character? It goes episode by episode. The thing’s 121 pages, showing when various characters got screen time. It walks through why he thinks the show worked and what makes it unique. But the most wild thing to note is that it’s all hand-labeled. He watched episodes on his couch with a spreadsheet open, pausing every five seconds to label who’s on screen and who’s getting laughs. The whole thing is astonishing: a human did this manually before AI.

David Rosenthal Wow. I have The Marine Biologist up right now. There are 23 scenes in The Marine Biologist.

Ben Gilbert Yeah, it’s crazy.

David Rosenthal There you go. Seinfeld and the internet, made for each other.

Ben Gilbert My second carve-out is Buck’s in Woodside.

David Rosenthal Oh, yeah.

Ben Gilbert Incredible restaurant. David and I just went there for a meeting this week, and I was reminded of just how special that place is, especially if you like Silicon Valley lore and ephemera. They’ve got an Apple I up on the wall. They’ve got a signed Jensen jacket, the first one he ever wore on stage. You can tour around the place and get a history of the tech industry, which is very fun.

David Rosenthal It’s like a Silicon Valley version of Monk’s Café, you might say.

Ben Gilbert Yes. And my last carve-out is a company called Tin Can. My son is obsessed with it. He’s 3, but it’s more for 5-to-12-year-olds. It’s a phone, a landline with no screen that uses Wi-Fi, built for kids. They can call preprogrammed numbers, and if they need to call 911 or an emergency contact, it stays plugged in at home. It’s exactly the type of phone we had when we were kids, and they get to call other kids without all the smartphone stuff. The weird coda to this one is that somehow I ended up being the first investor in this company—

David Rosenthal No, yeah.

Ben Gilbert —because it was a completely different company first. It was the last check I wrote when I was a professional VC.

David Rosenthal You’re like the NBC network executive.

Ben Gilbert It accidentally pivoted and turned into this company—

David Rosenthal Yeah.

Ben Gilbert —and became this massive viral hit. They’re on Good Morning America. It’s the face of this movement around great ways for kids to communicate without screens, and my son is loving it. For a while, I was sitting on it, thinking that at some point I should carve out Tin Can, but I don’t want to be too self-promotional and promote a company I invested in. This thing is just really fun to watch all these kids use.

David Rosenthal Ah, so good.

Ben Gilbert

Among the books we read was Seinfeldia by Jennifer Keishin Armstrong.

David Rosenthal

Yep.

Ben Gilbert

Great, great book. And a few people to thank in particular.

David Rosenthal

Research thank-yous. Speaking of books for the show, first and foremost, thank you to Warren Littlefield, the NBC executive responsible for the decision to officially pick up Seinfeld. Warren spent a great amount of time with us, which was wonderful. He also wrote a fantastic oral history memoir of his time at NBC called Top of the Rock, which is well worth reading. It covers Seinfeld, Friends, Mad About You, Cheers—all the great stuff from NBC in that era.

Famously, right after Seinfeld ended, Warren got fired from NBC and went on to have an amazing second career as a producer. He executive-produced Fargo, The Handmaid’s Tale, Dopesick, and now The Testaments, which is doing incredibly well. It was great to talk to him. Thank you to Alec Berg, David Mandel, and Jeff Schaffer, 3 of the writers behind some of the most legendary episodes of Seinfeld, especially in the second half of the show.

Thank you to Jeremy Zimmer, former head of the UTA talent agency; Michael Lynton, former chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment; our friend Ravi Nandan at A24; and Brian McAndrews, a longtime television executive, first at Capital Cities/ABC and then at Disney. And thank you to our friend Jeremy Giuffre for helping inspire this episode with his original recommendation, which I made a carve-out on our last episode: Jerry Seinfeld’s movie Comedian.

Ben Gilbert

Thank you, Jeremy. I’ve got a couple of thank-yous: one to Arvind Navaratnam at Worldly Partners for his great mini-study on Seinfeld for this episode, and another to our good friend Danny Passman, an entertainment lawyer who has spent his whole career around deals in this industry. If you liked this episode, go check out other episodes on TV and entertainment. Taylor Swift, Oprah way back in the day. More recently, much higher quality episode because we got better over time, Disney part one and part two.

David Rosenthal Yep.

Ben Gilbert And, uh, for a tie-in on Coca-Cola.

David Rosenthal That’s right.

Ben Gilbert You can visit library.acquire.fm to get access to all the visuals associated with this episode, charts, tables, and illustrations. You can join the email list at acquire.fm/email. That’s where we will send out behind-the-scenes photos from research, episode corrections, and vote on future episode topics. And come talk about this episode with us and the whole community in Slack after you listen, acquired.fm/slack. With that, listeners, we’ll see you next time.

David Rosenthal We’ll see you next time.

Who got the truth? Is it you, is it you, is it you? Who got the truth now? Huh.
