item.title: Comfy Sunday Spaces v37: OAI/Anthropic Revenues, Neocloud volatility and Trading Philosophy
item.description: Flood and Kyle reprice AI growth after OpenAI and Anthropic revenue claims disappoint expectations. They argue AI financing helped set the marginal price of money, then discuss cash, Bitcoin, and crash prep. Semiconductor multiples and prediction-market valuations look rich unless cash flows justify ownership.
item.content:encoded:
thinkingusd · Flood · 2026-10-18 · 106 min · 原语言 EN

Flood and Kyle reprice AI growth after OpenAI and Anthropic revenue claims disappoint expectations. They argue AI financing helped set the marginal price of money, then discuss cash, Bitcoin, and crash prep. Semiconductor multiples and prediction-market valuations look rich unless cash flows justify ownership.

TL;DR

  • Lower revenue expectations are testing an AI trade priced for exceptional growth. Flood contrasts OpenAI’s rumored $70 billion annualized run rate with its subsequently stated $50 billion, while Anthropic’s leaked roughly $16.8 billion Q3 revenue leaves questions around $100 billion ARR expectations. These remain unaudited claims, but the repricing already hit Nebius, CoreWeave and IREN, reportedly down 30–50% over two weeks: extraordinary technology still faces the “laws of financial gravity.”
  • Kyle’s central macro claim is that AI’s demand for financing is setting the marginal price of money. The 10-year Treasury reached roughly 5.3%, yet yields subsequently fell alongside AI stocks despite hot CPI and PPI releases. His mechanism: less anticipated AI borrowing frees capital elsewhere; a genuine AI rebound could push yields back toward their highs. Developers who believe they are “building God” will keep borrowing until financing costs constrain them.
  • An Anthropic IPO could succeed while draining capital from existing AI holdings. Kyle expects roughly $5 trillion of equity supply over the next year across major offerings and subsequent unlocks, competing for finite risk capital. Circle’s post-IPO surge illustrates his mechanism: investors seeking “the pure AI play” may sell infrastructure proxies to buy the labs themselves, regardless of whether those proxies’ businesses deteriorate.
  • Flood’s defensive position is primarily cash, with a willingness to reverse when the thesis changes. He reports roughly 70% cash versus a usual 80% net-long posture without a strong thesis, retaining smaller Bitcoin and Hyperliquid positions. Flood says he has not seen Bitcoin outperform strongly through material equity drawdowns; Kyle adds that he has never seen it stay flat, much less rise, during one. Renewed equity conviction or inflationary support for AI could change Flood’s view. “I’m gonna wait for the next pitch.”
  • Crash preparation means accessible capital and rehearsed decisions before prices dislocate. Kyle separates buying forced-liquidation rebounds from accumulating durable holdings, while Flood warns that resting bids 10–20% below market still liquidated leveraged traders when altcoins fell 60–70%. Flood’s illustrative shopping level is HYPE at $40, where he would begin buying incrementally. Their framing: “markets are pop quizzes.”
  • Cheap semiconductor multiples may reflect peak earnings rather than overlooked value. Flood describes memory producers earning extraordinary margins while end-user AI economics remain expensive; the market may correctly anticipate that upstream profits will normalize. His valuation test is deliberately uncomfortable: “is every human on Earth gonna spend three thousand dollars a year on AI?” The broader discipline is distinguishing cash flows that justify ownership from stories that merely attract another buyer.
  • Higher rates could eventually strengthen the debasement case rather than undermine it. Kyle follows Jeffrey Gundlach’s framework: sufficiently high sovereign debt can turn attractive Treasury yields into a warning about fiscal sustainability, potentially weakening the dollar and supporting gold, Bitcoin and property. AI distress could also invite inflationary intervention framed as strategic competition with China, which he considers “extremely constructive for Bitcoin and debasement trades.”
  • Prediction-market growth does not settle either valuation or legal durability. Flood calls Polymarket’s $20 billion valuation excessive, including at $10 billion, and prefers ordinary exchange multiples; Kyle pushes back that regulatory uncertainty makes a confident valuation difficult. Kyle sees gambling businesses as relevant comparables. Flood argues crypto needs protections “codified into law” before a possible political reversal in 2028.

Digest

1. Private AI labs create public-market information risk

  • Flood’s opening frustration is informational: enormous public-market exposure rests on two private companies whose revenue, spending and balance sheets outsiders cannot inspect. Even some investors lack information rights. Someone who learns that lab revenue is slowing could make informed trades in public beneficiaries before everyone else. His complaint is “a tremendous amount of asymmetric information,” rather than an accusation that either company falsified its numbers.
  • Flood floats a forcing function for companies raising outside capital at this scale: tens of billions in revenue and hundreds of billions raised might justify public ownership and disclosure. He also suggests allowing annual reporting to reduce short-term pressure. Kyle’s disagreement is explicit: “completely unbothered.” A trillion-dollar furniture manufacturer, he argues, should retain the autonomy to remain private.
  • Kyle’s concern instead follows the technology’s externalities: the labs monetize knowledge contributed across the public web while their products can affect everyone. He cites Anthropic’s proposed donation of up to 20% of its shares to Trump Accounts as an attempt to distribute economic upside without voting rights. Separately, Flood describes cryptography fears, reported hacking, and REA, a reverse-engineering tool he says can use AI to break down compiled programs. Those are Flood’s examples of externalities and potential harms.

2. Annualized run rates leave major questions about revenue and margins

  • Flood stresses that the figures under discussion are rumors and unaudited disclosures. OpenAI’s whispered $70 billion ARR became a company-stated $50 billion. Annualization itself deserves scrutiny: $1 million earned on one day can become a $365 million annualized figure without establishing that the next year will produce that revenue. Markets initially shrugged off the revision before AI names weakened.
  • Anthropic’s investor-meeting leak put Q3 revenue around $16.8 billion, or roughly $17 billion, against earlier discussion of $100 billion ARR. Flood’s possible reconciliation is approximately $25 billion revenue in Q4, supporting that annualized rate. That would require another roughly 50% sequential increase, similar to Q2–Q3, but the earlier period included “token maxing.” He also distinguishes rising costs for heavy API use from falling prices per token.
  • Flood gives the bull case its strongest form: these might be “the best businesses on Earth,” with profitability obscured by pre-training. He cites inference as only 37% of data-center usage; shifting 90–100% toward inference could produce a massive gross-margin business. The question is whether those economics survive when the spending that maintains frontier performance stops.
  • The bear case is commoditization: without continued pre-training, users might migrate to free open-source models or subsidized competitors. Flood’s analogy is economy air travel, where passengers largely want the same destination and acceptable delivery rather than a particular carrier. If the “end product, the end state” dominates purchasing decisions, frontier intelligence may struggle to retain premium economics for ordinary tasks.

3. Neoclouds sit inside an amplified spending chain

  • Kyle separates outside customer demand from transactions within the AI complex. His estimate is roughly $250 billion in annualized spending by customers outside that complex, amplified into trillions as companies purchase from one another. Nvidia hardware enters CoreWeave facilities, networking comes from Broadcom, and servers consume AMD or Intel CPUs and memory. That “amplification factor” makes many securities sensitive to the same underlying demand.
  • Kyle thinks some earlier growth reflected Chinese model distillation that the labs knowingly tolerated because it generated revenue and helped fundraising. In his explanation, blocking those customers subsequently flattens growth and unsettles downstream suppliers. This is his interpretation of the revenue trajectory; the discussion supplies no internal company evidence establishing it.
  • Flood reports Nebius, CoreWeave and IREN falling roughly 30–50% over two weeks, even with the broader market still up around 15% year to date. Kyle points to widening credit-default-swap protection on CoreWeave and Oracle as investors identify potential casualties. His concern is what happens if the labs are “only like seventy percent as good as we thought they were.”
  • Neither claims a trading edge in those names. Financing structures, construction delays, political obstruction and contractual responsibility require specialist knowledge they say they lack.

4. AI financing may now govern the cost of money

  • Kyle recalls the 10-year Treasury reaching approximately 5.3%, alongside a rate hike, while equities initially resisted the pressure. Then hot CPI and PPI arrived, yet Treasury yields fell as AI sold off. His provocative reading is that inflation is not currently the dominant marginal variable; anticipated borrowing for AI is driving the market’s pricing of capital.
  • The relevant distinction, in Kyle’s framework, is whether next year requires $500 billion or $1 trillion of AI borrowing. Strong demand makes financing expensive and competes with other borrowers. An AI slowdown reduces that competition, making capital more available to governments and businesses outside the sector. Falling yields can therefore accompany deteriorating expectations for AI rather than better inflation news.
  • His conditional test is concrete: if the sell-off proves to have been a fund liquidation and AI stocks recover, Treasury yields should probably return toward their highs. If AI continues unwinding, financing should keep getting cheaper, potentially reaching the two-year Treasury and expectations for no further hikes. Neither outcome is presented as certain.
  • Kyle believes developers who think they are “building God” will borrow every available dollar to accelerate, whether motivated by AGI or competition with China. Higher financing costs finally impose a ceiling. That is why he says fixed-income investors are currently “in the driver’s seat”: their pricing of default risk and funding determines what the rest of the trade can sustain.

5. An AI IPO can rally while starving its proxies

  • Anthropic’s S-1 remains the major unresolved catalyst. Flood allows that it could reveal “the greatest company on earth” and squeeze bears. Kyle is more suspicious of delays: Polymarket’s probability of an IPO that year fell from roughly 94% in early September to around 70%, with only about 50% for completion by November’s end. He also cites limited information-sharing and renewed safety concerns.
  • Flood discusses a rumored $1.5 trillion valuation versus an earlier $2 trillion ambition, with approximately $200 billion sought. Kyle combines potential Anthropic and OpenAI issuance, subsequent unlocks and SpaceX supply into roughly $5 trillion of equity looking for buyers over the next year. These are prospective supply estimates, not completed offerings, but they underpin his caution toward risk assets.
  • Kyle’s best analogy is Circle: investors wanted a pure stablecoin business rather than partial exposure through Coinbase or PayPal, and the shares surged within three weeks. Portfolio allocation to a theme could overwhelm valuation. He expects similar demand for “the pure AI play,” potentially making Anthropic perform very well while investors sell correlated infrastructure holdings to fund purchases.
  • Flood also watches existing companies issuing equity to finance capital expenditure. Management is choosing to sell ownership rather than borrow more; that counterparty decision deserves attention. He does not treat it as an automatic instruction to liquidate, but as another reason to reconsider sizing while the market works out AI’s eventual economics.

6. Flood’s cash position follows his equity thesis

  • Flood reports approximately 70% cash, retaining Hyperliquid and Bitcoin in substantially smaller quantities. The context matters: without a strong thesis, he typically runs around 80% net long because of his underlying enthusiasm for crypto. He also says Bitcoin sold during the reduction delivered almost a $2,000 gain per coin. Cash is his current allocation decision: “I’m gonna wait for the next pitch.”
  • Flood says that in nearly a decade and a half in crypto, he has not seen Bitcoin trade exceptionally strongly while equities sold off materially—10%, 15% or 20%. Kyle adds that he has never seen Bitcoin remain flat, much less rise, through such a decline. Its continuous trading and liquidity often make the drawdown larger. Betting on an exceptional decoupling is therefore insufficient reason for Flood to retain his usual exposure.
  • A bullish change in equities would likely bring rapid crypto re-entry; highly inflationary preferential financing for AI could also change Flood’s view. Their defensive posture includes low-double-digit-percentage shorts, rather than a huge crash bet. Flood considers a 10% market decline the following week exceptionally unlikely, and Kyle emphasizes that their equity framework operates over approximately six months.

7. A thesis needs an invalidation and a matching time horizon

  • Flood wants an identifiable price level, fact or state change that proves a thesis wrong. Otherwise, recognition can arrive after substantial losses. His own sensitivity to rising rates comes from complacency in 2022, when his portfolio was “eviscerated.” He also warns that social feeds reinforce positioning: liking one bearish CoreWeave post caused his feed to fill with similar arguments.
  • Winning frequently is a different objective from making money. Flood cites fellow trader Basics TNZ reporting roughly a 30% win rate despite substantial profits; sizing the strongest opportunities can dominate the result. His requirement is emotional flexibility: losses become more damaging when a trader cannot admit error or change exposure.
  • Kyle’s timeframe warning is that a six-month thesis can coexist with painful daily reversals, including 3–4% rallies and 10% up weeks. Flood’s example is Hyperliquid: buying in single digits and selling around $30 worked, but approaching $100 required enduring major tests, including Jelly Jelly and competition from Lighter. A short-term trading rule can interrupt a longer-term investment thesis.
  • Flood and Kyle manage separate books and can disagree, so one visible wallet does not represent every position or view. Flood also rejects taking trades to defend an online reputation. “You get paid for being fluid and responding to state changes,” rather than letting social pressure choose the trade.

8. Crash preparation starts with capital that can actually move

  • Kyle’s first rule is to avoid being incapacitated on the day. Capital behind a seven- or 30-day staking unlock cannot fund an immediate opportunity. Then distinguish two strategies: buying a forced-deleveraging overshoot, perhaps in a leveraged ETF such as SOXL, or accumulating assets intended for holding over one to three years. Those require different selection and exit decisions.
  • His rehearsal scenario runs from a terrible Anthropic S-1 through missed spending commitments, distressed neoclouds, trouble at Oracle and Nvidia’s backstops creating contagion. The purpose is to pre-decide a response while calm. He explicitly says such a dramatic sequence “almost certainly won’t happen”; preparation is useful without making the scenario a forecast.
  • Flood’s cautionary example is traders leaving bids 10–20% below market before altcoins fell 60–70%, liquidating even 2×-leveraged positions. Cross-margin accounts can also fail during a momentary 90% drop. Venue outages and congested chains matter independently of insolvency: capital on the wrong platform can leave a trader unable to act during the crucial hour.
  • Flood’s illustrative plan is HYPE at $40: begin buying a specified dollar amount every minute and welcome lower prices, because he considers levels underneath attractive. A shopping list does not require unattended limit orders. “Markets are pop quizzes”: preparation can determine whether a rare dislocation produces double-digit gains or losses, rather than leaving the trader frozen at the screen.

9. Falling markets force stories back toward cash flows

  • Kyle describes ownership fatigue after a stock falls in 18 of 20 weeks: “Why the fuck do I own this?” His framework is that markets oscillate between cash flows and stories. Prices can climb as high as a persuasive future allows, but durable bottoms require an ownership case based on being paid back within a reasonable period and with acceptable risk.
  • Zoom supplies his historical example: the story that offices, classrooms and business communication would permanently migrate to one remote platform supported extraordinary expectations. “The stories work until they don’t.” In a prolonged decline, investors may prefer businesses whose valuations need less storytelling, even at the cost of sacrificing upside.
  • Flood’s tweet cited companies moving from $50 million to $10 billion valuations within months. He says that implies $9.95 billion of value creation by a relatively small team. Kyle calls it effective storytelling. Flood adds that a VC’s claimed 1× downside protection depends on an acquisition actually occurring. Their preferred reading includes Buffett and Howard Marks for longer-term allocation judgment, rather than weekly market calls.

10. Debt stress could reverse the usual response to higher rates

  • Asked whether the 1970s oil shock, rate increases and gold’s more-than-tenfold rise offer a useful parallel, Kyle says historical comparisons will likely fail here. He follows Jeffrey Gundlach’s framework: normally higher Treasury yields attract investors away from non-yielding gold, but sufficiently large government debt can make higher rates look like a sustainability warning instead of an attractive opportunity.
  • If debt-service costs consume an alarming share of tax revenue, Kyle thinks the result is “probably dollar down” and probably supportive of gold, Bitcoin and even property. Separately, worsening AI distress could invite extraordinary support framed around beating China. He sees that potential intervention as constructive for debasement trades, which helps explain why he is less anxious about crypto’s longer-term position than about equities.

11. Prediction-market valuations depend on law as well as growth

  • Flood considers Kalshi reasonable but is publicly bearish Polymarket at $20 billion and even $10 billion. His comparison is an exchange: he cites Nasdaq around 8× and suggests 5–10× as reasonable multiples, rather than 20×, 40× or 100×. The sector may grow, but implementation and competition leave him broadly neutral to somewhat bearish on current companies at their valuations.
  • Kyle’s pushback is “I don’t know that it’s way overvalued,” because legal uncertainty makes the business itself difficult to handicap: the operators might not have a business in two years. Robinhood’s prediction revenue attracted growth enthusiasm, but he sees much activity substituting for exchanges or sports betting. MGM and DraftKings therefore look like relevant comparables, implying lower valuations than private markets currently assign.
  • On the midterms, Flood distinguishes ordinary political gridlock, which markets often welcome, from crypto’s need for affirmative legal protection. Without legislation such as the CLARITY Act, a Democratic presidency in 2028 could reverse today’s tolerance; prediction markets are particularly exposed. Flood’s intuition is that Democrats probably win the midterms and will then be favored for 2028, rather than that either outcome is certain.

12. Cheap chip earnings and expensive AI services can coexist

  • Asked whether institutions are simply chasing stories like retail traders, Flood says valuation depends on where one looks. He describes SK Hynix and Micron producing extraordinary earnings, citing roughly 90% net margins and enough profit to repurchase their shares at current prices in about three years. Earlier, Kyle noted some chip names trading at approximately 3–4× earnings. Those securities can look strikingly cheap.
  • The catch is overearning: circular spending can make supplier profits unusually strong, while low multiples signal that the market doubts their durability. Flood says the market may be right to price chip companies cheaply. Conversely, assessing Google, Microsoft, Amazon or Meta solely on AI revenue against AI spending would make those activities look extremely expensive; their other businesses soften the consolidated picture.
  • Flood does expect AI revenue to rise as people learn productive uses over time. His unresolved test is the scale of spending required to justify expectations: “is every human on Earth gonna spend three thousand dollars a year on AI?” Otherwise, as he puts it, “a lot of the math isn’t mathing.”

Full transcript

Flood

It’s been a pretty exciting week in markets. We try to schedule Sunday Spaces around periods of volatility, or sometimes periods where there’s a lack of volatility and we think something interesting might happen. This was obviously a week with a tremendous amount of volatility, specifically in the AI trade.

Speaker 1

I think let’s start with a lot of the headlines that came out in the last week, week and a half. OpenAI ARR was revised from the whisper number of $70 billion down to its self-claimed $50 billion. Then there were the leaked numbers from the Anthropic investor meeting, which I guess will eventually make it into its S-1 if it files one and actually tries to IPO. And then a lot of the inflation numbers came out: CPI and PPI were crazy hot.

Flood

There was a lot of data in the last week, and markets didn’t care at all until they cared a lot. Maybe let’s go into that.

It’s very clear that quite a bit of the market is reliant on 2 private companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. Whether people realize it or not, quite a bit of GDP growth is downstream of, or has a direct overlap with, some of the spending these 2 companies are doing. Specifically, that’s spending on data centers and revenue generated by other hyperscalers and companies around the world paying for the fantastic services these 2 companies provide.

It’s unclear, and there’s quite a bit of discussion around whether these businesses are profitable. Anthropic—which is… Well, hold on. Before we jump into it, it’s important to say that it’s slightly frustrating that so much of the U.S. economy is based on these 2 private companies. They’re not small; they’re some of the biggest companies in the entire world by market cap, not necessarily by revenue.

Anthropic is slated to go public at presumably a $1.5 trillion market cap, which would put it among the top 10 companies in the world, almost—just below Broadcom. So much of U.S. spending and growth, and pretty much the only industry that’s growing, has been AI and AI-related spending. It comprises so much of the index at this point, and it’s basically the trade that has dominated everything.

The Case for Going Public

Before we get into the actual figures and what we’re looking at, I think it’s important to say that what’s frustrating about trying to speculate in markets right now is that there’s a tremendous amount of asymmetric information. We have no idea what the actual revenues of OpenAI or Anthropic are. In fact, some investors in OpenAI and Anthropic don’t even have information rights, so they can’t get the companies’ revenues, net profitability, total spending, or even their balance sheets in real time.

You have protections as a private company in the United States, and that’s how the law works. But we can still comment on whether that’s fair. The beautiful thing about public markets is that there’s a standard of reporting. If you misrepresent your company’s financials, lie, or do something illegal, you go to jail. That still happens with private companies, obviously, but there’s quite a bit of leeway.

We’re not saying Anthropic or OpenAI are lying about their revenues. But it’s quite frustrating that people who have access to that information may be making very informed decisions in public markets. If someone knew that OpenAI or Anthropic’s revenues were slowing down, presumably that would affect their future spending, and they might short companies that are direct or indirect beneficiaries of the rapid, ravenous spending by these 2 massive frontier labs.

Again, this is less about markets, sentiment, or trading, and more about frustrations I’ve had personally. Kyle, I don’t know how you feel about it, but it does sort of blur the line. I know we say “crime is legal,” and joke about these things. I personally don’t joke about them. It’s quite different from public markets, where you’re not allowed to have asymmetric information on a company.

You can do research and spend quite a bit of time trying to become a very informed market participant. But it feels quite unfair at times that certain market participants have access to information about these 2 massive private companies, especially when we’re trying to navigate these fairly complex and sometimes theoretical markets. I just wanted to open with some of that. I know I had an interesting week on Twitter, as many of you have seen.

At a certain point, I think it’s important to consider this, especially if these companies are seeking outside funding. There’s a big difference if it’s a family business that’s been compounding over generations and generations. I suppose that can be grandfathered in and remain private. But a new frontier technology company being allowed to stay private and become one of the largest companies in the world, affecting so much of the market that everybody is exposed to, feels like something that might be looked at in hindsight.

People might say, “If a company has tens of billions of dollars in revenue and has raised hundreds of billions of dollars of capital, maybe it’s sort of a public good. Outside investors should have the opportunity to invest, and this company should be forced to go public.” There are forcing functions that made companies like Facebook go public back in 2009, or whenever it went public, based on the number of investors. People at Facebook essentially launched these SPVs to get around the rule because Facebook really didn’t want to go public. But they ended up being forced to go public by the SEC.

I’m a free markets guy, but I do think it’s important that the public is able to share in quite a bit of the upside and speculate if they choose to. Additionally, maybe public markets should be a bit more efficient, where reporting can happen once a year. That way, companies aren’t as short-term oriented. Companies could choose to report every quarter or once a year, with a little more flexibility, and still be liquid, tradable instruments. I think that would probably be a reasonable change.

Markets have changed considerably since these rules and regulations were created. Some of the SEC rules we follow were made almost a hundred years ago, because of speculation in the 1920s. Again, I just wanted to put that out there. It’s not really relevant to what we’re thinking about markets; it’s more about my philosophy on markets in general.

It’s quite frustrating that someone like Situational Awareness, or people with exposure to Anthropic or the ability to get that information, could have asymmetric information and make really informed decisions in markets. It does feel quite unfair. Anyways, Kyle, what are your thoughts?

Speaker 1

I’m completely unbothered by any of that. I just don’t feel any need to—I don’t feel any reason why a company should be forced to go public. I think they have the autonomy to do what they want to do.

ARR is different from revenue. It’s a bit of a confusing metric. It’s annualized run rate. What does that mean? You could take the last day of revenue and project an ARR. If you made $1 million that day, your ARR would be $365 million over the course of a year. If you take the last week, then multiply it by 52, and so on and so forth.

It’s not disingenuous, but it’s non-GAAP accounting. It’s kind of saying, “We make this amount of money, and if we continue to make money at this rate, this is what we would make for the rest of the year,” or something like that. Typically, it’s year or year to date.

Speaker 1 Yeah. Okay. When you come into a day like that, the first thing you want to do is make sure you don’t get your ass kicked that day. What does that mean? It means you don’t want your capital tied up in things that are illiquid, where you can’t realize any cash from them.

In a crypto sense, if you’re behind some sort of staking unlock where your capital is always 7 or 30 days away from you, tough shit. You’re not going to be able to participate in a productive way. You want to make sure you have very instant access to your money. That’s how you’re going to be able to capitalize.

Beyond that, I think it’s really an asset selection game. You have to say, “Look, what do I want to buy here?” There are going to be a lot of things that go down by an amount that’s clearly wrong. They’re clearly going to reach their terminal price through some sort of forced deleveraging. Then you’d expect that when the deleveraging occurs, they snap back to something more reasonable, albeit at a price substantially lower than where they started.

You have 2 strategies. You can bottom fish for these things and say, “Look, good shot that something like SOXL, a leveraged ETF product, ends up way overshooting,” and then buy something like that. Or you can say, “Look, I have durable views on a couple of assets in this space. I have a few things I want to buy here that I intend on selling for long-term capital gains in a year or 2 or 3.” Then you just buy them at a good price.

You have to make sure you run that playbook for yourself ahead of time, before anything like this ever happens, because you’re not going to feel calm or in control. You’re not going to feel like you have a lot of time to sit down and contemplate these things when it’s happening. I think it’s a good drill to rehearse the what-ifs. Just say, “Look, what if we had a lot of stuff? What if the Anthropic S-1 comes out and it’s horrific, and investors panic, and the debt guys sell stuff down, and there’s this domino effect where the neoclouds look like they’re going to default, OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t going to make their spending commitments, Oracle’s in a tough spot, Nvidia backstopped a lot of these guys, and there’s this contagion?” In that moment, how would you respond?

Just running that playbook as a rehearsal will bring you a lot of calm, because as markets go down, you say, “Look, I’ve prepared for this. I’m ready for this.” If it doesn’t happen—and it almost certainly won’t happen, at least not in any sort of dramatic capacity—then no harm, no foul.

Flood These are important things to think about, and this is where you, as a trader, make money: other people won’t be thinking carefully about potential tail risks or things that could happen during periods of extreme volatility and low liquidity, but you will, if you have the foresight to prepare.
