Speaker 2 金老师，请问能听到吗？

Shanghao Jin 可以，你说。

Speaker 2 你好，金老师。我是中途加进来的，前面的部分没听到，我回去再复习一下。我有一个问题想问，您对 CRWV 这家公司的看法有没有变化？这家公司未来看起来有比较大的不确定性，我们是适合把它当成一张彩票，还是说在当前价格下，可以占据一个不低的仓位？想问一下。

Shanghao Jin 我只能说我自己的看法。你怎么投资肯定是自己的 view，每个人风险偏好不一样，这肯定要自己看。我肯定不会把它当成一个重要仓位。我甚至卖掉 Google，也没有直接去买所谓的半导体，这是整个仓位分布的问题，每个人的仓位分布可能不一样。

CRWV 这只股票，最近资金方和台资验证了 TSMC 订单、TSMC 供应链以后，认为它业绩很好。我掌握这个信息，是因为它业绩很好，但它没有报出预期。上季业绩的时候没有报出这个预期。那最后的 gap 出在哪里？是它有产能但没有报出来，还是产能中间打了折扣？这个不太清楚。但我倾向于现在大家都低了。我肯定在这个时间点倾向于看多。看多的话可能会跌两天，但如果看空，跌两天你也不会买。

当然，彩票类的股票还有不少，比如 WOOF 也是彩票类的股票。别人拿到的钱已经跟市值一样，国防股给它的钱跟市值差不多，它该跌还是一样得跌。所以现在的跌法其实跟基本面没什么关系。你不应该因为基本面进去买或者做空。你做空肯定是因为 CDS spread 变宽，大家要砸盘，但你不知道要砸多久。

还有一个比较确定的买盘信号，我觉得就是听到哪个基金爆仓了，你就可以进去。特别是大 hedge fund 谁爆仓了，我觉得一般这种砸盘都是砸到有人死掉就结束。

Speaker 2 所以我们不能光看它跌得多深、跌了多少，还是要看它的确定性？

Shanghao Jin 对。不是，我说现在原来别人都没涨，它没涨、别人都涨，是一种机会。现在它跌了，别人跌得更多，有很多股票跌得比它还惨。基本面很好的股票跌得比它惨很多。

Speaker 2 是的，比如 INTC 这样的股票，确定性更高，所以我们可以放更多仓位在这些上面？

Shanghao Jin 对。INTC 我会放比较大的仓位。

Speaker 2 好的，谢谢您的解答。

Shanghao Jin 嗯。

Speaker 2 好。

Shanghao Jin 我后面自己的具体仓位可能就不说了。我再 take 两个问题吧，然后就下线了，我准备睡觉。

Speaker 3 金老师您好，可以听到吗？

Shanghao Jin 可以，你说。

Speaker 3 我想请教两个完全不相关的问题。一个是您觉得 12 月份以后通胀压力会小很多，这个我不太明白，您可以讲得仔细一点吗？第二个是关于 tariff 的问题。还有一个是您为什么觉得 Anthropic 会破发？尤其如果它为了上市把估值降到 1.5 倍 trailing，我理解它降估值是为了让后市交易更好一点，为什么您觉得它还是不行？

Shanghao Jin 你等一下，我吃口东西。

Speaker 3 没事。

Shanghao Jin 你现在到底是 40 倍 PS 还是 35 倍 PS，对市场交易来说没有差别。我也可以给你炒到 50 倍、100 倍，也可以砸到 20 倍。本身这个交易里情绪性就很强。你有两个选择：降价，或者加规模。在这种情况下只有这两条选择，要不就别干。

Speaker 3 嗯。

Shanghao Jin 你既然选择降价，就表示你很 desperate。你很想融。

Speaker 3 很想融。

Shanghao Jin 对，你很想融，很绝望，很 desperate。

Speaker 3 嗯。

Shanghao Jin 你很绝望，融完以后就很容易破发。一般来说，IPO deal 很 desperate，结果都不会特别好。很久以前有个类似的 deal，叫 Facebook，现在叫 Meta。当时也是比较大，不是 best home lead，但反正卖到 retail 去。我觉得卖到 retail 去就说明它融的量特别大，融了不少。现在看起来都无所谓，但当时融的量比较大，受众面比较广。受众面比较广的 IPO 一般也不会特别好。包括 SpaceX 也暴跌，跌了挺多，都是这样。

一般什么样的 IPO 会比较火？不是看发行价，而是看买方是不是 long-term money，是不是有大量优质投资人。你都不愿意给 hedge fund allocation，allocation 抢不到，最后不给他们 allocation，这种 deal 就会比较好。你都降价 25% 了，还在乎谁投吗？你里面挤进来多少对冲基金？所以这种交易一般上市以后不会太好。这是我个人感觉。

Speaker 3 好。那通胀呢？您讲讲为什么 12 月份以后可能就没什么通胀压力了。

Shanghao Jin 通胀比较大的部分，核心通胀的大头，是关税。关税的影响有滞后性。当时加了关税，滞后的影响高峰可能是今年 3 月、4 月。所以你要把全年算进去，再过一段时间，现在已经每个月都在下降，这个数据很明确。接下来关税就不怎么增加了，除非再新加。

不是加原来的关税，是要新加。就像油价一样，你要再产生通胀，就得再往上涨。

Speaker 3 对。

Shanghao Jin 从数据上来看，关税的影响在往下走。整个关税对核心通胀的影响大概是 0.8%。

Speaker 3 哦，那非常——

Shanghao Jin 是个大头，比油这些东西重要多了。

Speaker 3 好的，谢谢金老师，谢谢精彩讲解。

Speaker 4 金老师你好。

Shanghao Jin 你好。

Speaker 4 我想问一下美国电力供应上限的问题。美国明年的电力审批有一个明显的天花板，包括 BE 的装机量也有上限。明年、后年会不会因为电力问题导致很多项目被砍，进而让半导体被砍单？

Shanghao Jin 我了解下来，明年不会，后年不知道。明年不会。我了解下来大家都有储备，多多少少都有。这也是为什么我现在这个时间比较看多的原因之一。

看 2027 年，如果现在看 2027 年，2028 年还太远。现在是 2026 年，至少现在看 2027 年，整个 2027 年大的投入方 CSP，有几件事情是准备好的。第一，买卡是有准备的，至少已经知道从哪里买到卡。第二，电是有准备的。比如我差多少电，准备了哪些电条，联网不够的怎么办，原来有储备但没联网的怎么办，如果消耗到某个程度，准备去外面用什么方案。比如燃气涡轮也好，或者用 BE 的方案也好，大家都有几个电力方案，知道能源要砍的时候怎么做。这个限制在明年，大家都有准备。

第三，钱是有准备的。我明年准备发多少债，发 4,200 亿债，已经把 operating cash flow 计算进去。这三方面都是有明确准备的。他们都是大公司，跟 2000 年互联网公司想着就投、乱买服务器不是一回事。他们都明确做过自己的需求打算和预期，然后再去做这件事。不能把 2000 年的情况套过来。两者的负责程度差距非常大。

Speaker 4 好的，谢谢金老师，没别的问题了。

Speaker 5 金老师你好，我有两个问题。第一个，从 equity story 来看，Anthropic 现在 MoM 降速到大概 5%，这样平推的话，隐含一年 YoY 大概只有 80% 到 90%。但 Anthropic 明年和后年要框的算力大概都是翻倍，所以在市场还不知道 CSP 的 post-training 营收之前，市场担心供应过剩，这个 equity story 是不是短期有基本面的负面影响？

第二个问题是关于 post-training。我不太清楚 post-training 是不是指 CSP 看着客户的资料，选定特定垂类，然后自己来 train？

Shanghao Jin 不是，不是。

Speaker 5 那目前 YoY 的需求，至少上一季 Microsoft 和 Amazon 都说是三位数。扣掉 Frontier Labs 的份额，因为它们 YoY 也大概是三位数，剩下的需求大概也至少是 80% 到三位数。我可以这样理解需求增长吗？

Shanghao Jin 我给你说一下。先说第一个问题，是不是供应过剩。供应过剩有几个层面。第一个是 token 层面是不是供应过剩。我觉得 token 供应过剩不太会发生。真是 token 供应过剩，租金就会下来。现在你看到租金下来了吗？比如 on-demand 机器租金下来了吗？你可以去看一下租赁价格。我这边也有一张租金表。短期租赁的价格至少要和长约价格差不多，才叫租金过剩。

但现在不是这样，短期租金其实是紧缺的。第二，训练需求也要看租金，因为训练需求平时要和推理需求比。训练很多是在周末做，所以周末的租金有没有下降，也代表了大家对训练的需求够不够。现在周末租金没有下降。那些说不要这么快训练模型的人，基本上还在私下训练，这个趋势非常明显。

所以回到第一个问题，是不是因和果？你说供应过剩，整个半导体行业或者 token 都是供应过剩，所以导致下跌，根本不是这么回事。供应过剩造成下跌，是因为租金倒挂了，然后供应过剩，最后才跌，这才是因果。现在的原因跟半导体或者整个 AI 行业的基本面没有关系，而是流动性出了问题，利率出了问题，导致 CDS 变高，大家把 CoreWeave 的 CDS 炒起来。这是一段让你相信的故事，跟事实没有关系。当然很多人会相信，短期也可以相信，但我心里很清楚这是胡扯。这个故事能维持多久，取决于市场上有多少人相信、它能吹多久、能拿钱砸多久。

第二个问题是 post-training 需求。Microsoft 那边年初大概是 20 亿，现在大概 200 亿这个水平。你可以关注 Amazon 和 Microsoft 怎么讲 corporate AI 的需求。我听说挺多，知道应该挺强，可以看它们上一次业绩，上次业绩也讲到这个问题。

这个需求主要来自哪里？比如我本身是个 SaaS 服务商，Amazon 也是，它有很多场景。我公司要做一件具体的事情，再聪明的模型也做不了，因为它没有我公司原来的数据。所以我可以把它放到 Microsoft 或 Amazon 上面做训练，让模型了解我自己的数据，然后用这个小模型干活。

原来要训练模型，必须让 OpenAI 帮你训。Codex 一直有这个口子，可以提供后训数据让它帮你做后训，现在好像把这个关了。

Speaker 5 嗯。

Shanghao Jin 你用 OpenAI 模型，就等于是数据都要交给 OpenAI。现在如果用 Microsoft 训练，哪怕它部署 GPT，它也可以自己部署，比如部署在自己的数据中心上。你会觉得更安全一点，因为 Labs 不管市值多少，还是比较新的公司。你愿意把自己的 know-how 都交给 OpenAI 吗？其实你不太敢。但你比较敢交给 Microsoft，它服务你的 SaaS 多年，要偷你的数据早就偷了。所以你可能会觉得更安全一点。后训的需求很大，因为你不后训就做不了事。

基本上你只能拿个模型，让五年级学生照着大模型抄，或者拿个博士生去硬想一个问题。你让它写一篇文章，写成你自己的口气，试试看，这个都很难。你要把你口气的东西标注完给它看，后训完以后，它才会写得更像样。否则哪怕给它看一眼你以前的文章，它也会把通用口气和你的口气混在一起。

Speaker 5 关于这点，需求我大概理解，但我比较担心，他们做训练的时候会不会没办法调用最先进的模型帮忙做 data labeling？

Shanghao Jin 不会，当然不会。我最后回答你，当然不会。我自己做过一个写小说的模型，用的是千万级的模型，写出来的效果肯定比 LLM、比 OpenAI 好。因为我做了后训，把网络小说的这些偏好标注进去，让它重新训练了一次。你用了一个更小的模型，但经过后训，写出来的东西就是比 LLM、OpenAI 更能看。

所以我说 AI 真正干活，最后还是数据、算力、模型结合起来。如果没后训，等于没有数据。

Speaker 6 谢谢。

Shanghao Jin 谢谢。

Speaker 7 金老师，我有几个问题。第一个，现在整个 A 股的光模块跌得特别惨，包括中际旭创、东山精密。中际旭创明年的 forward PE 应该只有 11 到 12 倍。我们都知道光模块缺得非常厉害。现在市场传的几个鬼故事，比如 FCC 的 65% 规定。最近我有渠道可以买到东山精密，它不是要在港股 IPO 吗？我觉得东山精密是不是更像美股的 AAOI，弹性更强，但基本面上可能没有中际旭创那么安全？

Shanghao Jin 我其实对 A 股估值没那么明确，因为我得把 A 股估值映射到美股，但这个不太准。所以我讲的不代表什么。你看我跟你说我来赌一把，但我又不敢买，所以你要知道我不是那么专业。

第二，东山那类公司和中际旭创相比，我可能更了解中际旭创一点。我觉得封装上面确实没有办法超越它。但它的鬼故事不是美国方面。我觉得真要有鬼故事，可能是中国方面。刚才最后其实讲过了，我觉得这个才是比较严重的问题。

中国这边，我听说最近政策上可能会救一下跌得太多的股票，短期内可能会有动作。但 A 股长期政策我也不确定。中际旭创的产业地位肯定没有问题，但如果它不能在境外建厂，又不能绕过 FCC，可能会有一些阻力，业务上会受到影响。

Speaker 7 谢谢。

Shanghao Jin 好的，不好意思，我让 beefcube 再说一个，然后我就下线了，我准备睡觉。

Speaker 6 金老师，谢谢。我想问一下，之前有人怀疑 Intel EMIB 的方法和台积电不一样。它是放一个基板，然后在基板上放一个小硅片。大家说这个东西难度不低，容易变形，可能会影响良率。现在这个情况怎么样？

Shanghao Jin 良率很好，没有问题。它的问题是基板良率不好，基板良率可能不好，会影响产能。

Speaker 6 但基板良率提高起来应该也不是很难吧？

Shanghao Jin 那你得让供货商提高，这不是你自己直接提高的，得供货商给你提高。它现在确实在供货商那里花了不少精力改善这个问题。基板良率不高，导致基板供货不多，进而导致出货有问题、出货量受影响。不是说封装出来的良率有问题，而是说我可能不能赚那么多钱。Intel 这边，我听说现在供货应该 OK，我个人觉得 OK。

Speaker 6 也就是说，它的良率提升是有时间线的，不是还在摸索阶段？

Shanghao Jin 对。不过基板良率提高这件事，你看成本占比没有那么高。你花钱就是了。提高良率就像 HBM 一样，你是甲方，花钱就能提高。

Speaker 6 明白了，谢谢。

Shanghao Jin 好，谢谢大家，今天先到这里。我睡觉去了，拜拜。

Speaker 6 拜拜。

来源：X Space

item.title: Managing $525 Billion by Rethinking Wealth Management | Kurt MacAlpine, Corient
item.description: Corient, now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions, applies a professional-services partnership to wealth management, with roughly 3,000 employees on one compensation plan and one P&L. Its roughly 50-deal engine targets founders approaching a $3–5B scale ceiling; the September 2–3, 2025 announcement of acquisitions of Europe’s largest and second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses advances MacAlpine’s global ambition.
item.content:encoded:
David Senra · David Senra、Kurt MacAlpine · 2026-10-18 · 80 min · 原语言 EN

Corient, now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions, applies a professional-services partnership to wealth management, with roughly 3,000 employees on one compensation plan and one P&L. Its roughly 50-deal engine targets founders approaching a $3–5B scale ceiling; the September 2–3, 2025 announcement of acquisitions of Europe’s largest and second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses advances MacAlpine’s global ambition.

TL;DR

  • Kurt MacAlpine built Corient—now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions—by diagnosing wealth management as “built on a fundamentally flawed structure” and rebuilding it as a professional-services partnership. In many advisory businesses, independent-contractor advisers can take clients from colleagues, leaving the client experience tied to the originating adviser rather than the firm. Corient applied a partnership model, drawing on examples such as McKinsey and law firms; MacAlpine calls it “the first true professional services partnership” applied to wealth management.
  • The alignment mechanics are central to Corient’s model: about 3,000 employees on one compensation plan with no exceptions, one P&L with no chargebacks, and a fee-only fiduciary standard. MacAlpine claims Corient is “the largest business in the world that operates under that standard of care,” so any larger firm has the ability to operate at a lower standard. Corient also owns aircraft for clients’ collective use, takes the balance-sheet risk and the risk associated with the monthly management fee, and charges clients based on usage.
  • The M&A engine—about 50 deals—targets entrepreneurs hitting a scale ceiling, not retirees cashing out. MacAlpine’s thesis: a wealth firm can reach $3–5B with a limited service set, but the investments required to reach $50–100B can make the risk-reward trade-off “out of balance.” Joining Corient lets founders become partners and access its services from day one while continuing to grow their businesses. Corient’s median partner is in their mid-40s, versus an industry median adviser probably in their early 60s.
  • The public-market chapter is a conviction case study: CI Financial was the best- or second-best-performing North American financial-services stock in 2021 and the second worst in 2022. MacAlpine used cash flow and leverage to fund the pivot, carrying 3–3.5 turns of debt. The debt was fixed-rate and without covenants, with some debt extending out to 30 years. With about 75% of the float active, including hedge funds and value mutual funds facing redemptions, he bought back shares he called “criminally undervalued” at $12–13: “we were buying and buying and buying and buying.”
  • The take-private highlights a public/private-market disconnect: MacAlpine says private-equity investors would recognize the buyback-and-transformation approach as “the standard blueprint” for operating businesses and extracting value. Mubadala Capital approached him, saying the buyback path would take about nine years and involve execution trade-offs. The deal closed August 12, 2025, with no incremental debt and either deleveraging or an equity infusion tied to it, no cost synergies, and no change of strategic direction.
  • On September 2–3, 2025, Corient announced it was buying the largest and second-largest ultra-high-net-worth wealth-management businesses in Europe. MacAlpine says no truly global UHNW wealth manager exists outside Corient: in his view, multi-jurisdictional banks’ regional P&Ls and compensation structures can make cross-border collaboration an “impossible situation.”
  • The operating philosophy is built around a long horizon: full day-one integration of acquisitions, brand advertising in every market where Corient operates, and a Miami headquarters chosen from a clean slate. MacAlpine wants “the forever business in ultra-high-net-worth wealth management”; he contrasts that with temporary owners thinking in 18–36-month increments and optimizing for an exit. Senra closes with his friend Sam Hinkie’s line: “The person with the longest-term view in the room wins.”

Digest

1. A first-time CEO at 39 takes over a Canadian asset manager and makes a hard right turn

  • MacAlpine’s framing of the business today: partner and CEO of Corient, “the largest multi-family office in the world and the largest non-bank wealth manager serving ultra-high-net-worth clients,” managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions.
  • The starting point was CI Financial, a Toronto Stock Exchange-listed Canadian asset manager that had been public for about 25 years, earning “several hundred million a year of EBITDA” almost entirely from Canadian mutual funds. MacAlpine said the outlook for mutual funds was tapering relative to areas such as ETFs and alternatives. The board hired him at 39, before he had been a CEO, after he outlined the transformation in the interview: launch a U.S. ultra-high-net-worth wealth business, with the hope of later globalizing it.
  • His philosophy on inertia: “Often times people get comfort when things aren’t changing. That’s when you should be the most uncomfortable... I’m the most nervous when things aren’t changing.” Bill Holland, a previous CEO and chairman, and Ray Chang had built scale in Canadian asset management through acquisitions focused on mutual funds—an earlier disruption of a subscale industry.

2. The diagnosis: a barbell industry built on a flawed structure

  • Three reasons MacAlpine chose UHNW wealth management. First, the tailwinds: “There’s more wealth being created today than ever. That wealth is more concentrated than ever. There’s more complexity tied to that wealth than ever. It’s transitioning generations faster than ever. And it’s more global than ever.”
  • Second, the barbell: large banks that theoretically can do everything but whose governance, bureaucracy, and internal conflicts mean “they give back a lot of the scale benefits that clients should ultimately be benefiting from”—versus small local firms doing exceptional work but facing scale limits on manager access, purchasing power, and services. “In between... there’s a tremendous amount of white space.”
  • Third, the structural flaw: almost all advisory businesses, in his view, are built around advisers who are “independent contractors sharing somebody’s brand, somebody’s technology, and somebody’s office space.” They compete for clients and can take clients from one another within the firm. “Most wealth businesses are built to serve advisers. We wanted to build a wealth business that was built to serve clients.”
  • The three tensions he maps: adviser-to-adviser silos; advisers versus front-office experts (tax, planning, and family-office services can act as cost centers, so the adviser asks whether bringing in an expert will have “a negative impact on me personally”); and compensation that rewards advisers for generating revenue and then hoarding it—“the more that you share, the less that you ultimately earn.” He sees the client as a loser, and the firm itself as another: these businesses become “platforms” rather than companies.

3. The fix: a professional-services partnership, drawing on consulting

  • MacAlpine’s insight came from asking what wealth advisers do: they run “the ultimate human capital business,” requiring EQ and IQ. He points to partnerships in management consulting, law, accounting, and many successful investment and advisory businesses. Wealth managers, he said, had not adopted that structure. “We created the first true professional services partnership and applied it to the wealth management industry.”
  • On ambition and focus, his view is that “human nature guides people towards optionality... you can be fine at a bunch of those things, but it’s very very hard to be world class ultimately at something.” Senra interjects: “I find optionality disgusting, by the way.” Corient’s aspiration since launch has been to be the best in the world at serving UHNW clients globally.

4. What “comprehensive” looks like: embedded tax expertise, trust companies, and aircraft

  • The stack behind the adviser “relationship quarterbacks”: global financial planning (“everything associated with your lifetime”), wealth transfer (“everything that extends beyond your natural life”), 175 people on the investment team split about 70% traditional and 30% alternative investments, and several trust companies, including use of South Dakota in the U.S. Corient also has more than 100 full-time accountants who provide tax advice and implementation and are embedded on wealth-advisory teams, including in trust structuring and investment conversations about harvesting losses.
  • The family-office services include bill pay, outsourced CFO services, customized reporting, concierge lending, complex residential real-estate projects, art management, and aviation. Corient owns aircraft for clients’ collective use, takes the balance-sheet risk of buying the assets and the risk associated with the monthly management fee, and clients pay based on use. Senra frames this as a “Costco shared-economy” model; MacAlpine describes the aircraft arrangement but does not explicitly say it is not a profit center.
  • The logic of bundling: planning, wealth transfer, investments, tax, and trusts can be treated “as a collective problem as opposed to five or six individual decisions,” which MacAlpine says can lead to “meaningfully better outcomes.” But “you can’t do it if you have a structure in place that prevents you from being able to achieve that.”

5. “Conflict-free” defined: fiduciary standard plus less structural friction

  • MacAlpine claims Corient is “the only truly conflict-free business in wealth management,” on two axes. Standard of care: Corient is fee-only and fiduciary, “operating essentially at the highest standard of care.” He claims it is “the largest business in the world that operates under that standard of care. So anyone larger than us has the ability to operate at a lower standard of care.”
  • Business model: about 3,000 people, “one compensation plan” with “no exceptions,” because different compensation can make it “very very hard for us to objectively serve a client.” And one P&L with no chargebacks, since segmented P&Ls and chargebacks “inherently create underlying friction” that can keep experts away from clients.
  • When Senra tests the north star—serving clients better regardless of industry norms—MacAlpine agrees: “Correct. Exactly.” He argues for deep specialization by client type: “the more specialized you are, the more relevant you are, the better advice that you can ultimately give.”

6. Why founders join: the $3–5B inflection point and the Rockefeller parallel

  • The scale pitch to clients: access to capacity-constrained managers, negotiated rates passed through to clients (“whenever we negotiate better rates for our clients, we pass those rates on”), potentially better lending rates, and services that a $5–15B wealth manager would find “virtually impossible” to offer at scale.
  • The pitch to founders: “I don’t think of it as us buying people’s firms. People are coming to be partners at Corient.” His inflection-point thesis: firms can reach $3–5B with a limited set of services, but the investments required to reach $50–100B can make “the risk-reward trade-off” get out of balance. Joining Corient offers access to its existing services while founders continue their entrepreneurial journey. Senra offers Rockefeller’s Standard Oil as a historical parallel—building a “company of founders” by opening the books and exchanging stock—and MacAlpine agrees with the comparison.
  • The demographic consequence is deliberate: the industry’s median adviser is “probably in the early 60s”; Corient’s median partner is in their mid-40s, and its median employee is in their 30s. “We’re not doing M&A to fund retirements. We’re doing M&A to bring on partners who will continue to grow their businesses.”
  • The partnership is also a screening mechanism: “we tend to be someone’s first choice or their last choice... it’s rare that we would come in second.” That self-selection supports the “strategic, cultural, and financial alignment” he says a human-capital business requires.

7. The public market hated it: best stock in 2021, second worst in 2022

  • The volatility, in MacAlpine’s approximate terms: “In 2021, we were the best or second-best-performing financial services stock in North America. In 2022, we were the second worst.” His explanation starts with fairness to the market: “public companies don’t typically love transformation stories,” and CI was using a Canadian mutual-fund business’s cash flow to build a new U.S. UHNW business.
  • The structural amplifier: strategic investors and indexes locked up roughly 25% of the float, leaving about 75% active. He describes hedge funds piling in during 2021 and leaving in 2022, while value-oriented mutual funds faced net redemptions: “every single morning people wake up having to sell your shares to fund redemptions.”
  • On leverage, he carried 3 to 3.5 turns of debt against an asset-manager comparison group where about 2 turns is a rule of thumb. He argues composition mattered more than the amount: the debt was fixed-rate and without covenants, typically with long durations, and some extended out to 30 years. “At no point during the journey did I change my conviction,” though he says he expected the business success and diversification benefits to show up in the share price faster.
  • Senra’s parallels are Bezos, whom he recalls quoting Ben Graham during Amazon’s early stock decline, and his friend Adam, the founder of AppLovin. Senra says he thinks AppLovin’s value fell from about $28B to $3B; he recalls Adam borrowing “another $5 billion or something” to buy back stock while people around him thought it was crazy, and says Adam later described the outcome as worth $50–60B.

8. Buybacks at $12–13 and the public/private-market disconnect

  • Through his tenure, MacAlpine says CI was doing two things: building Corient and reducing the share count because he felt the shares were “criminally undervalued.” He saw forced selling as a buying opportunity: “that creates a tremendous buying opportunity... and we were buying and buying and buying and buying.” They bought many shares at $12 or $13, ultimately taking the company private.
  • The broader point: “If you describe that to a private equity investor, they would say that’s the standard blueprint under which we operate businesses and extract value.” He sees a disconnect between how people assess a business as owner-operators and how they assess its shares in public markets. Investors want diversification “without the time, investments, or capital required to do it,” he argues, but “that’s just not practical.”

9. Mubadala’s approach and a take-private with no synergies or strategic pivot

  • Mubadala Capital approached MacAlpine about two years before the conversation. Its message was that the buyback path would take about nine years and create trade-offs around executing the core strategy. “I agreed with 100% of that.”
  • Terms he emphasizes as evidence of alignment: announced in November 2024 and completed August 12, 2025, with no incremental debt and “deleveraging or an equity infusion” tied to it, no cost synergies, and no change of strategic direction. His verdict on the partner: “the best strategic partner on the planet” with equal ambition. He also says “a Canadian mutual fund company never really belonged in the public markets anyway.”
  • On September 2 or 3, 2025, Corient announced it was buying the largest and the second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses in Europe. MacAlpine says that would have been an impossible transaction to execute as a public company.

10. The global white space: multi-jurisdictional banks are not global wealth managers

  • MacAlpine’s claim is that “there are no global ultra-high-net-worth wealth managers in the world today” outside Corient, only multi-jurisdictional banks. His reasoning: offices in multiple jurisdictions can still operate as regional P&Ls. In his hypothetical, a billion-dollar family consolidates assets from four jurisdictions in Miami; three regional P&Ls lose assets while one gains. At the adviser level, he says, three people’s pay could go to zero for serving the client while one person’s pay could quadruple—an “impossible situation.”
  • Corient’s answer is the U.S. partnership model globalized: one compensation plan worldwide and one P&L, with clients served across jurisdictions rather than mapped to regional silos. Asked whether he is obsessed with incentives, MacAlpine reframes it: “I’m obsessed with alignment.” He says employees are paid for what they deliver, regardless of whether they joined through a direct hire in Seattle or an acquisition in San Diego.

11. Day-one integration, a crowdsourced name, and advertising for a forever business

  • Integration had three phases: accumulating scale during roughly the first 18 months, beginning the integration journey, and reaching today’s fully integrated state. MacAlpine thought people might prefer the first phase because it involved less change; instead, “people are most comfortable with the current state because they know exactly what they’re getting into.” Full integration means “on day one, you’re on our brand, you’re using our technology, you’re working in our offices... you’re on our comp, you’re on our benefits.” He adds that acquisitions should improve both sides: “I make you better and you make me better. If those aren’t true... it becomes a financial transaction.”
  • The naming story illustrates his integration philosophy. Rather than dictate a brand, he ran focus groups with about 75 participants, had the finalists mocked up under the same branding, and held a live vote at a partner town hall. “On day one, every person who wanted a voice in the process had one”; he says people embrace change better when they see their input reflected.
  • On marketing—prompted by Senra remembering Corient as the sole sponsor across four ad breaks of an interview he thinks was on CNBC’s “Wealth”—MacAlpine says the company advertises in every market where it operates to “short-circuit the discovery process.” He ties the spend to time horizon: “I think this should be the forever business in ultra-high-net-worth wealth management.” He contrasts that with temporary owners thinking in 18–36-month increments and “optimizing for a return and an exit,” rather than building a brand across generations. Senra closes with his friend Sam Hinkie’s line: “The person with the longest-term view in the room wins.”
  • Miami was a clean-slate headquarters choice. MacAlpine launched Corient around April 2020, chose the headquarters at the end of that year, and says he had no historical corporate tie directing him to a location. He cites Miami’s local engagement and welcoming environment, including Francis Suarez’s role as an ambassador for the city. His concern about local talent availability was answered at the time and, he says, has become less of a concern with subsequent migration. He says the choice has worked out beyond his expectations.
