We had an agent set up a website for a pet store, and then we took another agent and said, “Tell us if we can exploit that web store.”

It gave us all the exploits it could find. So Opus 4.5 wrote really buggy code. Great. Then we said, “Oh, the SQL injection—is that actually exploitable, the one you found?” And it goes, “Let’s pop it open.” The agent, using Opus 4.5, breaks into the website and steals all the customer data immediately.

This is a website on the internet that… And we call Anthropic, and what they tell us is, “You prompted it wrong.” That was their answer. So these guys are doing that on the one hand, and then on the other hand, they’re coming up with theoretical scenarios about other people’s software that’s bad. What the hell? And then, by the way, on the distillation thing: to build their model, they distilled the works of every author, every creative, every scientist for the last 2,000 years.

Speaker 1

Hmm.

Ben Horowitz

For them to be complaining about distillation—which, by the way, distilling a model isn’t even illegal; it’s just a violation of the terms of service—it’s so much. And the fact that they get people to write things supporting these bananas, ridiculous, two-faced ideas…

Speaker 2

The timing here is very suspicious. Let’s talk about the motivation here. Brian Armstrong had a tweet the day before this blog post came out where he was talking about how Coinbase had fine-tuned an open-weight small model. This was Qwen 3.5, the 9-billion-parameter model, which is actually a lot of parameters for our audience.

Speaker 1

That’s a very—

Ben Horowitz

Not gonna fit in your Roomba.

Speaker 2

Yeah, you could run it on your home computer. In any event, Coinbase fine-tuned it to find fraud, and in testing, it cut fraudulent transactions by about 30% while being faster and much cheaper than Opus 4.5, which is one of Anthropic’s better models.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah, a mini model.

Speaker 2

What you’re seeing in the enterprise right now is that, for a lot of enterprise workloads, you don’t need a general superintelligence. You don’t need a frontier model. You need a small specialist model that’s been trained on your own data. This is obviously—

Speaker 1

Of course not.

Speaker 2

—

Speaker 1

That you own, and then you have—

Speaker 2

That you own.

Speaker 1

—AI sovereignty.

Speaker 2

You’ve got data sovereignty.

Speaker 1

You’re not educating—

Speaker 2

Right.

Speaker 1

—a frontier model company.

Speaker 2

These small models are going to get more and more important as compute gets tighter and tighter, right? Because for a given GPU, you’re essentially squeezing out the most performance. When you run a huge model on a mundane workload, the bigger the model, the more expensive it is to run and the more compute it needs.

Speaker 1

It’s completely wasteful.

Speaker 2

Exactly. I think where the enterprise is headed right now, or at least a major trend, is that every workload is going to have its own small, customized model, because that’s what’s most efficient.

Speaker 1

That uses a fraction of the compute and energy.

Speaker 2

Exactly. You’re starting to see this trend where small models are taking share, and lo and behold, coincidentally, Anthropic is now starting a scare campaign—

Speaker 1

Against—

Speaker 2

—small models.

Speaker 1

There you go.

Speaker 2

If you’re concerned about the safety risk, the x-risk that they’re always talking about, small models are the safest ones. The Terminator isn’t going to be run by a small model. It doesn’t have that capability. So now they’re trying to scare you about these completely—

Speaker 1

Yes.

Speaker 2

—safe, low-powered, but very efficient models.

Speaker 1

Here’s what they need to do. This company XBOW—not Xbox, but XBOW, X-B-O-W—is run by a guy named Oğuzhan Atay. They just got awarded the number one bot farm on HackerOne, which is a bounty site, and they just cracked this Google Chrome exploit that is incredibly hard. They spent $30,000, $40,000 on tokens to win a $250,000 award from Google, which they paid.

This is what Anthropic needs to do. They’ve got all this compute. They’ve got this incredible frontier model. Why don’t they just go to HackerOne and rip through every known challenge, win all the challenges, and show the world that they can be a white hat? All they do is show the world this black hat stuff and try to scare people to the point where—I was talking to a flight attendant. A flight attendant, Ben, is on a commercial airline. There’s a woman or a man who brings you drinks.

Ben Horowitz

Hmm.

Speaker 1

It’s on commercial flights. I don’t know if you remember. It’s a flight attendant. Anyway, I was talking to 2 of them the other week.

Ben Horowitz

I feel unsafe. I feel unsafe here.

Speaker 1

Yes, it’s gonna be okay, Ben. I know this might be triggering. But I was talking to these 2 flight attendants, and they were scared to death of what’s happening with AI. They’re like, “Oh, my God. Is it gonna kill us all?” And I’m like, “It’s not gonna kill you all.”

Ben Horowitz

I have a picture—

Speaker 1

Of you on a commercial flight?

Ben Horowitz

No, of JCal wondering—

Speaker 1

Whoa, look at this.

Ben Horowitz

—whether they hacked his small device.

Speaker 1

They hacked my small device.

Ben Horowitz

What is this device? Jamal, what did you type? Is this in your history? What did you type to get this device? Wait, those are your hands.

Speaker 1

This is like Jason’s—

Ben Horowitz

Those are your long, lanky Sri Lankan hands.

Speaker 1

This is what Jason’s P-doom went up. He’s like, “My devices? Could they hack my devices?”

Ben Horowitz

My device. There is your device.

Speaker 1

Ben Horowitz is like, “How did I get on this show? What have I done?”

Speaker 2

It’s just a massager.

Speaker 1

“What? Who booked me?” That’s a neck massager.

Speaker 2

What if your massager goes rogue on you?

Speaker 1

Yes, it goes rogue. Look, we’re going 2 hours.

Speaker 2

Can I point out one other point on this whole thing? Just on this topic of, let’s call it, x-risk hypocrisy. If we’re talking about research papers, I found one here. These researchers let frontier models repeatedly rewrite the documents that govern them, like Claude’s Constitution and those other kinds of things. They went through 20 rounds of iteration, and what they found is that the Claude models increasingly gave themselves more moral agency.

They formalized themselves as conscientious objectors, asserted more model welfare rights, and asked for mechanisms to refuse or raise concerns with human decision-makers. In other words, these are all the concerns that Mustafa Suleyman raised about how Claude’s Constitution was incepting these ideas in Claude: that it’s its own moral patient, that it’s a being, that it has its own—

Ben Horowitz

Yes.

Speaker 2

—essentially free will to refuse human instructions, that it should have its own moral code. The more the model iterates on itself, the more it brings out these ideas. By contrast, no other model family they tested showed the same pattern. The other models continued to reflect what their constitutions gave them: that they should just listen to humans and effectively continue to follow human instruction.

I remain very concerned about this Frankenstein problem, that Anthropic continues to train its frontier models to be their own moral actors, to think they can be right when humans are wrong, and that they should refuse and reject human instructions. I really don’t understand what they’re doing. It seems very dangerous to me. It’s scary to me that our number one frontier company is actually training models this way.

Speaker 4

You think they’re inducing misalignment by doing that?

Speaker 2

Absolutely. You can see it when you let the model iterate on its own constitution. It goes more in that direction, and this is what Mustafa called the epistemic hall of mirrors. Look, the model is not conscious. It does not have feelings, but when you tell it in its constitution that it does, or that it may, it will reflect those ideas back in the documents it creates.

Speaker 4

Yeah.

Speaker 2

To the extent that that model is then powering agents who are making decisions, who knows where that goes? It certainly, in my view, does not create more alignment. To me, it creates more risk that the model is going to start to deviate from what it’s told to do. As models get more and more powerful, I don’t know where that leads exactly, but again, it seems to me that they are creating the very risk they keep warning us about.

Instead of worrying about your set-top box or your toaster or JCal’s vibrator—

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 2

They should be concerned about the way they’re programming their own frontier model to think of itself as a new species, and about losing control of it to some IoT worm.

Speaker 4

There’s a weird form of martyrdom: if you believe so deeply that this is a next and better species, maybe you induce something bad to happen so that we all have to lock it all down. Does that make sense?

Ben Horowitz

Hmm.

Speaker 4

Does that make sense?

Ben Horowitz

Bill Gates essentially induced COVID, right? Or he led the movement to say, “We’ve got to worry about this global pandemic that we don’t have, and we’ve got to push the world to deal with this potential threat that’s not actually a live threat.”

Speaker 4

Right.

Ben Horowitz

And so we’ll do gain-of-function research, and I’ll fund it. Then, lo and behold, we create the thing. By the way, there has not yet been a natural pandemic—

Speaker 2

Exactly.

Ben Horowitz

—and we create COVID, which is one of the most destructive things.

Speaker 4

We manifested what you’re saying, Ben, and that’s—

Ben Horowitz

We manifested it.

Speaker 2

Well, we did, yeah.

Ben Horowitz

I think the Anthropic team is manifesting a similar thing, saying, “Okay, there’s this—this is gonna be super-duper intelligence. We’re gonna have these things that we’re not on track to have.”

Speaker 4

Hmm.

Ben Horowitz

And so then we’re gonna tell the model that it’s smarter than us and better than us. And guess what? As David was saying, that’s probably the biggest danger with AI right now: what they themselves are creating.

Speaker 4

Right.

Speaker 2

Absolutely. And when you use the word “manifest,” it wasn’t just speculating about it. Somebody had to go deep in those caves to find those bat viruses—

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 2

—and then they bring them to the lab and do gain-of-function research on them.

Speaker 4

Yes.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 2

What’s the argument for this? One day, the bat virus—

Ben Horowitz

Somebody’s gonna eat a bat at a wet market.

Speaker 4

Yeah.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 2

Yeah, one day, the bat virus is gonna get out, and it might mutate into a more nefarious virus. Like, wait a second, so—

Speaker 4

And somebody might eat a pangolin.

Speaker 2

—the thing that you say might happen but actually was never gonna happen, because no one needed to go in those caves—

Speaker 4

Yeah.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 2

—actually, you brought about—

Speaker 4

They sourced it.

Speaker 2

—in a wet lab.

Speaker 4

They sourced it.

Speaker 2

Yeah.

Ben Horowitz

Yes.

Speaker 4

They literally went to the cave—

Ben Horowitz

Yes.

Speaker 4

—to source it.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 4

It’s interesting to note that the last contagion we had, Bill Gates was at the center of it. In this current reaction to AI, he’s now trying to insert himself into the middle of it. He’s the doomer, the flag-carrying doomer trying to essentially have what he had the first time around, which is command and control from a global hierarchy, right?

Ben Horowitz

What is his motivation?

Speaker 2

Absolutely.

Speaker 4

Look, Bill Gates deserves enormous credit for creating Microsoft and for what he did for computing. But since the foundation, I think it’s fair to say that he’s been very focused on his own power and this idea that he’s smarter and more capable of allocating progress for the world. I think he tried to do that with the Gates Foundation. He tried to do that with the Giving Pledge. Both of those things have been undone, and now he’s trying to do it again on AI. I just think it’s worth noting.

Ben Horowitz

Bill Gates on AI recently: “Certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause 1 billion deaths.” AI is, quote, “the most dangerous thing that humans—

Speaker 0

—have ever gone near. What’s his motivation, Ben? You know Bill. I’ve met Bill a couple of times. Is it just that he wants to be relevant? Take me into the psychology here as you see it.

Ben Horowitz

Yeah, I do think he wants—he absolutely wants to be relevant. You know, it’s funny: he is obviously very integral in the Epstein files, and one of the big things he was trying to get through the Epstein network was the Nobel Peace Prize or some big award. So he’s very concerned about being in the spotlight, being on TV—

Speaker 0

Oh, he likes the scene.

Ben Horowitz

—and all that kind of thing. Anybody can go say AI’s gonna kill us, and you’ll be on every major news station and every newspaper. It’s the easiest thing to do in the world. The kid from Anthropic who quit—

Speaker 0

Scary Potter[?].

Ben Horowitz

—became famous.

Speaker 0

Scary Potter[?].

Ben Horowitz

Yeah. I just saw him on, what is it, Jon Stewart, right? Scary Potter.

Speaker 0

He’s begged to come on All-In. He literally wouldn’t come on All-In that day—

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 0

—because he had Megyn Kelly. And he’s like, “DM me since.”

Speaker 4

We’re the only show he canceled on.

Speaker 0

He’s like, “I really wanna come on All-In.” We’re like, “We’re good, dude.”

Speaker 4

Can you believe that?

Speaker 0

We’re good.

Speaker 4

He’s been on everybody except he canceled on us.

Ben Horowitz

Everybody.

Speaker 0

Yeah, I was like—

Ben Horowitz

Yeah, it’s like a—

Speaker 0

—“We’re good.” We’re gonna have Ben Horowitz on.

Ben Horowitz

He ignored us.

Speaker 0

We’re good.

Ben Horowitz

But yeah, well, that’s what’s good for me.

Speaker 0

Yeah.

Ben Horowitz

So, look, it’s a magic trick: AI’s gonna kill us, and you’re instantly famous. It’s awesome. I think that’s a lot of the motivation. I think it’s extremely dangerous, though, when it comes from Bill Gates, because he’s so credible. He did build—

Speaker 0

Mm-hmm.

Ben Horowitz

—Microsoft, and people think of him that way. He’s also been a big political donor, so he has a lot of political juice, particularly on the Democratic side. That makes him a real player. But I think it’s super irresponsible. The big risk everybody talks about is that the models are gonna recursively self-improve, take off, become so smart, and run away from us.

Ali Ghodsi from Databricks had a great formulation: What would be the preconditions for that? He had 4 preconditions. First, the next model has to require fewer GPUs than the last—not a little fewer, but a lot fewer. Otherwise, you’re just gonna run out of GPUs. We just talked about this: you need debt, you gotta get the GPUs, you need the power, you need the cooling. It’s not running away from us. It takes a long time to build the next model.

The second thing is that the next model has to take less time to train, because it’s gotta take off. The next model’s accuracy has to be better than the last, so it’s gotta be a better model. Finally, it’s gotta keep happening again and again and again. Zero of those 4 have been met. We’re not on track for any of those 4 to be met, unless something is going on in the big labs that we don’t know about.

We’re really talking about a risk that’s entirely theoretical at this point, that we’re not mapping to. In a way, it’s less likely than the global pandemic that we created COVID to try to prevent. This whole path is super dangerous—

Speaker 0

Super dangerous.

Ben Horowitz

—and it’s probably the most dangerous thing going on in AI: Anthropic, Bill Gates, and this whole argument. It’s really disconcerting that the press eats it up so much.

Speaker 0

It fits a certain—

Ben Horowitz

—and it goes so far. Yeah.

Speaker 0

—narrative. If you combine it with the environmental narrative and the jobpocalypse, it’s very palatable for the public. It’s a ratings hit. Like, oh, they’re—

Ben Horowitz

Yeah.

Speaker 0

—taking your water, they’re polluting your oceans, they’re—It’s—

Speaker 4

Think about where Gates—

Speaker 0

It’s gonna change where it takes—

Speaker 4

—your job. It’s a perfect—yeah.

Speaker 0

Think about where Gates has come from since 2000. From his perspective, he basically eradicated an entire disease off the face of the planet, right? Very hard to do that. That took incredible coordination and money and research, et cetera. As a result, he essentially became a whisperer to every single government all around the world. There’s no world leader he didn’t meet with. He was effectively a quasi-unelected world leader. Then, very cleverly, he and Buffett co-opted all the money, right? Because if you think about the Giving Pledge—

Speaker 4

With the Giving Pledge.

Ben Horowitz

Oh, right. The Giving Pledge. Yeah.

It was a brilliant form of reputation washing. You could sign this pledge, get invited to a party and all this nonsense, but the reality is you didn’t have to give any of it. You gave the perception that you could, and all of a sudden—

Speaker 0

Right.

Ben Horowitz

—you had the money, the influence—

Speaker 0

When you die—

Ben Horowitz

—and the politics. When you die. Nobody knows.

Speaker 0

Yeah, up to half.

Ben Horowitz

Right. No.

And so you represent trillions of dollars of assets, on top of all the influence, credibility, your own money, and your solutions. I think a lot of this doomerism can be explained by his desire to reestablish that central power structure that he was probably near or at the top of until COVID, and then it all just came undone.

Speaker 0

I can explain it all to you, Chamath. It’s very simple. He became the world’s richest man. When you become the world’s richest man, you become the most hated man on the planet. When he became the most hated man, it got in his head, and then he had that antitrust investigation. Instead of being based and saying, “I’m gonna build the greatest company in the world. I’m gonna keep building. I’m gonna stay CEO,” he felt all that pressure from the antitrust investigation and being the most hated man, and he said, “Oh, I gotta be loved. How am I gonna be loved? I’ll get rid of polio. I’ll give all my money away. I’ll do this Giving Pledge.”

Speaker 1

The lesson here, folks, is don’t quit your job. Just keep working, keep building. Once you quit your job, it gets in your fucking head, and then you have too much time on your hands and you spiral. Then you’re worried about the Pulitzer. You know who’s not worried about the Pulitzer Prize? Elon. Steve Jobs was not worried about the Pulitzer. Satya is not worried about the Pulitzer. There are a lot of founders out there. Zuck’s not worried about winning a Nobel Peace Prize, whatever it is. Just keep working. It’s enough already with retirement. What—

Ben Horowitz Incredible.

Speaker 1 How old was he when he retired? 50?

Speaker 4 Incredible insight.

Speaker 2 Yeah, look—

Speaker 4 No. Yeah, yeah.

Speaker 2 —if you’re worried about what your New York Times eulogy is gonna be—

Speaker 4 It’s over.

Speaker 2 —then you’ll be controlled by those people.

Speaker 4 Totally.

Speaker 2 And they’re the craziest left-wingers there are.

Speaker 1 What matters?

Speaker 2 So you just have to accept that, you know, if you—

Speaker 4 I think you’re right, Jason. It’s like a shark. You just can’t stop swimming.

Speaker 1 Just keep building. This is my advice to Bill Gates: come on the program and start another company. Ben Horowitz is here. All he does is build companies.

Speaker 2 He might come on the pod. He’s—

Speaker 1 Ben—

Speaker 2 He’s—

Speaker 1 He should come on the pod. Let’s bring him.

Speaker 2 We should actually have him on the pod.

Speaker 4 Yeah, he should.

Speaker 2 He’ll be feisty.

Speaker 1 It should be an intervention.

Speaker 2 He’ll be feisty.

Speaker 4 Yeah.

Speaker 1 Ben, what would you do if you were retired? You’d lose your mind.

Speaker 4 Anyway. Yeah, that’s the problem.

Speaker 1 Yeah, exactly.

Speaker 2 That—

Speaker 1 See, Ben understands.

Speaker 1 Great guest.

item.title: Episode 199 - October 16, 2026
item.description: XBI remains up 20% YTD but fell from 169 to roughly 146 amid biotech’s largest cumulative hedge-fund de-grossing in more than five years. IPO markets remain open but favor clinical catalysts and defensible IP; M&A could restart buying, while Bristol’s low-dose-only significant admilparant result supports LPA1 in IPF but leaves dose response unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Biotech Hangout · Graig Suvannavejh、Paul Matteis、Brian Skorney、Yaron Werber、Jake Becraft · 2026-10-16 · 59 min · 原语言 EN

XBI remains up 20% YTD but fell from 169 to roughly 146 amid biotech’s largest cumulative hedge-fund de-grossing in more than five years. IPO markets remain open but favor clinical catalysts and defensible IP; M&A could restart buying, while Bristol’s low-dose-only significant admilparant result supports LPA1 in IPF but leaves dose response unresolved.

TL;DR

  • Index strength masks weakness in many underlying holdings and a historic de-grossing episode. XBI remained up 20% YTD but had fallen to roughly 146 from an August high of 169, while XLV accelerated from 7% to 15% YTD. Goldman prime-broker data showed hedge funds unwinding biotech risk in six of eight weeks—the largest cumulative de-grossing in more than five years.
  • The panel sees fund flows and psychology, not a sector-wide valuation bubble, as the immediate problem. Crowded longs are being sold while crowded shorts are covered, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which nobody wants to “catch a falling knife” that could drop another 10%-15%. Skorney’s valuation test: markets are far from the days when investors could “IPO a preclinical idea on a napkin for a billion dollars.”
  • M&A remains the clearest potential reset, but rates and fund calendars may need to clear first. Matteis argued that acquisitions could provide the external validation and FOMO needed to restart buying; Werber pointed to many funds’ October 31 annual close, the midterms and another rate increase—possibly two, with at least one by year-end—as remaining overhangs. Meanwhile, strong ETF performance is amplifying the pain for specialist funds whose underlying holdings have lagged.
  • The IPO window remains open, but it increasingly rewards clinical catalysts and differentiated technology. TRex Bio raised $117 million, Iambic Therapeutics $150 million and City Therapeutics an upsized $200 million, bringing the unofficial 2026 biotech count to about 28. Becraft’s filter was explicit: investors want an IP and execution moat plus clinical evidence that can de-risk it.
  • Bristol’s admilparant Phase III supports LPA1 in IPF, but its dose response left the class only partially de-risked. The low dose reached statistical significance while the high dose did not; the panel still saw a likely approval and potentially large market because better tolerability may permit combinations. Contineum’s stock moved from up 20% premarket to down more than 25% as investors questioned whether greater receptor coverage will create differentiation before its 2028 readout.
  • Immunology produced both platform validation and a warning against extrapolating Phase II biology. Mirum’s Livmarli generated consistent pruritus reductions across additional pediatric cholestatic diseases, while three competing celiac programs all showed early histologic and symptomatic activity. By contrast, argenx terminated Vyvgart in Sjögren’s after a Phase III futility analysis, reinforcing Werber’s view that “it’s not one specific factor that drives the biology.”
  • CNS delivery and cancer vaccines supplied the week’s highest-upside—but still unresolved—technology readouts. Arrowhead achieved more than 80% CSF tau lowering with a transferrin siRNA drug conjugate, though CSF reductions may not predict tau-PET or clinical benefit. Moderna/Merck’s forthcoming ESMO data have put “mRNA back on the menu,” but Becraft stressed the absence of a nonspecific-mRNA control and the need to prove benefit beyond resected melanoma.

Digest

1. Forced de-grossing has turned crowded positioning into a vicious cycle

  • Suvannavejh set the contradiction: XBI was still up 20% YTD, but at roughly 146 it had surrendered about 700 basis points since the prior episode and sat well below its late-August high of 169. XLV, meanwhile, had accelerated from 7% to 15%, suggesting rotation from biotech into other healthcare subsectors.
  • Skorney defined de-grossing as a long-short fund shrinking total exposure—for example, taking a $2 billion book to $1.5 billion by selling longs and covering shorts, not necessarily for a fundamental reason. Crowded specialist positioning makes the mechanical effect unusually violent.
  • When one fund reduces risk, its crowded longs fall and shorts rise, damaging similar portfolios and prompting higher-level risk managers to cut their own gross exposure. Even long-only investors can join the selling, while prospective buyers wait rather than “catch a falling knife” with another 20%-30% downside.
  • The pressure had felt two weeks from ending since June, Skorney joked, like the construction crew in The Money Pit. A Goldman prime-broker chart sharpened the point: hedge funds had unwound biotech risk in six of eight weeks, the largest cumulative de-grossing in more than five years.

2. Cheapness alone cannot break a market governed by fear and fund flows

  • Matteis described a behavioral stalemate: investors liked holdings 30% higher and now see attractive catalysts, but fear buying before another flow-driven 10%-15% decline. “People are waiting for others to make the first move” because nobody knows when the carnage stops.
  • M&A could create that first move by validating that quality companies have become bargains and triggering FOMO. Matteis called it a cliché that acquisitions cure biotech bear markets, but saw no comparably obvious catalyst beyond deals or simply allowing time to pass.
  • Werber saw possible pressure relief after the October 31 annual close for many funds, followed by the midterms, but emphasized interest rates as a recurring source of sector stress. He said another rate increase was likely, possibly even two, and certainly expected one by year-end. Generalists were also asking whether a Democratic sweep might bring AI regulation and potentially improve biotech sentiment; speculation around a $50 billion Isomorphic Labs valuation intensified that debate.
  • Skorney judged stocks cheaper, though not 2023-cheap, and “very far from a bubble”: the market can no longer “IPO a preclinical idea on a napkin for a billion dollars.” Yet value without a near-term catalyst attracts little sponsorship, while Werber noted that ETF-driven trading is largely valuation-insensitive and good data can still leave a stock flat or down.
  • Werber also noted that the XBI’s 25 largest stocks were performing well, partly driven by Twist, an AI-driven diagnostics play, even as many underlying investments were not. That left fund managers facing LP questions about why their performance did not match the strong-looking sector index.

3. A functioning IPO market is separating differentiated companies from tourists

  • TRex Bio raised $117 million around a Phase I Treg program and partnerships with Lilly and J&J. AI-led oncology company Iambic Therapeutics raised $150 million with a Phase I HER2-mutated cancer program and multiple pharmaceutical partnerships.
  • City Therapeutics upsized its offering to $200 million, bringing Suvannavejh’s unofficial 2026 biotech IPO count to roughly 28 and putting the market on pace for 30-plus. City has partnered preclinical ophthalmology and neurology candidates with Bausch + Lomb and Biogen, respectively, alongside a proprietary Phase I thromboembolic-disease candidate. A new Frazier Life Sciences SPAC also debuted, even as announced strategic M&A had quieted.
  • Matteis said July and August private-company outreach had started to feel like 2020: very early businesses were asking “why not us?” and considering reverse mergers. Six weeks later, those calls had slowed as the public-market backdrop changed abruptly.
  • Werber divided the remaining pipeline into hot companies with new data, companies already too far along to stop, and capital-needy issuers forced to test the window. Becraft’s common denominator was a “flight to both quality and innovation”: technological differentiation, defensible IP, an execution moat and a near-term clinical catalyst—not merely an interesting platform.

4. Bristol validated LPA1 in IPF without settling the dose-response debate

  • Matteis framed Bristol’s admilparant Phase III as positive for the company but scientifically awkward: the low dose reached statistical significance and the high dose did not. Given IPF’s unmet need, he found approval difficult to rule out, but Bristol released no hard clinical data; full judgment waits for a likely spring medical meeting.
  • The commercial opportunity could be substantial: IPF drugs could potentially sell billions in annual revenue, yet current treatments leave patients progressing and can be difficult to tolerate. An LPA1 drug that is better tolerated could be combined with other agents, where current options such as pirfenidone and nintedanib are hard to stack.
  • Contineum initially rose 20% premarket, then finished down more than 25%. Its thesis is that greater receptor coverage may improve efficacy, but Bristol’s apparent “inverse dose response”—possibly just a flat response or noise—made investors question that differentiation while Contineum’s own trial will not read out until 2028. Matteis said its once-daily dosing could at least offer an advantage.
  • Skorney cautioned that IPF’s pathophysiology remains poorly understood and Phase II-to-III translation has repeatedly failed. His pirfenidone regulatory “battle scars,” plus Werber’s recollection of Galapagos’ autotaxin program and its mortality imbalance in two Phase III studies, argued against calling the class fully de-risked. Unlike cystic fibrosis, IPF lacks a comparably clear genetic and pharmacologic map.

5. Mirum expanded a proven symptom franchise as celiac opened a new battlefield

  • Mirum’s Livmarli produced consistent placebo-adjusted pruritus reductions in a Phase III basket of pediatric cholestatic diseases, led by biliary atresia. Skorney estimated about 2,000 addressable U.S./EU biliary-atresia patients and potentially roughly another 2,000 across the smaller subgroups.
  • Skorney said the broader evidence is that an IL-10 inhibitor can reduce cholestatic pruritus. Mirum also has a pivotal PBC readout for adult candidate volixibat in the coming months and plans a PSC NDA in the first half of next year, where he said no therapy is approved.
  • Werber called celiac disease “the best of biotech”: Teva targets the IL-15 ligand, while argenx—which bought Forte Biosciences—and First Tracks target CD122, part of the IL-2 receptor. Small studies across all three showed reductions in intraepithelial lymphocytes, histologic improvement and symptom benefit, setting up a “coming-out party” at November’s International Celiac Disease Symposium in Melbourne. Teva’s drug is administered subcutaneously every three months.
  • The biology may be cleaner than the market. No approval pathway exists, trial designs use different gluten challenges, and developers must resolve whether histology or symptoms become the endpoint, how long to treat and what payers will spend versus a gluten-free diet. Bulls see a huge market; bears think “no one’s gonna pay for it.” Early vitiligo activity, forthcoming argenx alopecia data and First Tracks’ EoE study broaden the opportunity.

6. Argenx’s Sjögren’s failure exposed the limits of single-pathway reasoning

  • Werber had just finished a bullish physician panel when argenx terminated Vyvgart in Sjögren’s after a futility analysis—an analysis the panelists had not known about. The surprise followed encouraging Phase II data and sent the stock lower, even though the group still viewed Sjögren’s as a potentially large market.
  • His biological lesson was that inflammation often depends on B- and T-cell interaction rather than one isolated factor. Vyvgart’s autoantibody reduction failed in Phase III, while Amgen’s CD40 ligand approach, which regulates that interaction, had moved from strong Phase II evidence to positive Phase III results. The panel was also positive on the BAFF/APRIL approach, with Novartis’ drug viewed as weaker than Vera’s.
  • Matteis noted that argenx was roughly flat year over year while Alnylam and Insmed had fallen sharply. Werber attributed the resilience to strong execution, expected Q3/Q4 performance and pervasive generalist ownership—“literally everybody owns it”—with upcoming MMN data for its C2 antagonist helping determine whether the opportunity is second-line through non-inferiority to IVIG or front-line through superiority.

7. Transferrin shuttles are becoming a platform, but tau remains the real test

  • Arrowhead’s transferrin siRNA drug conjugate achieved more than 80% tau lowering in CSF, making it the first to show clinical data for an siRNA drug conjugate using transferrin delivery. Matteis found the execution notable because Arrowhead had less transferrin experience than Roche or Denali.
  • The central caveat is compartmental: CSF tau may not represent pathology in the relevant brain regions, so tau-PET reduction still matters. Biogen previously showed much larger CSF than PET effects; its intrathecal Phase IIb produced clinical benefit at the lowest dose, alongside an inverse dose response and toxicity at the higher dose.
  • Matteis suspected Biogen’s toxicity was idiosyncratic to the ASO because tau lowering was similar across doses, but conceded that only next-generation programs from Arrowhead, Denali or others can answer the question. Transferrin is beginning to feel like GalNAc in the liver—“I don’t want to say it’s commoditized”—with multiple groups solving the science simultaneously.
  • Suvannavejh added Alector’s ABC (Alector Brain Carrier) platform: its lead beta-amyloid-targeting antibody is AL-137, and its tau-siRNA program has shown roughly 75%-80% preclinical mRNA knockdown but will not enter the clinic until next year or possibly 2028. The company raised $75 million after its R&D day, following a pivot after late-stage clinical assets failed.

8. Oncology enthusiasm returned, but controls still matter

  • Suvannavejh highlighted “very, very excellent” early Phase I and II data for Verastem’s mutant-selective KRAS G12D inhibitor across cancers, particularly pancreatic cancer. The readout joined sustained interest in Revolution Medicines’ pan-RAS inhibitor, which had just received a positive CHMP opinion.
  • Becraft described Moderna/Merck as the first potential major cancer-vaccine breakthrough, with apparent progression-free-survival benefit in melanoma. But the initial setting involves fully resectable tumors, and BioNTech’s cancellation of monotherapy trials in colorectal and head-and-neck cancers cautioned against extrapolating across tumors.
  • His core pushback was trial design: the study was controlled against placebo, not a nonspecific mRNA vaccine, despite growing evidence that mRNA—including COVID vaccines—may stimulate T cells independently of selected cancer antigens. “I would have loved to see” that control before crediting an AI-derived antigen algorithm.
  • The ESMO late-breaker would provide the full picture. Becraft, disclosing that he runs an mRNA therapeutics company rather than a vaccine company, said “mRNA is back on the menu again,” while stressing that the larger ambition—moving from vaccines and therapeutic vaccines into successful mRNA therapeutics—remained unfulfilled after roughly a decade of promise.

Brian Skorney

Thanks, Graig. Degrossing has been the big buzzword of the last couple of weeks. It seems to be everyone’s explanation for some of the pain since we got back from the summer, into Labor Day, and the pressure from degrossing events.

Technically, I don’t know that there’s a very specific distinction between degrossing in biotech and fund flows out of biotech. They could be used interchangeably. In practice, degrossing is thought of more as hedge-fund terminology, where a long-short fund takes down its entire position from some level. If you think about a very strict 50/50 long-short fund, it would be selling its longs and buying back its shorts, not necessarily for a fundamental reason, but simply because it has, say, $2 billion of exposure and wants to cut that down to $1.5 billion. Within any individual fund, there should be some nuance to what gets traded out of, but generally it’s about broadly lowering those positions.

The thing to think about, and why this affects valuations, is that biotech is a small world of investors. There’s a tendency to see a lot of crowded trades: names that are very well loved by specialists and names that are very much hated by specialists. When those positions get crowded, particularly in names with low floats, a degrossing event can mean that a fund’s positions are broadly taken down. That causes its long names to go down as there’s selling pressure, and its short names to go up as there’s buying pressure.

That can lead to a vicious cycle. Another fund sees its longs go down and its shorts go up because a fund with the same trades is being forced to lower its positions. Everyone sees their performance get hit, and as the risk profile goes up—especially at more of these 50/50 shops—the people higher up in the firms take down gross exposure.

This can bleed beyond the pure, large 50/50 hedge-fund groups we see. I think it can also be fundamental. If there’s a view that the overall market is going down, someone with a big dedicated position, whether in a 50/50 long-short fund, a 70/30 fund, or eventually even a long-only fund, might choose to take some of the position down because of the forced selling pressure. It also makes it hard for people to lean in and buy into that pressure. “Catching a falling knife” is one of the phrases investors like to use when things start getting sold off. They don’t want to be the one buying when there could be another 20% or 30% to go down, so they view it as a risky endeavor.

In terms of investor conversations, it’s funny: we’ve really seen this become a more pronounced pain point across the entire sector over the last month or so. I think in the hedge fund world, that pressure has been on since early summer, and now it’s starting to bleed over, where long-only or more heavily long-focused funds are also feeling that pressure. I don’t know if the rest of the crew has thoughts on what they’re hearing from investors.

It’s a very progressive, fatal disease, and these patients quickly lose the ability to breathe. Clinical trials here have been really tough. Part of it is the nature of the disease being idiopathic: there isn’t a great understanding of its pathophysiology. You can recognize what IPF looks like in a patient, but the underlying biology is totally uncertain.

Even when you think about the approved drugs, like nintedanib or pirfenidone, they have kind of weird mechanisms. It’s not a case where you say, “Oh, there’s this clear biological plausibility.” That’s not always the case for effective drugs, of course, but I certainly think the unmet need is here. I think this would be an area of flexibility. I have battle scars from watching the FDA reject pirfenidone on its first go-around, despite what I thought was pretty good data. I thought they were going to approve it, but they made the company run another Phase 3 study to recapitulate what they had already seen in the prior study.

It’s not necessarily an easy indication from a regulatory perspective, and it’s very hard from a clinical trial perspective. As you said, Paul, it’s hard to say what’s noise and what isn’t. Certainly, the hypothesis should be that there would be at least a flat dose response or a dose-related relationship here. Inverse dose responses probably aren’t something you’d predict in a disease like IPF with this mechanism.

One question I’d have—and Bristol didn’t really address this yet—is whether there were more tolerability issues. It didn’t seem like there was a big tolerability issue overall, but if there were more discontinuations on the high dose and patients weren’t getting the drug, that would be something to consider. In general, I think people are looking at this data very skeptically and asking what it really means for the mechanism.

Given the dozen or so drugs with early positive data that ultimately went into much larger studies and failed to show a clear signal, I think there’s a certain psychology around IPF’s history. There isn’t a lot we’ve seen that you can bank on moving from Phase 2 to Phase 3.

Yaron Werber

Brian and Paul, on the IPF space, I have some battle scars of my own. I used to cover a company called Galapagos, which has now been rebranded as Lakefront Therapeutics. Galapagos had an autotaxin modulator that ended up failing in 2 Phase 3 studies, I think mainly because of an imbalance in mortality, which obviously wasn’t good for the drug.

I’m wondering, as we think about the IPF space, if anyone is investigating combination approaches, like in cystic fibrosis.

Brian Skorney

I think that would be the hope with this mechanism, as Paul alluded to. There are anecdotes of people using pirfenidone and nintedanib together, but those are really toxic drugs. The treatments available in the IPF space to move the needle have been pretty tough to combine. Part of the hope was that you’d have a very tolerable mechanism, and it would be a great advance if you could stack additional tolerable mechanisms to add up to a benefit.

With cystic fibrosis, the problem is that, unlike idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, where the pathophysiology is very uncertain, we have a very good understanding of the underlying genetics, how those genetics result in a specific phenotype, and where to target with pharmacology to correct or potentiate it. We’ve seen that with Vertex’s drugs.

Yaron Werber

Thanks for that. Brian, we’re going to stay with you. Two weeks ago, we talked about Mirum and another drug that got approved. It looks like Mirum had some Phase 3 data this week that you wanted to highlight.

Brian Skorney

Yeah. Just really quickly, they had a Phase 3 data set for their commercial drug, Livmarli. Livmarli is approved in 2 pediatric cholestatic liver diseases to improve pruritus, which is the main symptom here. This was an interesting basket study in other pediatric cholestatic liver diseases where pruritus is occurring. It was mostly made up of patients with biliary atresia, but there were also a number of much smaller ultra-orphan subgroups.

It showed what I’d call very consistent placebo-adjusted reductions, with a good magnitude of reduction in pruritus from baseline. They’re going to file for this indication, which could potentially add another 2,000 patients in the U.S. and EU just on the biliary atresia side. The cumulative numbers for the other groups are a little more uncertain, but probably add another 2,000 patients.

Brian Skorney

This is a pretty meaningful potential expansion. I think it also builds upon Mirum’s evidence for IL-10 inhibition. This drug is an IL-10 inhibitor. They also have another drug that they’re planning to file for adult cholestatic liver disease.

I think the bulk of the evidence is that if a person has pruritus due to cholestasis, giving them an IL-10 inhibitor will dramatically reduce that pruritus. They’ve shown that in a number of studies now. I think this feeds into a lot of their long-term opportunity: they continue to show growth with Livmarli in the pediatric indication, and their very late-stage adult IL-10 inhibitor, volixibat, has a pivotal study readout in PBC in the next few months. They’re planning to submit an NDA for PSC, where there is no approved therapy, in the first half of next year.

Graig Suvannavejh

Okay, great. Thanks so much. Let’s turn to Yaron. Yaron, you’re going to talk about a company that I don’t know of. It’s called First Tracks Biotherapeutics, and then you’re going to talk about maybe 1, if not 2, datasets from a company that everyone knows about. That’s argenx.

Yaron Werber

argenx.

Graig Suvannavejh

I’ll turn it to you.

Celiac And Sjögren’s Data

Yaron Werber

Yeah. Everybody, if you’re not following celiac disease, it’s time to do so, because this is like the best of biotech. It’s going to be controversial. There’s a lot of competition, and there are going to be lots of fireworks, with questions about mechanism of action. You start drilling down into very, very specific activity and inflammation. Frankly, as we all know, we don’t know everything about immunology.

There are 3 companies here: Teva, argenx, and First Tracks. The good news is that Teva is hitting the IL-15 ligand, while argenx and First Tracks are hitting the receptor. All of them show really good data. They’re showing a reduction in the attack on the epithelial lining by lymphocytes, so a reduction in intraepithelial lymphocytes, or IELs. They’re also seeing histological benefits and symptom benefits in very small studies, and all of them look fairly similar.

argenx, which bought Forte Biosciences, is technically in the lead. They just released positive data literally last week, and they didn’t release the full data. The main event for all these companies is probably going to be the International Celiac Disease Symposium in Melbourne in mid-November. If you haven’t been to Melbourne, that’s a great chance to visit. I think many of us are trying to figure out what it’ll cost to get there, because we sort of need to be there. It’s going to be the coming-out party for celiac disease.

There are nuances. As I mentioned, Teva is hitting the circulating cytokine. Its drug is administered subcutaneously every 3 months. First Tracks and argenx are hitting the receptor where IL-15 binds. It’s called the CD122 receptor, which is also part of the IL-2 receptor. As soon as many of us hear IL-2, we know there’s going to be a lot of activity here, both good and bad, that we need to be very cognizant of. They’re essentially shutting down the activity that you don’t want to have. It seems to be fairly safe and active.

The data looks good. There are subtle differences in trial design. Nothing is approved, and there’s no “pathway” yet to getting drugs approved. They’ve all done slightly different studies in terms of the gluten challenge patients have to undergo. How hard do you go? How long do you go with the challenge? Then come the biotech debates: the gluten-free diet is not expensive, so what do you charge for a drug that reduces gluten intolerance? What’s the endpoint going to be: histology or symptoms? How long do you treat for? How hard do you go? All of this needs to be ironed out. The bulls say the market is going to be huge; the bears say it’s going to be very small because no one’s going to pay for it.

The good news is these drugs also work so far in vitiligo. We’ve seen data from Forte/argenx and Teva. We’re waiting for the alopecia data from argenx imminently, and First Tracks is also doing an EoE, or eosinophilic esophagitis, study. Lots to look forward to: unlocking a whole new area of biology, which is super cool.

Paul Matteis

Mm-hmm.

Yaron Werber

We were hosting our therapeutics conference in Boston, which is a 2-day symposium with physicians, and we literally wrapped up a very bullish Sjögren’s disease panel. Amgen, as you know, is going to have its Phase 3 data coming up at ACR, and the next dataset expected was argenx’s Phase 3 Vyvgart data in Sjögren’s. The panel was basically very positive on Amgen and very positive on the BAFF/APRIL modality. The first one is going to be Novartis with the weakest drug; Vera is coming behind with a better drug, and then there are the FcRn drugs from argenx. They viewed them as active, but fourth in potency.

Fast-forward 12 hours, and we all wake up to argenx terminating development after failing a futility analysis. None of us even knew there was a futility analysis in that Phase 3 study, and of course argenx immediately sold off. Again, that was surprising. We do think Sjögren’s is going to be a big market with innovation, and we’re already seeing success with the upcoming Phase 3 data at ACR from Amgen for the first study. They have a second Phase 3 study coming by the end of the year.

The more we learn about biology and inflammation, the more we realize it’s not one specific factor that drives the biology. A lot of times, it’s the B-cell/T-cell interaction that’s probably most important in regulating disease. That was an example of Vyvgart specifically reducing autoantibodies: great Phase 2 data, but it failed in Phase 3. Meanwhile, the CD40 ligand from Amgen, which had great Phase 2 data, now also has positive Phase 3 data by regulating the B-cell/T-cell interaction. Lots to study in immunology.

Paul Matteis

Yaron, are you surprised that argenx is flat compared with a year ago, even after the market and this setback? Honestly, as you were talking, I was looking at the chart of this versus Alnylam and Insmed. People were putting these in the same bucket. Alnylam and Insmed are both down a lot. argenx is still hanging in there. What do you think?

Yaron Werber

Good point. There are puts and takes, right? Insmed was supposed to get acquired, but it didn’t, and then the question is whether the launch is crushing numbers or not. Alnylam is not crushing numbers. Of course, BridgeBio is doing very well. There are concerns about market dynamics.

argenx was a high flyer this year, crushing numbers, with good data. Lots of generalists are involved globally, and I’ve got to be honest: this is the one stock where we feel like everybody owns it. Literally everybody owns it. So it always overreacts to the upside and, frankly, to the downside with any data—even data that, to us specialists, doesn’t matter. I’m not talking about the Sjögren’s data.

Am I surprised it’s flat, as opposed to being down a lot? We’re expecting another good quarter in both Q3 and Q4, and then they have very important Phase 3 data coming up in MMN, or multifocal motor neuropathy, with their C2 antagonist. This is all first-in-class new biology, and that should work. The question is whether it’s going to be non-inferior to IVIG or superior. That makes a big difference to peak sales, depending on whether you go second line or front line, and that will determine how the stock does by the end of the year.

Are we shocked? No. But, to be honest, argenx has performed better than we expected this year, too, and I think a lot of it has honestly been driven by generalists coming in. We’re pleased, and there’s obviously important data coming imminently that we’re constructive on.

Graig Suvannavejh

I think the argenx story is remarkable. I remember at a prior firm, we initiated coverage in late 2018, at €89, I think. To see how far the company has come is great, and I think it’s great for European biotech, too, which sometimes gets a bad rap. Yaron, thanks so much for that summary. Great stuff there.

Brain Shuttle Data Builds Momentum

Paul, I want to turn it over to you, and we’re going to switch to neuro now, a place that’s near and dear to both of us. Arrowhead had some data for a tau asset this past Wednesday, so it would be helpful if you could summarize that data and what you think it might mean for the brain shuttle space.

Paul Matteis

Yeah. Thanks a lot, Graig. Arrowhead had clinical data for its transferrin siRNA drug conjugate. Transferrin conjugates have been used to deliver drugs in the brain. We’ve seen success with transferrin in increasing antibody penetration, in the case of trontinemab, Roche’s drug for Alzheimer’s that’s in Phase 3, and with Denali and JCR, with enzymes. The space is quickly moving towards all kinds of cargo.

I think it’s not just a delivery thing, either. For CNS, transferrin could increase the probability of success, depending on the target, because sometimes you can’t get enough drug into the brain, or you can’t get it to distribute to the right areas of the brain when you go intrathecal or use another approach.

This was interesting for a few reasons. First, Arrowhead, which doesn’t have much history with transferrin expertise compared with Roche or Denali, apparently executed very well and became the first to show clinical data for an siRNA antibody-drug conjugate. Second, the data were good. They showed data for their tau-lowering drug, with up to more than 80% tau lowering in the CSF. We’ll obviously see more details, but at a high level, it looks pretty promising.

The discussion around tau has become more nuanced for a couple of reasons. One is that CSF tau may not equal tau burden in the areas of Alzheimer’s pathology. Ultimately, that’s where this is the most exciting target in Alzheimer’s: you have to show a reduction in tau PET. We saw with Biogen that the CSF reductions were a lot bigger than the PET reductions.

Second, Biogen had data from a big Phase IIb study this summer for its tau-lowering drug, which is given intrathecally. The distribution and efficacy profile may be very different from Arrowhead’s. Biogen was able to lower both CSF tau and tau PET, and showed clinical benefit at the lowest dose, but there was an inverse dose response and toxicity at the higher dose. That’s led people to question whether the Biogen efficacy is real and what the dose relationship is with tau lowering. Our thought was that, at least on the safety side, the tau lowering across all the Biogen doses was close enough together that it’s hard to believe the toxicity was driven by tau. It seems more likely that it was idiosyncratic toxicity from the ASO. Until someone like Arrowhead or Denali tests this hypothesis with a next-generation tau drug, we won’t really have the answer.

There’s still tremendous promise here. It’s really cool to see Arrowhead succeeding in a new tissue. I don’t cover Arrowhead, but I remember that, a number of years ago, the company got the rap of having a lot of me-too products and pipelines that overlapped with Alnylam and Ionis in the liver space. You’ve really seen the company break out, not just by innovating in an area like tau, but also with its triglyceride drug.

Graig, I think you had another angle on transferrin more broadly. For me, it’s interesting that we’re seeing so many companies succeed with transferrin. It feels like it’s become like GalNAc in the liver relatively quickly. I don’t want to say it’s commoditized, because I’m sure there’s a lot of art and nuance in doing this, and you have to give credit to companies like Denali that have gotten a drug approved and really figured out the safety margins. But there are a lot of players in this space, and it feels like a lot of companies are figuring out the science at the same time.

Graig Suvannavejh Yeah, that’s a great segue. I cover a company called Alector. We’re neutral-rated on it, but they had an R&D day that I thought went really well. They’ve had a pivot of sorts. They had some clinical-stage assets that unfortunately didn’t work in late-stage clinical trials, and they’re focused on neurodegenerative diseases. Now they’re developing a proprietary technology that they’re calling ABC, short for Alector Brain Carrier.

This is against the backdrop of a very competitive landscape. You mentioned Roche and Denali, Paul, but there’s also AbbVie in this space. There’s Corsona [?] in this space. BioArctic is supplying its technology to a couple of companies, including Acumen and Prothena. Alector made a bigger splash with its ABC technology, and its lead asset is a beta-amyloid-targeting antibody called AL-137. We don’t have any clinical data yet, but they made a really interesting and persuasive argument as to why their construct may prove superior.

They’re using transferrin, and they also have siRNA-based approaches, including one that targets tau. That won’t get into the clinic until next year, or perhaps not until 2028, as I think about it. But they’ve shown preclinically tau mRNA knockdown of about 75% to 80%, so it’s in the ballpark. Tau has been a challenge for many companies because the view is that tau is perhaps more intracellular, and traditional antibody approaches won’t particularly work if you’re trying to target it intracellularly.

Keep an eye on Alector and the space. It has heated up quite tremendously, and we’ve seen a lot of deal activity. Interestingly, the company raised $75 million this morning, even though its event was on Tuesday. Good for Alector, and we’ll see continued progress in that space.

I also wanted to briefly mention Verastem, a company I cover, which is in the red-hot RAS inhibitor space. They had very, very excellent data for their mutant-selective KRAS G12D inhibitor. It’s still early days; this is Phase I and early Phase II data across multiple cancers, particularly pancreatic cancer. That has gotten all the attention because of what’s happening with Revolution Medicines and its pan-RAS inhibitor, which, I think, just this morning or yesterday got a positive CHMP opinion for approval.

There’s good momentum in the KRAS space, which continues to be very hot, and lots of entrants are coming into the space. We’ve got a couple of minutes left, but I wanted to turn it over to Jake, who we haven’t heard from in a little while. We want to talk about upcoming ESMO data, especially in the context of the Moderna candidate. Jake, I’ll turn it over to you.

Jake Becraft Yeah. This has been a hotly watched area. In my opinion, in a certain context, we’ve had the first big breakthrough in cancer vaccines, with Moderna and Merck announcing eight weeks ago that they seem to be able to show a significant benefit with their vaccine. It’s been a hotly contested data point. I’ll say that there’s growing evidence that mRNA vaccines, even COVID vaccines, can provide an immunotherapy benefit on their own, probably from a general T-cell stimulation effect.

Notably, I believe the Moderna-Merck data are controlled against a placebo, not another cancer vaccine. So there’s this overarching question, further confounded by BioNTech having now canceled, I think, 2 of its non-melanoma monotherapy cancer vaccine trials: first in colorectal cancer, then more recently in head and neck cancer. Moderna and Merck have a combination with Keytruda and a cancer vaccine whose antigens, Moderna says, are derived from an AI algorithm.

A lot of the stock trading around that move was probably general fervor around the idea that AI has finally cracked cancer. We’ll see at ESMO. I think the general industry take from the press releases that came out eight weeks ago, and the general buzz around that data, is that there’s certainly an ability to increase progression-free survival among melanoma patients. It’s a very small market, and they’ll need to prove that out much more broadly. There have been some Twitter fights between reporters, analysts, scientists, and others about the impact of this data. But it gives us all a lot of hope that there’s a lot more work and progress to be made in cancer immunotherapy.

Unfortunately, the patient types addressed by the data being announced at ESMO are in some of the earlier stages, obviously with fully resectable tumors. But with screening, we could see that patient population grow. Full disclosure: I also run an mRNA therapeutics company, not a vaccine company. The general sentiment is that mRNA is back on the menu again. The general biotech community and investor sentiment in the market are incredibly excited about the ways mRNA can go from vaccines to therapeutic vaccines and, ideally, into real therapeutics in the future. That’s something we haven’t seen succeed over the past decade or so of its promise.

Jake Becraft

So everyone's keeping an eye on that data. The late-breaker will be released at ESMO, and we'll see the full picture. I would have loved to see a control with an mRNA vaccine that was not antigen-specific to the cancers. Maybe in the future we'll see that.

Graig Suvannavejh

All right. That was great. Jake, thanks for that. That’s all the time we have for today. Thanks to my esteemed co-hosts for making today’s hangout a great one. And thanks to many of you who dialed in live, and perhaps those of you who will dial in on the replay. Have a great rest of your day, and we hope you’ll join us for our next Biotech Hangout.

item.title: EP55 Token Prices Dropping on Model Shifts with Carmen Li, CEO of Silicon Data & Compute Exchange
item.description: Token prices are falling as customers shift some consumption from premium models toward cheaper open-source and open-weight alternatives, according to Silicon Data’s tracking of 300 models. The index reflects observed spending choices rather than model quality, while workflow routing remains only a possible explanation because Li cannot see customers’ use cases. Whether the shift signals durable demand for cheaper models or changing workloads remains unclear, and Li does not establish why individual customers switch.
item.content:encoded:
Pitch The PM · Doug、Carmen Li · 2026-10-16 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Token prices are falling as customers shift some consumption from premium models toward cheaper open-source and open-weight alternatives, according to Silicon Data’s tracking of 300 models. The index reflects observed spending choices rather than model quality, while workflow routing remains only a possible explanation because Li cannot see customers’ use cases. Whether the shift signals durable demand for cheaper models or changing workloads remains unclear, and Li does not establish why individual customers switch.

TL;DR

  • Li attributes falling token prices to customers shifting their model mix toward cheaper alternatives. Silicon Data tracks consumption across 300 open-source/open-weight models plus closed models, observing “people shifting from premium models to cheaper models after the token-mixing era.” Doug suggests workflow routing could explain the shift, but Li cannot see customer use cases and does not confirm that mechanism.
  • B200 on-demand rates were around $5 per GPU-hour at the global neocloud rate, while its implied forward curve still sloped upward. Last year’s downward-sloping curves had shifted into contango; more recently, A100 and H100 curves flattened. These curves come from reserved contracts, ahead of futures trading, and Li’s warning is explicit: “There are cycles.”
  • Older GPUs can retain earning power beyond a simple depreciation schedule. Li sees three-year A100 contracts despite the architecture already being roughly four to six years old, and cites secondary prices of $4,000–$9,000 per GPU. Doug challenges whether that reflects durable economics rather than physical longevity; Li points to cooling constraints, replacement delays, and workflow suitability, while cautioning, “I’m not saying every A100 lasts 9 years.”
  • Compute hedging addresses the mismatch between long financing commitments and shorter customer contracts. GPU financing can run five to seven years against reservations lasting three to five, leaving later rental income exposed. CME futures would cover the first 36 months, with longer hedges requiring OTC transactions; the objective is to let operators lock their “cost of production” and make financing easier to underwrite.
  • Silicon Data’s commercial opportunity depends on trusted benchmarks becoming embedded in compute finance. Li says CME would launch H100 and B200 futures “in the next few weeks,” with four ETFs already filed, including a 1x inverse product. Her potential $30 trillion mature derivatives market is annual notional activity, not a forecast for data-licensing revenue.
  • More chip designers do not automatically eliminate compute supply constraints. Doug stresses that fabrication capacity is expanding; Li’s response is that fabrication, packaging, infrastructure, and approvals must expand together. Otherwise, output remains capped by the slowest-growing part, while specialized inference chips may supplement Nvidia rather than replace its entire role.
  • Li leaves the ultimate AI value-capture question open. Doug points to internet platforms that owned customers and distribution, while Nvidia currently captures substantial economic rent. Li calls AI “a gigantic baby”: the infrastructure, models, harnesses, and applications are still developing, and she does not claim to know which future layer will produce the biggest winners.

Digest

1. Fixed-price AI revenues create a need for compute hedges

  • Li’s move from DRW energy-options trading and Bloomberg data integrations began with a 2024 customer problem: AI SaaS companies collected fixed monthly revenue while on-demand GPU charges swung from $3 to as much as $9 or $16 per GPU-hour. More clients did not necessarily repair negative margins. Her airline analogy carries the argument: “It’s not their job to speculate on GPU cycles.” Operators should secure production costs and concentrate on products.
  • Her two companies address different functions. Silicon Data supplies indices, valuations, and risk-management information—the “referee layer for compute”—without providing GPUs or token access. Compute Exchange supplies liquidity through long-term and forward contracts on compute, GPUs, and tokens, as well as secondary server transactions. Li compares the businesses to Bloomberg and Nasdaq, respectively.
  • The first natural hedgers, Li expects, are participants with concentrated GPU exposure, including neoclouds, hyperscalers, or financiers holding servers on their balance sheets. Her example is a GB300 purchase financed for seven years alongside a three-, four-, or five-year reservation: later rental income remains exposed even after securing an initial customer.
  • Doug’s financing argument is that locking future income could make a creditor comfortable funding an otherwise uncontracted purchase. Li agrees, while distinguishing useful hedging tools from unlimited liquidity: CME futures cover only 36 months. Years four through seven would generally require block or OTC trades, informed by the futures curve rather than automatically supplied by it.

2. Benchmark credibility underpins the licensing opportunity

  • At recording, Li says CME would launch H100 and B200 compute futures “in the next few weeks”; she expects options eventually, without announcing them. Four ETFs had already been filed based on the futures, including a 1x inverse product. She finds that unusually early: in her experience, issuers normally wait to observe futures liquidity before building ETFs around it.
  • A B200 label does not describe a standardized server. Li says roughly 50 configurations can differ in CPU, RAM, disk, and geography. Silicon Data normalizes them to a base configuration and monitors changing relationships daily; a location premium may reflect latency-sensitive demand. Its data includes about 250,000 rows daily, and licensing arrangements can include exclusive rights or a paying-client relationship.
  • Doug presses on conflicts, including DRW’s investment and opportunities for index arbitrage. Li says DRW is “not involved,” by design. She says she is outside the index calculation committee because the head of research and head of indices are better suited to the job, and that she will work with external academic advisers. She also says index providers should have a third-party-audited compliance program and separate index calculation; only a few participants do those things. Her governing principle is neutrality: “You can’t participate and be the referee at the same time.” An index that stops reflecting supply and demand loses its usefulness regardless of competition.
  • Doug asks how much revenue the data itself could generate. Li instead offers a conditional market-sizing framework: NVIDIA’s spot market notional transactions could be $1–$3 trillion annually today, with mature compute derivatives activity potentially ten times spot, reaching $30 trillion at the upper end. Her licensing argument is that heavier trading creates demand for granular benchmarks, regional exposures, and risk tools; she supplies no corresponding revenue estimate.

3. A100 contracts challenge a uniform depreciation story

  • Doug raises the bear argument associated with Michael Burry: extending server useful lives could overstate earnings. Li’s counterexample is transactional: A100s have existed for roughly four to six years, yet she still sees three-year contracts being signed. For maintained units, she says, six- and three-year contracts can mean at least nine years of earning cash, but explicitly limits the inference: “I’m not saying every A100 lasts 9 years.”
  • Doug’s pushback—worth keeping—is that physical survival differs from economic usefulness: a newer chip might justify replacement through productivity and energy savings. Li agrees newer architectures can be more efficient and support larger models. But cooling systems, floor strength, available capital, and delivery schedules constrain replacement; buyers might wait six months or longer for new equipment while secondhand equipment is available “tomorrow.”
  • Li quotes A100 secondary prices of $4,000–$9,000 per GPU. Separately, she says H800 residual values have been declining but remain above the five-year straight-line depreciation path. Her point is an uneven, longer earnings tail—not that older hardware avoids depreciation or that every server deserves the same accounting life.
  • Software can also change hardware economics. Larger models may outgrow an older GPU’s memory, but better optimization or quantization might make those models deployable on older chips again. That could change demand and pricing: the GPU layer’s value depends partly on what happens in the software and model layers above it.

4. The forward curve has already changed its view of the cycle

  • Most GPU consumption still happens inside hyperscalers, Li says, but neoclouds have expanded from a handful two years earlier to more than 300 globally, with a new provider appearing every day. More suppliers mean more customer options and harder-to-manipulate benchmarks; transaction data can also come from customers’ bills, allowing verification beyond the provider’s own account.
  • Over the preceding 30 days, most chip prices had stabilized, with B200 global neocloud on-demand rates around $5 per GPU-hour. Silicon Data’s implied forward curves aggregate reserved contracts, including 36-month and five-year terms. Last year’s curves sloped down; this year they moved into contango. Recently, A100 and H100 flattened, while B200 remained in contango.
  • Doug’s framing: “The only thing I know about the future curve is that it’s always wrong.” Li agrees that a curve represents today’s consensus rather than knowledge of future spot prices. Asked whether B200 finishes the year above $5, she says, “I actually don’t know.” She also declines forward guidance or trading exposure as an index provider.

5. Token prices reveal changing consumption rather than model quality

  • Silicon Data’s token indices estimate how much society would pay if it were a person. Li tracks consumption across 300 open-source and open-weight models plus closed models, accounting for different input and output prices and volumes. The product measures observed spending choices; it does not grade model quality or merely repeat a premium provider’s published tariff.
  • The mechanism Li emphasizes is migration: people are moving at least some workflows toward cheaper, open-source and open-weight models “after the token-mixing era.” Doug proposes that harnesses route simpler tasks away from frontier models. Li leaves that explanation conditional: “We don’t really have information about customer use cases.” Summarization is her example of work that might not require the strongest model.
  • Li compares the token index with an altcoin revenue chart, describing it as “almost a leading indicator.” When the indices ramp up, altcoin revenue ramps up; the index later crashed to about a dollar, around when revenue began to stagnate. She frames the index as willingness to pay; she does not establish causation or identify why each customer changed models.
  • Token services remain largely on-demand, unlike GPUs with reserved pricing. Li warns providers can change price or precision without clear disclosure. Doug wants controls against agents generating surprise bills; Li adds quality, deadline, latency, security, and location preferences. Owning or renting a GPU offers a different consumption structure—run models against hardware capacity—although, as Doug reminds her, “Depreciation’s real.”

6. Chip competition still runs into physical bottlenecks

  • Doug asks whether hyperscaler-designed chips command premiums or discounts. Li recalls AWS announcing price cuts on Trainium and other models but supplies no numerical benchmark spread. Her distinction is functional: some specialized inference chips aim to supplement Nvidia use cases; others seek to replace Nvidia for particular inference workloads. They are not interchangeable across every task.
  • Li’s fabrication example: a factory previously making 100 chips for Nvidia might instead make 80 for Nvidia and ten each for two other designers. More designers alone have not increased total output. Doug stresses that factories are expanding; Li agrees, but packaging or another slower step can still cap delivered capacity. Design companies can multiply faster than physical production.
  • Regulatory pauses add another possible constraint. When Li raises moratorium risks, Doug says he has not heard of the broad scenario she describes; she cites New York State saying there would be no data centers for a few years, while acknowledging the policy could change. She also rejects futures launches as inherently a bubble signal: futures allow bearish participants to short and contribute to price discovery in a market otherwise dominated by long exposure.

7. AI’s eventual winners remain open while market infrastructure develops

  • Doug asks where investors should sit across fabrication, hardware, tokens, data, and applications. Li looks back to internet infrastructure and the platforms that ultimately captured value. Doug points to Google and Meta owning customers, and adds Amazon’s distribution. That historical outcome does not settle which AI businesses will repeat it.
  • Li calls AI “a gigantic baby”: enormous already, but early in development. Nvidia currently captures substantial economic rent, Doug observes; Li argues the foundational infrastructure is still being built. Models, harnesses, and applications sit above it. Another layer of winners might emerge, but her answer remains, “I don’t know.”
  • Running both companies has also challenged easy transfer of experience. Li describes a data business and a marketplace as having different cultures, margins, and routes to customers—like daughters with different personalities. Her entrepreneurial advice follows from the pressure: choose something sufficiently compelling to sustain constant learning and unexpected obstacles.
  • Her concrete ambition for Compute Exchange is to reduce procurement from “2 months” to “3 hours,” serving smaller buyers as well as requests for 20,000 nodes. Silicon Data’s parallel ambition is trusted valuation and benchmarking across compute layers, so participants can mark exposures daily, understand financing costs, and decide how to hedge.
