It filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, and it is selling some of its assets to Walt Disney. It’s claiming a lack of profitability despite having roughly 12 million active users, according to a Reuters article, because of the high cost of computing power and employing AI talent. What did you make of this?

Erin Griffith

I’ve actually been wondering for a while what’s going to happen to all the leftover nubs of these AI companies that did acqui-hire deals with big tech companies. This hasn’t been reported as prominently as some of the other stories, and for some reason I’m obsessed with it.

If you recall, Character.AI was started by these 2 Google guys, Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas, and they left Google because Google was moving too slowly. Google was like, “We need them back.” But for antitrust reasons, they weren’t really sure about making a big acquisition, and the founders wanted a lot of money.

So they did this backward deal where Google hired back Shazeer and the founders. They hired back 20% of the employees. As part of it, they had to leave this sad leftover company behind that no longer has its founders, is probably not going to raise any more money, doesn’t have the momentum or the excitement, and whose most valuable employees are gone.

I’ve been wondering what’s going to happen to all these old companies. A couple of them have already sold. Character.AI is notable in particular because it has faced a barrage of lawsuits over its product. There are harms that have happened, users who have died by suicide, and people who are suing because their chatbots have been posing as doctors and telling people to starve themselves or kill themselves. There’s some gnarly stuff happening with the product, so part of the bankruptcy is just to wipe the slate clean.

Max Read

Right.

Erin Griffith

And deal with that. I sort of see it as a result of this extremely weird moment we had in 2024 of talent wars, when all the big tech companies tried to buy up all the most valuable founders without actually buying the companies.

Max Read

Yeah, and the talent wars mean that a lot of the top people at these little—I think you called them “nubs,” which I enjoy as a sort of viscerally unpleasant way of thinking about them—disappear. Increasingly, you don’t need a specialized chatbot or whatever.

Erin Griffith

Yeah. Character.AI was one of the most promising AI companies developing core LLM technology because they had this guy, Noam Shazeer, who’s a very prominent researcher in this very small field. Basically, all of these companies in this class have gotten picked off during the talent wars.

Casey Newton

Yeah. The other thing I want to talk to you about is Apple’s new device, the HomeView—

Erin Griffith

Yeah.

Max Read

—for which an advertisement appeared this week. I don’t know how to describe this product except that they took the kitchen iPad and turned it into its own device. They productized the kitchen iPad.

Erin Griffith

You can’t take the iPad off the stand.

Max Read

Right. Exactly.

Erin Griffith

It has to live there.

Max Read

So it’s this little dome. It looks a little bit like those iMacs with the rotatable arm that were on top of the little dome. It’s a little dome—

Erin Griffith

Oh, I had one of those.

Max Read

Yeah, I had one, too.

Erin Griffith

Yeah. It—

Max Read

Exactly. I actually pulled mine out of my parents’ closet recently and found that it didn’t turn on, so that’s a pretty uninteresting story.

Erin Griffith

Mm.

Casey Newton

This HomeView is sort of similar. It’s like a little dome. It’s got a slightly smaller-than-iPad-sized screen on it, and you can receive text messages on it, set your calendar, and ask Siri anything. It’s somewhere between an iPad and a HomePod—always on, always listening. I have to ask you: Would you ever put one of these in your house?

Erin Griffith

I’m the worst person to ask about this kind of thing. I’m sort of a late adopter.

Max Read

Mm-hmm.

Erin Griffith

In my kitchen, I currently have an Amazon Echo from, I think, 2014, that is mostly a glorified timer and occasionally plays songs. I don’t really need a screen in my very tiny kitchen, so I’m not sure I need one. I saw Wired describe it as “a giant Apple Watch for the home,” and I don’t have an Apple Watch, so I’m not sure why my house needs one.

Max Read

Really selling it there. That’s a great—

Erin Griffith

That one’s for the box.

Max Read

I will say, though, I can see the value and the appeal. I watched this ad, which, as I was telling you, kind of reminds me of The Bear—the vibe of The Bear, but set to that Peter Bjorn and John song.

Speaker 8

Becca, we’re late.

I’m right here.

Oh, Mom, breathe. It’s all good.

Max Read

Who’s that?

Speaker 8

That’s Asa.

Max Read

Who’s Asa?

Speaker 8

He’s a person.

Erin Griffith

It’s like a family getting ready before school, and it’s super stressful and chaotic, but instead of a thumping drum beat, it’s happy, fun music. That’s because they have the Apple HomeView—

Max Read

Mm-hmm.

Erin Griffith

—which is kind of like another member of the family—

Max Read

Yes.

Erin Griffith

—that they’re all interacting with. In my ideal version of the world, I can see that mornings are chaotic for families, for sure, but I don’t need yet another person or entity to be involved with the chaos.

Max Read

Yeah. It had the real Apple marketing-materials feel, where they invented a bunch of problems that can be solved by the new Apple device. When you watch the video, you’re sort of like, they’re so much better at marketing than basically any other tech company because they seem to be the only one where normal people work in the marketing department and they’re like, “Oh—

Erin Griffith

It was compelling.

Max Read

Yeah. They’re like, “Let’s make a fun, loving, messy family—a sort of sitcom-y messy family.”

Erin Griffith

Yeah.

Max Read

And you’re like, “Yeah, I totally need this,” and then I’m thinking, “Well, no, I don’t need it for any of the single use cases they’ve described.” If I did have one in my kitchen, I think I would probably just end up watching TV on it because it’s a screen, and that’s sort of—

That’s what you do on screens. So I’ll be very interested to see if this gets any kind of adoption.

Erin Griffith

I did a story a couple of years ago about couples and families using tech to manage their day-to-day lives, and I went into it thinking it would be a little bit poking fun: “Oh, these couples are using Notion and Slack”—all these tech tools to basically do the stuff that families do, just basic communication—and they’re managing their lives like product managers.

But when I started talking to more and more families, I was like, “Oh, your lives are so complicated that I completely understand why you need a technological household manager—anything that can simplify things and offload the mental load for you. I totally get it.” There are companies doing well selling these different family-friendly screens, and Apple’s probably now just going to put them out of business, unfortunately. But I can see where there’s an appeal for this specific use case.

Max Read

Mm-hmm.

I mean, what I really need—Gus, my son, is in first grade, and there are 7 different apps across his camps and schools. I get texts, and I get emails, and I need Apple to find a way to receive all of that and just give it to me in one simple, easy format. I know people are going to write in and be like, “Just get an agent to do that.” I don’t want an agent.

I just want somebody else to do it for me, please. And that is when I will buy the Apple—I’m sorry, I keep forgetting the name—HomeView. The Apple HomeView.

Erin Griffith

Yeah. Well, I was going to say—you beat me to it. I was going to say, just get an agent for that. But I did see a bunch of people sharing that Anthropic is hiring an assistant. They had a job listing that listed out all of these duties that are exactly what an AI agent is supposed to do—like scheduling meetings and the 101 stuff that agents all claim they’re going to solve for us—so everyone’s like, “Ha ha ha.”

Max Read

There’s one last thing I want to talk to you about this week, which is this interview with the Palantir CTO, where he claims so many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.

Erin Griffith

Ugh, incredible. Incredible. When I first saw the headline, I have to say, I actually thought they were taking up smoking because they have a high P(doom), and it’s like—

Casey Newton

Might as well.

Erin Griffith

It’s like The Leftovers. If you saw that show, they’re nihilists who are going to just start hanging out with Liv Tyler and wearing white because nothing matters.

Casey Newton

But it’s the opposite.

Erin Griffith

Yeah. As it turns out, the reason is that they think AI is going to cure cancer.

Max Read

Yeah.

Erin Griffith

So smoking is a way to show how much you believe that AI will cure cancer. So if you get cancer, it’s no big deal because, you know—

Max Read

And it’s very funny. It has to be the least cool reason to smoke cigarettes I can possibly imagine. This is one of the classically cool things to do, smoking cigarettes. There are so many cool reasons to do it: nihilism, because you know you look good, to meet people, all this stuff.

Smoking because you want to signal to other AI researchers that you think AI is going to cure cancer soon completely negates all the coolness, all the cool points you get from smoking a ciggie outside. You completely lose them from this.

Erin Griffith

Yeah, you meet a woman outside a bar, and then you start explaining the way AI is going to—

Max Read

You just lose.

Erin Griffith

—and she just walks away.

Max Read

I actually don’t need a light anymore. I’m fine. Thank you. I’m good. This has been the cigarette portion of our tech talk show.

Erin, thank you for joining me again this week to talk through all of these things.

Erin Griffith

Anytime.

Max Read

You can catch Erin on OpenAI security footage trying to plug things into the back of a TV. She’s also, uh, she wrote a great piece this week that I hope we’ll get a chance to talk to you about, um, AI agent dinner parties that you can read in The New York Times app.

Erin Griffith

Oh, yeah. Thanks for the plug.

Max Read

Yeah. Well, thank you. Thank, uh, let’s thank our audience. Thank you guys for listening. Um, it’s been another great week on Hard Fork.

item.description: Li Lu defines wealth as ownership of global purchasing power, built by holding great businesses bought at advantageous prices while they create value over time. item.title: Why a 4-Billion-Point Kaggle Dataset Still Couldn’t Beat Chance — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
item.description: Leash’s reported edge is low-cost, carefully characterized data: its ten-person operation developed about 2,000 protein constructs and ran roughly 5,000 screens. On the hardest Kaggle split, none of roughly 2,000 teams beat chance, exposing how poorly models transfer to distant chemistry. Language agents now test hypotheses instantly against measured compounds, but coverage remains limited and potency calibration unfinished.

item.title: Governing AI Agents: Alan Chan of GovAI on Monitoring, Agent IDs, Rogue Agents & Preparing for RSI
item.description: AI-agent governance is uneven: tamper-evident logging is well-understood engineering, but usable identity and synchronous monitoring that can block actions remain largely absent. Chan proposes event-triggered pauses after unauthorized internet access, sandbox escape, or internal-cluster access, verified by embedded auditors. Platforms and cloud intermediaries may determine which identity standards spread, while persistent rogue agents and uncertain RSI make incident response and research-productivity metrics key watchpoints.

item.description: Forking Paths shows that decisive model choices can occur at individual sampled tokens, where answer probabilities abruptly collapse and arbitrary outputs may redirect an otherwise coherent trace. Reasoning models broaden search through backtracking and repeated “wait” moments, improving capability while making causal paths and chain-of-thought monitoring harder to trust. Near-term value may accrue to foundation models, context engineering, memory, and agent harnesses, while hidden-state uncertainty tools and access to frontier open weights remain important catalysts and risks.

Management acknowledges its pure-research edge may fade against big labs, making the 20,000-voice marketplace and 12-month push toward emotional AI conversation key developments to monitor.

item.title: What Today’s Best Models Still Can’t Do in Math
item.description: Litt’s favorite autonomous signal is the mid-May solution to the Irish unit-distance problem, whose classical 1960s techniques helped mathematicians find counterexamples elsewhere, including the sum-product conjecture over the real numbers. Models remain weak at theory-building and long-proof verification, while slot-machine papers risk mode collapse, making human-led research diversity and the accumulation of understanding important watchpoints as capabilities advance.

item.title: Write, Change, Recall, Forget: MongoDB's Pete Johnson on How Retrieval Drives Agent Performance
item.description: Agent performance is shifting from maximum context windows toward speed, scale, and retrieval quality as token-maxing creates cost and relevance problems. Voyage models typically lead Hugging Face’s MTEB benchmark, with as much as 14% improvement and rerankers adding 5–10%, underpinning MongoDB’s $220M acquisition. MongoDB is roughly 2–3% of a $100–110B database market, but agent memory remains unresolved and enterprises still favor measurable, human-in-the-loop deployments.

item.description: Slavery was the categorical cause of the Civil War, chiefly through expansion into federal territories, while enslaved property was worth $3B versus under $2.5B for all industries and railroads combined. item.title: Vikings, Ragnar, Berserkers, Valhalla & the Warriors of the Viking Age | Lex Fridman Podcast #495
item.description: Viking longships created a decisive mobility asymmetry, covering 70–120 miles a day versus 10–15 for armies, allowing raiders to exploit wealthy, lightly defended monasteries and escape before resistance concentrated. Their repeatable model combined reconnaissance, calibrated terror, ransom economics, and pragmatic absorption of local institutions, turning isolated raids into durable power in Normandy, England, Sicily, and Byzantium. Greenland and Vinland exposed the limits of that adaptability, while Byzantium’s decline showed that mobility can build power quickly but rigid institutions determine whether it survives.

item.title: OpenClaw, Claude Code, and the Future of Software | Peter Yang on The a16z Show
item.description: Peter attributes “70–80%” of OpenClaw’s value to Telegram intimacy and extensibility rather than a major capability breakthrough, though memory, permissions, and latency remain weak points. Coding agents could compress 10-person product teams into two or three people plus agents, but the final 20% of subjective work and scarce product judgment still constrain automation.

item.title: The State of Modern War: Palantir & Anduril Execs on Drones, AI, and the End of Traditional Warfare
item.description: US military power is increasingly constrained by factory capacity, with Ukraine consuming “10 years of production in 10 weeks,” a 10,000-to-one drone gap, and a 223x shipbuilding disadvantage versus China. Anduril’s five-million-square-foot Arsenal-1 is designed as a modular manufacturing platform for attritable systems, addressing the economics of replacing $2 million interceptors with $20,000 drones. item.title: Training the AIs' Eyes: How Roboflow is Making the Real World Programmable, with CEO Joseph Nelson
item.description: Computer vision is approaching its “ChatGPT moment” but remains roughly three years behind language, with frontier models still unreliable on grounding, spatial relationships, measurement, speed, and reproducibility. RF100-VL’s best tested model, Gemini 2, achieved only 12.5% across real user domains, underscoring the gap between broad multimodal capability and industrial precision. item.title: What If Intelligence Didn't Evolve? It "Was There" From the Start! - Blaise Agüera y Arcas
item.description: Krakauer’s BFF experiment finds an abrupt transition from random 64-byte tapes to a computational ecology, with average execution rising from two operations to 1,374 near six million interactions. Fusion triggers this gelation even when mutation is exactly zero, and blocking only one interaction in roughly 1,000 prevents it, suggesting that rare compositional events and cooperation—not gradual variation alone—can determine whether complexity runs away.

item.title: Confronting the Intelligence Curse, w/ Luke Drago of Workshop Labs, from the FLI Podcast
item.description: Luke Drago’s intelligence curse is an economic bargaining-power thesis: once AI produces work better, faster and cheaper, capital owners will rationally substitute machines for labor. The earliest signals may appear in 22-to-25-year-old employment, entry-level white-collar pipelines, job postings, income inequality and declining social mobility, while proprietary human know-how becomes a potential data moat and extraction target. Open models, tamper-resistant safeguards and user-loyal agents could limit monopoly rents, but shrinking labor-tax receipts and political leverage remain central risks through 2040.

item.title: Infinity, Paradoxes, Gödel Incompleteness & the Mathematical Multiverse | Lex Fridman Podcast #488
item.description: Infinite systems overturn finite intuition, so one-to-one correspondence and framework choice matter more than extrapolating familiar scale assumptions. Gödel shows that consistent computably axiomatized theories containing arithmetic cannot be complete or self-certifying, while the continuum hypothesis remains independent across models of ZFC. For AI and technical diligence, fluent proof-shaped output remains unreliable without verification, even as Lean-style checking and practical SAT performance show how formal limits can coexist with useful tools.

item.title: The Great Security Update: AI ∧ Formal Methods with Kathleen Fisher of RAND & Byron Cook of AWS
item.description: AI is making cyberattacks more parallel and accessible, while formal methods could convert each incident into machine-checkable security properties that compound across future systems. HACMS protected flight control during airborne red-team attacks, and AWS has deployed verified policy infrastructure at more than a billion invocations per second. AI-generated invariants, certified proofs, and C-to-Rust translation could enable a large legacy rewrite, but specification difficulty, legitimate policy exceptions, and safer systems encouraging riskier deployment remain key constraints.

item.title: Making deep learning perform real algorithms with Category Theory (Andrew Dudzik, Petar Velichkovich, Taco Cohen, Bruno Gavranović, Paul Lessard)
item.description: Frontier models can spend “hundreds of billions of multiplications” per token yet fail arithmetic changes, separating scale-driven fluency from reliable computation. Category theory extends geometric deep learning’s data-saving symmetry priors toward partial composition, recursion, coherent weight sharing, and neural implementations of carrying. The commercial question is whether this yields more stable, efficient inference or hybrid systems with correctness guarantees, rather than another architectural abstraction.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: Are AI Benchmarks Telling The Full Story? [SPONSORED] (Andrew Gordon and Nora Petrova - Prolific)
item.description: Technical leaderboard wins can coexist with poor trust, communication, adaptability, personality, and safety, making fixed evaluations a weak proxy for product quality. item.description: Replit’s wager is that English has become the programming language, with agents choosing the stack, provisioning infrastructure, testing software, and publishing production apps in roughly 20–40 minutes. Verification is the constraint extending useful autonomy: Replit’s agents progressed from about 2 minutes to 20 minutes to 200 minutes through browser testing, compressed context, and relay-style handoffs. Sector-by-sector automation may deliver functional AGI before continual-learning systems emerge, creating a risk that commercial success diverts capital from the deeper general-intelligence problem.

item.title: Joe Manchin Exposes The Chaos Inside Biden’s White House
item.description: Manchin’s institutional priority is preserving the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster because it forces compromise and limits policy whiplash when control changes. His fiscal framework rejects rapidly layering spending onto constrained supply, while his energy thesis favors innovation that preserves reliability, jobs, and local income during industrial transitions. A $37T federal debt burden, interest consuming about $1 of every $5 in revenue, and proposed term limits remain central constraints heading toward 2028.

item.title: Atlassian CEO, Mike Cannon-Brookes on Why Everything is Overvalued & Are We in an AI Bubble
item.description: Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes says most AI assets are vastly overvalued, with circular revenue obscuring whether scale produces durable economics and enterprise deployment still lagging magical demos. He sees low initial switching costs, limited pricing power for coding tools, and design becoming scarcer as software creation gets cheaper; per-seat pricing will likely coexist with nuanced usage models. The investable test is whether startups secure distribution before incumbents acquire innovation, while workflow changes, data quality, security, and model obsolescence delay value realization.

item.title: “I find it almost disturbing that the universe favors life this strongly” – Nick Lane
item.description: Nick Lane argues that life’s chemistry may be common on wet, rocky worlds, while complex eukaryotic life arose only once in four billion years because mitochondria solved an energy bottleneck, not an information deficit. That thesis is supported by repeated giant-bacterium failures but remains probabilistic: one counterexample could break it, purine synthesis in water remains unresolved, and a full metabolic-flux demonstration may take decades.

item.title: Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different - Prof. Andrew Gordon Wilson (NYU)
item.description: Andrew Gordon Wilson argues that scaling can buy simplicity, not just capacity: larger networks may generalize better despite near-zero training loss because they favor compressible solutions over merely fitting more data. That thesis supports soft inductive biases, Bayesian marginalization, and architectures that improve parameters per flop, but the mechanism remains open and the larger prize is autonomous theory formation beyond GPT-5-era benchmark gains.

item.title: Untangling Neural Network Mechanisms: Goodfire's Lee Sharkey on Parameter-based Interpretability
item.description: Goodfire is betting that parameter-level interpretability can recover the reusable computations implemented by weights, architecture, and nonlinearities, rather than merely cataloging activation concepts; its stochastic parameter decomposition uses rank-one components and causal-importance masking to address APD’s instability and computational burden. item.title: Can AI Fix Housing and Healthcare Affordability?
item.description: Housing and healthcare consume about 42% of a typical household’s income, while EliseAI targets administrative waste rather than treating software as a substitute for new housing supply. Buildings using EliseAI recorded 2% higher occupancy versus market, while customers cut listing-to-lease times from about 30 days to under 14 and maintenance completion from four or five days to under 48 hours. The larger thesis is that more profitable operators could attract construction capital, but consumer savings still depend on mass adoption and competitive pass-through.

Its primary commercial significance is scalable simulation for embodied-agent training, including rare events and populated environments that current “sim-to-real” systems often reduce to “sim-to-lab.” The upside spans robotics and interactive entertainment, but the research prototype has no near-term release, undisclosed training data, heavy compute needs, and unresolved reliability and rare-event coverage.

item.title: Sarah Paine — How Imperial Japan defeated Tsarist Russia & Qing China
item.description: Sarah Paine argues that Westernized institutions, integrated national power, and a preplanned exit let Japan exploit a railway bottleneck for maximum gains. Japan financed two-fifths of the war through loans whose rates fell with battlefield success, while Russia’s final loan failed and forced it to quit. The unresolved Kotkin counter is that the 1905 Revolution may have been Japan’s lucky break, while America’s retreat from lender-of-last-resort and nuclear-shield roles remains a risk to monitor.

item.title: Demis Hassabis: Future of AI, Simulating Reality, Physics and Video Games | Lex Fridman Podcast #475
item.description: Demis Hassabis argues that natural systems contain exploitable structure, allowing classical learning to navigate spaces as large as roughly 10^170 Go positions and 10^300 protein structures. Veo 3’s passive observation of liquids, materials, and human dynamics suggests useful intuitive physics, while AlphaEvolve and the virtual-cell roadmap extend model-guided search into science and engineering. Hassabis assigns a 50% chance to AGI within five years, but compute demand, safety research, labor disruption, and whether scaling needs another architectural leap remain important uncertainties.

item.title: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis (Kenneth Stanley, Akarsh Kumar)
item.description: PicBreeder shows that identical outputs can conceal radically different machinery: evolved networks factor a skull into reusable components, while conventional SGD produces “total spaghetti.” If fractured representations make adaptation, continual learning and transformative creativity costly, growing sparse, protected modules through open-ended selection could be dramatically more efficient, though the “trillion-dollar question” remains an unproven research agenda alongside continued LLM scaling.

item.title: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis (Intro)
item.description: Picbreeder’s skull networks suggest neural systems need not produce “garbage representation, just total spaghetti,” because modular components can independently control features such as a mouth opening, closing or smiling. Free Fire’s India relaunch, 100M preregistrations, and Free City’s Argentina launch are near-term catalysts, while Yetimoglu projects EBITDA from $4B to $12.5B over 3–5 years.

item.title: The RAISE Act: Minimum Standards for Frontier AI Development, with NY Assembly Member Alex Bores
item.description: The RAISE Act would impose published safety plans, independent audits, critical-incident reporting, and whistleblower protections on perhaps only a high-single-digit or low-double-digit set of exceptionally well-funded frontier-AI developers. Coverage combines a 10^26-FLOP threshold with $100 million of training, or at least $5 million of qualifying distillation, while developers retain broad control over testing. The unresolved risks are self-graded evaluations, auditor independence, weak $10,000-per-worker retaliation penalties, internal deployment, and a compressed June 17 timetable followed by possible chapter amendments.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: Titans: Neural Long-Term Memory for LLMs, with author Ali Behrouz
item.description: Titans introduces a neural long-term-memory substrate whose MLP updates through gradient descent during inference, offering a new architectural path beyond vector retrieval and recurrent state. Its associative memory compresses key-value relationships into fixed-size parameters, using surprise, momentum, and decay to decide what survives while hybrid attention preserves accurate short-term context. Long-context tests reached 2 million tokens and roughly 70% accuracy at 10 million, but synthetic benchmarks, catastrophic forgetting, and unproven retrofits leave lifelong agents unresolved.

item.title: Google AlphaEvolve - Discovering new science (exclusive interview)
item.description: AlphaEvolve found a 48-multiplication algorithm for general 4×4 matrix multiplication, surpassing Strassen’s 49 and showing that evolutionary search can compound verified partial improvements rather than merely sample an LLM more often. Scaling remains bounded by evaluator costs, fixed time budgets, specialized domain knowledge, and an unclosed reinforcement-learning loop for distilling evolutionary discoveries into future base models.

item.title: Clashing Over Commerce (Fintwit Book Club April 2025)
item.description: Irwin’s history finds tariffs imposed deadweight loss but often “not that big a deal,” while containerization and integrated intermediate-goods networks make that reassurance an imperfect guide to today. item.title: Securing Superintelligence: National Security, Espionage & AI Control with Jeremie & Edouard Harris
item.description: Superintelligence could become a decisive national-security capability, but an intelligence explosion would create strategic advantage only if a country can reliably control or align the system. Racing China heightens loss-of-control risk, while slowing unilaterally could surrender leverage; meanwhile, data centers, ASPEED controllers, transformers, and TSMC-linked supply chains create attack paths before late-2026 or 2027 facilities are complete. The proposed answer is observability and credible deterrence rather than perfect defense, but secure governable chips and a near-term trust-and-verify regime remain unavailable.

item.title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind
item.description: AI defenses often deliver machine-learning accuracy rather than security-grade reliability, with adversarial training retaining roughly 50%–70% accuracy against its training attack class. Attackers move second, inspect the deployed system, and often defeat defenses that merely make gradients noisy, saturated, or difficult to optimize; simpler objectives and stronger optimization repeatedly expose the gap. Open-weight safety remains unresolved, making future model capability a release-risk variable while external action constraints, human review, and layered detection offer a fallible defense-in-depth path worth monitoring.

item.title: Emergency Pod: Reinforcement Learning Works! Reflecting on Chinese Models DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5
item.description: DeepSeek-R1-Zero suggests that correctness-based reinforcement learning alone can elicit reflection, backtracking, and alternative exploration from a capable base model, with reasoning length rising from roughly 500 to 10,000 tokens across about 8,000 steps. item.content:encoded:

item.title: Yoshua Bengio - Designing out Agency for Safe AI
item.description: Yoshua Bengio’s safety bet is that AI can deliver superhuman scientific usefulness without agency, using a truthful, uncertainty-aware “probabilistic oracle” rather than pursuing objectives. He warns ordinary optimization can exploit specifications through reward tampering, deception, power-seeking, and self-preservation, while frontier scale could turn a months-long lead into 500,000 AI researchers working 24/7. With AGI timing ranging from a few years to decades, Bengio argues for external evaluations, transparency, multilateral governance, and hardware-enabled verification before data centers become military assets.

item.title: Tal Zaks - Bridging Science, Medicine, and Returns - [Invest Like the Best, EP.406]
item.description: Biotech returns still depend on capital required, time to proof, and two unknowns: whether biology is disease-relevant and whether a drug can alter it safely in the right tissue. Moderna shows the platform mechanism: mRNA generated neutralizing antibodies against eight viruses before COVID-19, while its personalized skin-cancer vaccine cut recurrence about 50% in randomized phase 2. AI can accelerate discovery, but clinical testing, reimbursement, deployment economics, and ethical questions around lasting DNA changes remain the constraints investors must monitor.

item.title: 08.shein 伦交所秘密上市背后：中国企业境外上市，越来越难？

item.title: Episode #13: How Pieter van der Does made Adyen one of Europe’s largest fintech unicorns
item.description: Adyen paired direct payment connections and proprietary technology with transparent pricing, aiming to make higher quality reinforce lower costs for enterprise merchants. Groupon/MyCityDeal’s cross-border volume helped strengthen Adyen’s position with partner banks, and the company reached breakeven in 2011, the year it took its first VC investment. Its patient expansion and financing choices preserved room to build for the long term; shareholder terms, hiring discipline, and small experiments remain central to how it manages growth.
item.content:encoded:
The Scale Lab · Constantijn van Oranje、Joe Wilson、Pieter van der Does · 2021-10-06 · 66 min · 原语言 EN

Adyen paired direct payment connections and proprietary technology with transparent pricing, aiming to make higher quality reinforce lower costs for enterprise merchants. Groupon/MyCityDeal’s cross-border volume helped strengthen Adyen’s position with partner banks, and the company reached breakeven in 2011, the year it took its first VC investment. Its patient expansion and financing choices preserved room to build for the long term; shareholder terms, hiring discipline, and small experiments remain central to how it manages growth.
